Loire: overall cool; Central Vineyards (Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé) are inland and continental; the coast is maritime. Northern limit for its grapes -> big vintage variation; high rainfall -> fungal disease. Best sites: southerly, mid-slope, facing the river (heat and reflected light). Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé: chalky, well-drained, stony soils; Pouilly-Fumé often said to be subtly smoky.

Sauternes AOC: sweet white from botrytis-concentrated grapes; Sémillon most important because particularly susceptible to botrytis. Sweet, medium to high alcohol, full body, high acidity; pronounced apricot plus oak (smoke, vanilla). Very good/outstanding; ages for many years to dried fruit, honey, caramel.

Bordeaux: moderate climate, high rainfall (Atlantic). Most widely planted variety. Left Bank (west/south of Gironde/Garonne: Médoc, Graves, Sauternes); Right Bank (north/east of Gironde and Dordogne: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol). Bordeaux AOC and Bordeaux Supérieur AOC typically Merlot-dominated. Most famous Merlot-dominated: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol; full body, pronounced black fruit, oak; age to dried fruit, tobacco.

Sauternes CAUSAL CHAIN: Garonne + Ciron rivers -> misty autumns -> noble rot on fully ripe grapes; level varies by year; passerillage concentrates sugar when rot is scarce. Selective hand-picking. Barsac may use its own name or Sauternes.

Sauternes: Sémillon chosen for its thin skin and affinity for noble rot; Sauvignon Blanc adds the acidity sweet wines need; Muscadelle a little grapey-floral. Best fermented and matured in new oak for up to three years.

1855 Classification: Médoc reds in five ranks; top rank Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Mouton Rothschild, plus Haut-Brion from Graves. Sauternes in three ranks, Château d'Yquem at the top. Listed châteaux = crus classés.

mentions.text: Sweetness: dry = none detectable; off-dry = tiny detectable amount; medium = distinct sugar but generally not sweet enough for most desserts; sweet = sugar is the prominent feature (e.g. Sauternes, Port).
Sweet wines (e.g. Sauternes): well chilled, 6-8°C (43-46°F)

Noble rot (Botrytis cinerea) - same fungus as grey rot. Needs fully ripe grapes first, then misty humid mornings and sunny dry afternoons. Adds its own honey, apricot, citrus zest flavours. Used for Sauternes, Tokaji, BA and TBA.

Dry; frost a concern; crus riper

facts.text: More likely to show oak than Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc; suffered from heavily oaked 1980s-90s styles; Chablis popular (unoaked, labelled by region) (p. 71).
Burgundy: cool Chablis in the north, moderate Côte d'Or, Mâconnais in the south.

Chablis AOC (village appellation): cool; dry, light to medium body, high acid, apple, lemon, wet stones. Premier/Grand Cru on south/south-west-facing hillsides: riper, more flavourful. Frost a key concern. With very few exceptions no detectable oak; inert vessels preserve delicacy.

Climate: cool continental around Chablis, moderate continental further south. Rain can disrupt flowering and harvest; Pinot Noir is particularly prone to grey rot; spring frosts (Chablis, as late as May) and summer hail are hazards.

Chablis: Chardonnay only; frost the main hazard (sprinklers, heaters). Village Chablis often on north-facing or flatter land; premier and grand cru on south-facing hillsides -> riper citrus, more body.

Hierarchy (2016 edition, may have changed): regional about half of output; commune about a third; 600+ premiers crus about a tenth (label says premier cru); grands crus just over 1% (33 in Côte d'Or, 1 in Chablis; vineyard name plus 'grand cru'). Reds at village level and above: Pinot Noir only.

mentions.text: Acidity: tingling, makes mouth water; more acid = more and longer watering. Sugar and acid mask each other (sweet wine acidity seems less obvious than e.g. Chablis), but mouth-watering is always the reliable guide. Alcohol burn can feel like acidity - check mouth-watering.
In the EU the grape variety does not necessarily appear on PDO labels (e.g. Chablis = Chardonnay). Outside the EU wines are commonly varietally labelled.

Continental: big seasonal swing, short summers, rapid autumn cool-down; spring frost risk (Chablis, Champagne); suits grapes that bud late (avoiding spring frost) and ripen early (before autumn cools). Continental summers are dry, so warm sites may need irrigation.

Aromatic (Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling): keep primary fruit - inert vessels (old foudres in Alsace), cool ferment, MLF blocked with SO2, bottle early. Non-aromatic (Chardonnay): may build character - some solids, new barriques, MLF (almost all premium white Burgundy, Chablis too), lees stirring. Cheap whites: clarified juice, cultured yeast, acid often added, sterile filtered.
GI = defined vineyard area, from a region (Bordeaux) to one vineyard (La Romanée). Trade deals protect GIs abroad (Australia dropped 'Chablis').

PDO: smaller, tight rules on varieties and methods; variety often not on label (Chablis, Meursault); traditional terms (AC) used. PGI: larger, looser, allows non-traditional varieties, variety usually shown; IGP replacing Vin de Pays. No GI: most flexible, multi-region or multi-country blends.

facts.text: Burgundy (Chapter 6, book p. 53), lowest to highest: Regional (Bourgogne AOC, the broadest: covers all of Burgundy) -> Village (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin AOC) -> Premier Cru (village name + Premier Cru; may name the vineyard) -> Grand Cru (own appellation; vineyard name + Grand Cru AOC; rarest, most age-worthy).
Village wines: better sited; more intensity, complexity, length. Côte de Nuits: Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges. Côte de Beaune: Beaune, Pommard.

Champagne: even in warm years sugar stays low and acid high -> ideal base. Chalk soils drain yet store water. Chardonnay (Côte des Blancs: light, high acid, floral, citrus); Pinot Noir (Montagne de Reims, Côte des Bar: body, backbone, red fruit); Meunier (Vallée de la Marne; buds late, avoids frost; fruity, for early drinking). Hand-picked; first pressing (cuvée) purest, later (taille).

Crus: Moulin-à-Vent, Morgon often most structured, can age; Fleurie, Brouilly lighter, perfumed. Many crus use normal crushed-fruit fermentation; some oak-aged, often in large vats.
Non-vintage: blend of several vintages (most Champagne). Vintage Champagne: exceptional years only (book p. 113).
Champagne and Cava do not have to mention PDO status on the label (book p. 115).
Champagne legal minimum on lees: 12 months (book p. 113).

facts.text: Champagne AOC: northern France; cool climate gives low-alcohol, high-acid base. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier. Most non-vintage (blends of vintages for consistency). Legal minimum 12 months on lees for the cheapest (apple, light autolytic). Very good: apple, lemon, toasted bread, biscuit. Vintage Champagne: exceptional years; long on lees plus bottle age; nuts and honey; small quantities, very high prices.
Champagne and Cava don't have to state PDO status on the label.

Champagne (2016 edition): NV min 15 months, 12 on lees; vintage 36 months. Prosecco: Glera, tank method; DOC vs Conegliano-Valdobbiadene DOCG.

mentions.text: Sparkling wines (e.g. Champagne): well chilled, 6-10°C (43-50°F)

Usually single-varietal (exception: sparkling such as Champagne). Often oak-matured but small new oak can overwhelm it; older and/or larger barrels often used. Best have subtle oak (smoke, cloves, vanilla).

Traditional method (e.g. Champagne, Cava): bottle sealed with crown cap -> second fermentation in bottle -> lees (must be removed or the wine is hazy) -> yeast autolysis (biscuit, bread; longer on lees = more intense) -> riddling (bottle moved slowly from horizontal to inverted; traditionally by hand, now mostly automated by gyropalette, a machine moving hundreds of bottles at once) -> disgorgement (neck frozen, ice plug of lees ejected) -> dosage (liqueur d'expédition: wine plus usually sugar; sets final sweetness) -> resealed with thick cork and wire cage.

Cava: Spanish term for traditional-method sparkling from certain regions; vast majority from Catalunya. Mainly local Spanish grapes; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also permitted (add fruit flavour and acidity). Warm climate -> grapes may be picked early to keep acid; base wine light apple and lemon. Shorter on lees than Champagne -> very subtle autolytic character. Big brands dominate; some smaller producers age long on lees.

South Africa, USA, Australia, NZ: best from coolest regions; often Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; slightly riper fruit than Champagne (extra sunlight and warmth); best are intense, complex, long finish. Cap Classique = South African traditional method (Champagne grapes or e.g. Chenin Blanc).

Continental: big seasonal swing, short summers, rapid autumn cool-down; spring frost risk (Chablis, Champagne); suits grapes that bud late (avoiding spring frost) and ripen early (before autumn cools). Continental summers are dry, so warm sites may need irrigation.

Rosé methods: direct pressing (often the palest), short maceration, blending red and white (L3: EU ban except rosé Champagne - 2016 edition, may have changed; L2 exam: 'not permitted in many parts of Europe').

Machine harvest: fast, works at night (cool fruit, less oxidation); unselective (MOG); flat or gentle slopes only; no whole bunches (Beaujolais, Champagne). Hand: selective, essential for noble rot; may be the only option on steep slopes.

facts.text: Rhône (Chapter 18, book p. 98): Côtes du Rhône AOC (covers the whole valley, but almost all from the south) -> Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC -> crus (North: Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Côte Rôtie, Condrieu; South: Châteauneuf-du-Pape).

Southern Rhône: valley flattens, warm southerly climate; blends with local grapes incl. Syrah. Côtes du Rhône (simple, medium body, red fruit, white pepper) -> Côtes du Rhône Villages -> Châteauneuf-du-Pape (full body, high alcohol; large round stones absorb heat by day and radiate it at night).
Mâconnais: fruity, mostly unoaked, simple (lemon, peach, melon) = Mâcon AOC. Pouilly-Fuissé: steep east and south-east slopes; concentrated stone and tropical fruit; often oak.
Pouilly-Fuissé, Saint-Véran: limestone suntrap slopes -> some of Burgundy's richest, ripest Chardonnay.

Rhône (Chapter 18, book p. 98): Côtes du Rhône AOC (covers the whole valley, but almost all from the south) -> Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC -> crus (North: Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Côte Rôtie, Condrieu; South: Châteauneuf-du-Pape).

Northern Rhône: only black grape permitted in AOC wines; narrow valley, steep slopes, moderate climate, aspect aids ripening; hand-worked, expensive. Côte Rôtie: far north, northern limit for ripening Syrah; exceptionally steep, stony slopes -> complex, peppery, long-lived; some (not all) co-ferment a little Viognier (floral). Hermitage: one steep south-facing hill. Crozes-Hermitage: larger, flatter, surrounds Hermitage; less intense, cheaper (higher yields, mechanisation).

Crus: Côte-Rôtie (most northerly; red only). Condrieu (100% Viognier). Hermitage (one steep south-facing hill; fullest reds). Crozes-Hermitage (largest; flat south = lighter, northern slopes = more concentrated). Cornas (warmest; 100% Syrah).

facts.text: Côte d'Or: moderate; more body, riper (peach, melon). Chardonnay focus is the Côte de Beaune: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. Oak fermentation/maturation and lees ageing add complexity and body. Premier and grand crus develop hazelnut, mushroom for decades; considered the pinnacle of Chardonnay.

Languedoc-Roussillon: Mediterranean coast of southern France, from the Spanish border to the Rhône; AOCs plus Pays d'Oc IGP; best may be barrel-fermented/matured (p. 69).
Languedoc-Roussillon: mostly too warm; best where cooled by altitude; tropical (passion fruit) and grass; Pays d'Oc IGP.

Languedoc-Roussillon: single-varietal Merlot at all quality levels, or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Syrah; Pays d'Oc IGP. California: styles from fruity, medium-bodied 'California' to concentrated, full-bodied Napa Valley and Sonoma; blends common but single-varietal Merlot important; pronounced oak (vanilla, coconut, smoke); best often in new barrels, high-volume producers use chips or staves. Chile Central Valley: warm, dry; high yields of fully ripe fruit every year; soft, medium-bodied, high-volume; altitude allows fresher styles. South Africa Stellenbosch: known for complex, age-worthy Bordeaux-variety reds; moderate to warm depending on altitude and sea breezes. Australia: blended with Cabernet, e.g. Margaret River. NZ: most Merlot comes from Hawke's Bay (North Island); moderate, plentiful rainfall; more widely grown there than Cabernet; single-varietal or blended with Cabernet; light to full-bodied.
Languedoc-Roussillon: warm, reliable; Pays d'Oc IGP.
Languedoc-Roussillon: ripens reliably; blends (e.g. Minervois AOC) or Pays d'Oc IGP.

Languedoc-Roussillon: Grenache important for south-of-France reds and rosés; Minervois AOC is one of the most important red AOCs (Grenache with Syrah etc.). Provence (east of Languedoc-Roussillon; Grenache often key in its rosé blends): dry, pale rosé, mostly Côtes de Provence AOC.
Languedoc: Pays d'Oc IGP; Limoux (altitude) premium oaked.
Pays d'Oc IGP: wider grape choice, varietal labels, big volumes of ripe fruity wine -> value.

facts.text: Black grape; wines almost exclusively from one region, Beaujolais (moderate climate, directly south of Burgundy).
High acidity, low to medium tannins, red fruit (raspberry, red cherry, red plum). Usually inert vessels; rarely shows oak.
Winemakers use techniques that maximise colour and minimise tannin; these can create banana and candy aromas.
Beaujolais wines: light to medium body, low to medium tannin, red fruit. Sometimes served lightly chilled. Most for immediate drinking; lose fresh fruit quickly.

CAUSAL CHAIN: Gamay can crop heavily -> best wines from GRANITE soils, low in nutrients -> lower yields -> more concentrated flavour. The north and west (Beaujolais Villages, crus) are granite hills; the south and east is an alluvial plain (Beaujolais AOC).
Gobelet: spur-pruned bush vines with shoots tied together vertically; more growers now use wires for mechanisation.

Basic Beaujolais and Beaujolais Nouveau: mostly carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration -> kirsch, banana, cinnamon. Nouveau released the third Thursday of November; only Beaujolais or Beaujolais Villages quality (never crus).
39 villages may use Beaujolais Villages; 10 crus have their own appellations.

mentions.text: Rhône (Chapter 18, book p. 98): One hierarchy across North and South Rhône, similar to Beaujolais (p. 98).
Light-bodied red (e.g. Beaujolais): room temperature or lightly chilled, 13-18°C (55-64°F)

Bush vines (untrellised, typically head-trained, spur-pruned) suit warm, dry, sunny regions like the Southern Rhône and Barossa; shade protects grapes. Beaujolais ties the shoots together ("gobelet").

Carbonic maceration: whole uncrushed bunches in a vat filled with CO2 -> fermentation inside each berry (intracellular). At about 2% alcohol skins split; grapes pressed; yeast finish off the skins. Extracts colour but little tannin; soft, fruity wines with kirsch, banana, bubble gum, cinnamon. Carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration is widely used on basic Beaujolais (and cheap Grenache) - likely behind L2's 'banana and candy'.

Northern Rhône: narrow, steep valley; moderate continental, similar to Beaujolais; noticeably cooler than the south. Best sites steep, south-facing, often in side valleys sheltered from the cold north wind, the mistral. Vines on individual stakes.

Machine harvest: fast, works at night (cool fruit, less oxidation); unselective (MOG); flat or gentle slopes only; no whole bunches (Beaujolais, Champagne). Hand: selective, essential for noble rot; may be the only option on steep slopes.

Many small geological faults mean soils change over short distances, often linked to subtle style differences (soil's exact role much debated).

Château: wine made from grapes grown on the producer's own land (not necessarily a grand building).
Grand Cru Classé / Cru Classé: wines from classifications ranking the best châteaux in some sub-regions.
Gironde Estuary = where the Garonne and Dordogne meet (p. 82).

Moderate maritime, warmed by the Gulf Stream: long season, ripening into October, spring frost rarely a problem. But Atlantic rain and humidity disrupt flowering and fruit set, promote rot, dilute flavour -> vintage variation. Landes forest and dunes shelter it from storms.
WHY blends: grapes flower and ripen at different times, so one frost or shower won't ruin everything.
Top reds: 225-litre barriques, sometimes 100% new. Second wines protect the grand vin.
EXAM NOTE: L2 needs only Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur, Cru Bourgeois, Grand Cru Classé.
Bordeaux Supérieur: slightly stricter rules, higher minimum alcohol; both mostly early-drinking medium-bodied reds.
Merlot: most planted; dominates cheap wines for softness.

mentions.text: Languedoc-Roussillon: single-varietal Merlot at all quality levels, or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Syrah; Pays d'Oc IGP. California: styles from fruity, medium-bodied 'California' to concentrated, full-bodied Napa Valley and Sonoma; blends common but single-varietal Merlot important; pronounced oak (vanilla, coconut, smoke); best often in new barrels, high-volume producers use chips or staves. Chile Central Valley: warm, dry; high yields of fully ripe fruit every year; soft, medium-bodied, high-volume; altitude allows fresher styles. South Africa Stellenbosch: known for complex, age-worthy Bordeaux-variety reds; moderate to warm depending on altitude and sea breezes. Australia: blended with Cabernet, e.g. Margaret River. NZ: most Merlot comes from Hawke's Bay (North Island); moderate, plentiful rainfall; more widely grown there than Cabernet; single-varietal or blended with Cabernet; light to full-bodied.

Carmenère: native to Bordeaux, now rare there; needs a long sunny season; struggles except in the warmest, sunniest Central Valley sites. Unripe: pungent green bell pepper, tomato leaf. Ripe: fresh blackberry. Deep colour, medium to high acid, high tannin, full body; oak softens tannins (coffee, chocolate). Ages to leather, earth. Widely grown in Chile. More commonly blended (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot) than single-varietal.

Maritime: low continentality, rain spread through the year; ripening continues late into autumn -> lets Bordeaux ripen thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon; but rain can harm flowering, fruit set and health.
Climate = average pattern over years; weather = this year's variation (Bordeaux varies a lot; Central Valley California barely).
GI = defined vineyard area, from a region (Bordeaux) to one vineyard (La Romanée). Trade deals protect GIs abroad (Australia dropped 'Chablis').

profiles.label: Bourgogne AOC
vals: Burgundy: cool north to moderate south
Drink young; can still be high priced

facts.text: Village wines: better sited; more intensity, complexity, length. Côte de Nuits: Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges. Côte de Beaune: Beaune, Pommard.
Provence: mostly pale, dry, light rosé (Côtes de Provence); Bandol reds from Mourvèdre.

Vouvray AOC (Loire): only Chenin permitted; dry, off-dry, medium, sweet and sparkling. Dry: fresh apple. Off-dry/medium labelled Demi-Sec. Sweeter: extra-ripe or botrytis grapes, stone/tropical fruit. Typically unoaked. Best age to honey, dried fruit.
Vouvray: cool, clay -> light-medium body, fruity, floral; rarely new oak; dry to sweet plus sparkling.

Syrah trellised (wind damage). Côtes du Rhône: over half of output. Villages: stricter alcohol and yields, more Grenache/Syrah/Mourvèdre; a named village needs 100% from it. Châteauneuf-du-Pape: largest cru, 13 varieties, first AC. Gigondas, Vacqueyras similar. Tavel: rosé only.

Moderate climate (Northern Rhône style, "Syrah"): medium body, fresh black cherry, blackberry, herbal notes, black pepper. Warm climate (Australian style, "Shiraz"): full body, high alcohol, cooked black fruit, liquorice. Outside France and Australia the name used hints at style.

Northern Rhône: only black grape permitted in AOC wines; narrow valley, steep slopes, moderate climate, aspect aids ripening; hand-worked, expensive. Côte Rôtie: far north, northern limit for ripening Syrah; exceptionally steep, stony slopes -> complex, peppery, long-lived; some (not all) co-ferment a little Viognier (floral). Hermitage: one steep south-facing hill. Crozes-Hermitage: larger, flatter, surrounds Hermitage; less intense, cheaper (higher yields, mechanisation).

Northern Rhône: narrow, steep valley; moderate continental, similar to Beaujolais; noticeably cooler than the south. Best sites steep, south-facing, often in side valleys sheltered from the cold north wind, the mistral. Vines on individual stakes.

mentions.text: Sauternes CAUSAL CHAIN: Garonne + Ciron rivers -> misty autumns -> noble rot on fully ripe grapes; level varies by year; passerillage concentrates sugar when rot is scarce. Selective hand-picking. Barsac may use its own name or Sauternes.

facts.text: Côte d'Or: moderate; more body, riper (peach, melon). Chardonnay focus is the Côte de Beaune: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. Oak fermentation/maturation and lees ageing add complexity and body. Premier and grand crus develop hazelnut, mushroom for decades; considered the pinnacle of Chardonnay.

Q-L2-06-01.stem: Which of these Burgundy village appellations is in the Côte de Beaune?

options.a: Pommard
options.b: Gevrey-Chambertin
options.c: Nuits-Saint-Georges
options.d: Chablis

notes.a: Correct: the book gives Beaune and Pommard as Côte de Beaune examples.
notes.b: Côte de Nuits (the northern half of the Côte d'Or).
notes.c: Côte de Nuits - the name is the clue.
notes.d: Chablis is a separate cool area in northern Burgundy, known for Chardonnay, not part of the Côte d'Or.

Q-L2-10-01.stem: A dry Chardonnay has high acidity, a light to medium body and flavours of green apple, lemon and wet stones. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Pays d'Oc
options.b: Chablis
options.c: Napa Valley
options.d: Margaret River

notes.a: Warm Languedoc-Roussillon gives ripe peach, pineapple and banana.
notes.b: Correct: the book describes Chablis as cool, giving dry, light- to medium-bodied wines with high acidity and apple, lemon, wet stones.
notes.c: Napa Chardonnay is described as full-bodied with pronounced tropical fruit and new-oak vanilla and spice.
notes.d: Warm (sea-breeze moderated); medium to full body with peach and pineapple.

Q-L2-15-01.stem: Why can Cabernet Sauvignon ripen successfully on Bordeaux's Left Bank despite the moderate maritime climate?

options.a: Gravel soils drain quickly and hold heat into the evening.
options.b: Morning fog from the Gironde estuary protects grapes from sunburn.
options.c: Clay soils hold enough water to carry vines through dry summers.
options.d: High altitude gives cool nights that help preserve acidity.

notes.a: Correct: the book gives both effects of gravel (drainage and heat retention).
notes.b: Not the book's explanation; the book credits the gravel soils.
notes.c: Not the book's explanation. (L3 p. 78: clay is the cooler Right Bank soil, where Merlot does better.)
notes.d: Altitude is not the explanation the book gives; it credits gravel soils.

Q-L2-14-01.stem: Which of these appellations would be LEAST likely to produce a Merlot-dominated red wine?

options.a: Saint-Émilion
options.b: Pomerol
options.c: Bordeaux AOC
options.d: Pauillac

notes.a: Right Bank: Merlot-dominated.
notes.b: Right Bank: among the most famous Merlot-dominated wines.
notes.c: The book says Bordeaux AOC and Bordeaux Supérieur are typically Merlot-dominated blends.
notes.d: Correct: a Left Bank (Haut-Médoc) appellation where Cabernet Sauvignon is typically dominant.

Q-L2-16-01.stem: Compared with a typical Northern Rhône Syrah, a typical Barossa Valley Shiraz is MOST likely to be:

options.a: lower in alcohol, with more herbal and floral notes from a cooler climate.
options.b: lighter-bodied, with fresh black fruit and more pronounced black pepper.
options.c: fuller-bodied, with cooked black fruit and often vanilla or coconut.
options.d: unoaked, lighter in tannin and intended to be drunk within a year.

notes.a: Warm Barossa gives riper grapes and higher alcohol.
notes.b: That is closer to the moderate-climate Northern Rhône style.
notes.c: Correct: the book describes Barossa Shiraz as full-bodied with high ripe tannins, cooked black fruit, black pepper and often vanilla/coconut oak.
notes.d: Barossa Shiraz commonly shows oak and the best can age.

Q-L2-15-02.stem: What does 'Bordeaux Supérieur' on a label indicate?

options.a: A Médoc château that is not classified as Grand Cru Classé.
options.b: A wine made only from grapes grown on the Right Bank.
options.c: Slightly stricter rules than Bordeaux AOC (yields, ageing, alcohol).
options.d: A château ranked in one of Bordeaux's official classifications.

notes.a: Closest to Cru Bourgeois: unclassified Médoc wines may APPLY to use that term.
notes.b: It can be made from grapes grown anywhere in Bordeaux.
notes.c: Correct: it can come from anywhere in Bordeaux, with slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol.
notes.d: That describes Grand Cru Classé / Cru Classé.

Q-L2-18-01.stem: Which pair of French GIs outside the Rhône Valley is listed for Grenache in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Minervois and Côtes de Provence
options.b: Minervois and Pays d'Oc
options.c: Fleurie and Minervois
options.d: Côtes de Provence and Châteauneuf-du-Pape

notes.a: Correct: Languedoc-Roussillon and Provence.
notes.b: Pays d'Oc blends can contain Grenache (L2 book p. 83), but Pays d'Oc is not one of the spec's Grenache GIs.
notes.c: Fleurie is a Beaujolais cru (Gamay).
notes.d: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is a Grenache GI, but it is IN the Southern Rhône, so the stem rules it out.

Q-L2-17-01.stem: Beaujolais winemakers often use techniques that maximise colour extraction while minimising tannin. Which aromas can these techniques create?

options.a: Leather and earth
options.b: Bread and biscuit
options.c: Vanilla and coconut
options.d: Banana and candy

notes.a: Tertiary aromas from ageing; most Beaujolais is drunk young.
notes.b: From lees/autolysis, not these red-winemaking techniques.
notes.c: These come from new oak; Gamay is usually made in inert vessels and rarely shows oak.
notes.d: Correct: stated in the book.

Q-L3-14-01.stem: Why does Merlot, rather than Cabernet Sauvignon, dominate in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol?

options.a: Their cooler clay soils suit Merlot; Cabernet struggles to ripen.
options.b: Their warm gravel soils cause Cabernet Sauvignon to over-ripen.
options.c: Appellation rules there forbid the planting of Cabernet Sauvignon.
options.d: Merlot ripens later, making full use of the long Atlantic autumn.

notes.a: Correct: per the L3 book.
notes.b: Gravel is the Left Bank soil, and it helps Cabernet ripen.
notes.c: No such ban; Cabernet Franc in particular is widely used in Saint-Émilion.
notes.d: Merlot is the variety that copes with the cooler soils; this reason is not given.

Q-L2-03-05.stem: What is the recommended service temperature for a light-bodied red such as Beaujolais?

options.a: Room temperature or lightly chilled, 13-18°C
options.b: Lightly chilled, like an oaked Chardonnay, 10-13°C
options.c: Well chilled, like a Sauternes, 6-8°C
options.d: Chilled, like a light white or rosé, 7-10°C

notes.a: Correct: as given in the L2 book's table.
notes.b: 10-13°C is for full-bodied whites such as oaked Chardonnay.
notes.c: 6-8°C, well chilled, is for sweet wines such as Sauternes.
notes.d: 7-10°C is for light- and medium-bodied whites and rosés.

Q-L2-03-07.stem: Which sequence lists these wines from the COLDEST to the WARMEST recommended service temperature?

options.a: Pinot Grigio, Sauternes, oaked Chardonnay, Shiraz
options.b: Pinot Grigio, oaked Chardonnay, Sauternes, Shiraz
options.c: Sauternes, Pinot Grigio, oaked Chardonnay, Shiraz
options.d: Sauternes, oaked Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Shiraz

notes.a: Sauternes (sweet, 6-8°C) is served colder than Pinot Grigio (7-10°C).
notes.b: Sauternes is the coldest of these (well chilled, 6-8°C).
notes.d: Oaked Chardonnay (lightly chilled, 10-13°C) is warmer than Pinot Grigio (7-10°C).

Q-L3-02-02.stem: Why do Muscadet and Champagne work well with oysters, according to the L3 book?

options.a: Oaked, full-bodied and high in alcohol
options.b: Unoaked, light in flavour and high in acidity
options.c: Off-dry, low in acidity and with light tannins
options.d: Sweet, aromatic and low in alcohol

notes.a: Oak bitterness clashes with umami, and big flavours would overwhelm oysters.
notes.b: Correct: no oak bitterness for umami to spoil, no overwhelming, fresh with lemon.
notes.c: Low acid would seem flat with lemon juice; the book stresses high acidity.
notes.d: Not the reasons given; the book cites unoaked, light flavour and high acidity.

Q-L2-04-32.stem: A Chardonnay from Languedoc-Roussillon is labelled 'Pays d'Oc IGP'. What does IGP tell you about it?

options.a: It is a PGI wine from a wide area with less strict rules.
options.b: It is a PDO wine from a small area with tightly defined rules.
options.c: It is a wine from a GI outside the European Union.
options.d: It is a late-harvest wine made from extra-ripe grapes.

notes.a: Correct: IGP is France's PGI term. PGIs give producers more flexibility over grapes and methods.
notes.b: That describes a PDO: AOC or AOP in France.
notes.c: France is in the EU; IGP is an EU PGI term.
notes.d: IGP is a GI category; the French late-harvest term is Vendanges tardives.

Q-L2-04-37.stem: A bottle of Chablis AOC does not mention Chardonnay on its label. Why is this?

options.a: EU PDO labels need not name the grape; Chablis must be Chardonnay.
options.b: Only wines from outside the EU are permitted to name their grape.
options.c: Chablis is a PGI wine, and PGI labels may not show grape varieties.
options.d: Chablis is always a blend, so no single grape variety can be named.

notes.a: Correct: the GI's rules fix the grape, so the name may be left off.
notes.b: EU wines can name grapes (e.g. Alsace); it is just more common outside the EU.
notes.c: Chablis is a PDO (AOC), and Pays d'Oc IGP wines are often varietal.
notes.d: Chablis wines must be made from Chardonnay.

Q-L3-04-07.stem: Which kind of grape variety does the L3 book say is better suited to a cool continental climate, such as Chablis or Champagne?

options.a: One that buds late and ripens late
options.b: One that buds early and ripens early
options.c: One that buds late and ripens early
options.d: One that buds early and ripens late

notes.a: Late budding helps, but late ripening risks the short summer and fast cool-down.
notes.b: Early ripening helps, but early budding exposes new shoots to spring frost.
notes.c: Correct: late budding avoids spring frost; early ripening beats the rapid autumn cool-down.
notes.d: The worst fit: frost risk in spring and too little time in autumn.

Q-L3-04-08.stem: How does a maritime climate help Bordeaux ripen thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon at its latitude?

options.a: It stays warm enough for ripening to go on far into autumn.
options.b: Its cold nights give the grapes more time to build sugar.
options.c: It has a big gap between summer and winter temperatures.
options.d: It gives hot, dry summers with almost no rain all year.

notes.a: Correct: low continentality and evenly spread rain moderate temperatures.
notes.b: Not the L3 explanation; it is the long, mild autumn that matters.
notes.c: That is high continentality (continental climate); maritime is low.
notes.d: Maritime rainfall is spread evenly through the year.

Q-L3-04-12.stem: Why are untrellised bush vines well suited to warm, dry, sunny regions such as the Southern Rhône and Barossa Valley?

options.a: Their dense shade improves airflow and cuts disease.
options.b: Their extra shade helps to protect the grapes.
options.c: They are easy to harvest by machine on flat land.
options.d: Their open canopy maximises sunlight on the grapes.

notes.a: Shade and poor airflow PROMOTE disease, a problem in cool or wet regions.
notes.b: Correct: in intense sun, shade guards the grapes against sunburn.
notes.c: Untrellised vines are not suitable for mechanical harvesting.
notes.d: Open trellised canopies (e.g. VSP) suit regions with LIMITED sunlight.

Q-L2-06-05.stem: Which of these puts the Burgundy appellation hierarchy in order from the bottom to the top?

options.a: Village, regional, premier cru, grand cru
options.b: Regional, village, grand cru, premier cru
options.c: Regional, village, premier cru, grand cru
options.d: Regional, premier cru, village, grand cru

notes.a: Regional appellations such as Bourgogne AOC are below the village appellations.
notes.b: Grand cru is the top of the hierarchy, above premier cru.
notes.c: Correct: Bourgogne AOC at the bottom, grand crus at the top.
notes.d: Premier cru vineyards lie WITHIN village appellations and rank above them.

Q-L2-06-06.stem: A label reads 'Gevrey-Chambertin Clos Saint-Jacques, Appellation Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Contrôlée'. What does this tell you about the wine?

options.a: It is from one premier cru vineyard in Gevrey-Chambertin.
options.b: It is a blend of premier crus from several Côte d'Or villages.
options.c: It is from a grand cru vineyard with its own appellation.
options.d: It is a regional wine that can come from all of Burgundy.

notes.a: Correct: Premier Cru goes with the village name; a single-vineyard wine may also name the vineyard.
notes.b: The label names one village and one vineyard, so it is not a multi-village blend.
notes.c: Grand cru labels show the vineyard name with 'Grand Cru', e.g. Le Chambertin Grand Cru.
notes.d: That describes Bourgogne AOC, the broadest regional appellation.

Q-L2-06-07.stem: Which statement about Burgundy's grand cru vineyards is NOT correct?

options.a: They make the rarest, most age-worthy Burgundies.
options.b: Their wines command exceptionally high prices.
options.c: Each has been awarded its own appellation.
options.d: They lie mostly on flat, fertile valley land.

notes.a: True: they give the most concentrated, complex wines with the greatest ageing potential.
notes.b: True: because of their quality and rarity.
notes.c: True: the vineyard name appears on the label with the term 'Grand Cru AOC'.
notes.d: Correct (the false statement): they are well-situated plots, commonly on south- or south-east-facing slopes.

Q-L2-06-08.stem: Compared with a typical red Bourgogne AOC, a red Pommard AOC is MOST LIKELY to show:

options.a: a lower price, as it is a broader area.
options.b: less ageing potential and less tannin.
options.c: more intensity, complexity and length.
options.d: lighter body and simpler, fresher fruit.

notes.a: Pommard is a single village, narrower than Bourgogne AOC, which covers all of Burgundy.
notes.b: Bourgogne AOC lacks the intensity to age; the best village wines can age in bottle.
notes.c: Correct: village vineyards are better sited and give more flavour intensity, complexity and length.
notes.d: That describes Bourgogne AOC: light to medium body, fresh red fruit, drink young.

Q-L2-06-09.stem: Which pair of Pinot Noir village appellations are BOTH in the Côte de Beaune?

options.a: Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges
options.b: Nuits-Saint-Georges and Beaune
options.c: Beaune and Pommard
options.d: Gevrey-Chambertin and Pommard

notes.a: Both are in the Côte de Nuits, the northern half of the Côte d'Or.
notes.b: Beaune is Côte de Beaune, but Nuits-Saint-Georges is in the Côte de Nuits.
notes.c: Correct: the book gives Beaune AOC and Pommard AOC as the Côte de Beaune examples.
notes.d: Pommard is Côte de Beaune, but Gevrey-Chambertin is in the Côte de Nuits.

Q-L2-06-10.stem: A red Burgundy is labelled 'Nuits-Saint-Georges AOC' with no other quality term. Which description fits it?

options.a: A grand cru wine from the Côte de Nuits
options.b: A regional wine from all over Burgundy
options.c: A village wine from the Côte de Beaune
options.d: A village wine from the Côte de Nuits

notes.a: Grand cru labels name the vineyard and state 'Grand Cru'; this names a village only.
notes.b: The broadest regional appellation is Bourgogne AOC.
notes.c: Wrong half: the Côte de Beaune examples are Beaune and Pommard.
notes.d: Correct: Nuits-Saint-Georges is a village appellation in the Côte de Nuits.

Q-L2-06-12.stem: Why are Burgundy's best Pinot Noir vineyards commonly on south- or south-east-facing slopes?

options.a: They are cooled by breezes from the Atlantic.
options.b: They receive less sunlight, slowing ripening.
options.c: They receive extra sunlight and warmth.
options.d: They have deeper and more fertile soils.

notes.a: Not the book's explanation; the benefit is extra sunlight and warmth.
notes.b: The reverse: these slopes get EXTRA sunlight, which a cool to moderate climate needs.
notes.c: Correct: this lets them produce concentrated, complex wines suitable for bottle ageing.
notes.d: The book links these sites to sunlight; fertile soils are not the reason given.

Q-L2-08-07.stem: The Pfalz is protected by mountains to the west and has a dry, sunny climate. What is the typical style of its Riesling?

options.a: Sweet and full-bodied
options.b: Off-dry and light-bodied
options.c: Medium-sweet and light-bodied
options.d: Dry and medium-bodied

notes.a: Not the typical style: the book gives Pfalz Riesling as dry and medium-bodied.
notes.b: Light body is the Mosel; a typical Pfalz Riesling is dry and medium-bodied.
notes.c: That is the typical Mosel style.
notes.d: Correct: climatically like an extension of Alsace, with similar wines.

Q-L2-08-08.stem: Why is Alsace one of the driest and sunniest wine regions in France?

options.a: Its vineyards sit at a high altitude, above the rain clouds.
options.b: The Vosges Mountains block rain-bearing westerly winds.
options.c: Warm Mediterranean winds blow in from the south.
options.d: The River Rhine reflects sunlight onto the slopes.

notes.a: The best vineyards are in the mountain foothills; altitude is not the reason given.
notes.b: Correct: dry autumns also extend ripening; best sites face east/south-east for morning sun.
notes.c: Not the book's explanation; the key is the Vosges rain shadow.
notes.d: Reflected river sunlight is described for the Mosel, not as the reason for Alsace.

Q-L3-06-01.stem: In Burgundy, why are premier and grand cru vineyards often mid-slope rather than on the flat land below?

options.a: Less frost risk and shallower, better-drained soils
options.b: More frequent rain that helps flowering go smoothly
options.c: Deeper, more fertile soils that give higher yields
options.d: Shelter from the prevailing easterly winds

notes.a: Correct: per the L3 book; they also tend to face south or east.
notes.b: Rain disrupts flowering in Burgundy; it is a hazard, not a benefit.
notes.c: The reverse: the deeper, more fertile soils are on the flat land.
notes.d: The best sites face south or east, protected from prevailing WESTERLY winds.

Q-L3-06-02.stem: According to the L3 book, how does the Côte de Nuits differ from the Côte de Beaune?

options.a: Nearly all the red grands crus are in the Côte de Nuits.
options.b: Its Pinot Noirs are generally lighter and fruitier.
options.c: Nearly all the white grands crus are in the Côte de Nuits.
options.d: It lies to the south of the Côte de Beaune.

notes.a: Correct: all red grands crus but one; it makes many of the fullest, longest-lived Pinots.
notes.b: The Côte de Beaune reds are described as generally fruitier.
notes.c: Reversed: all white grands crus but one are in the Côte de Beaune.
notes.d: The Côte de Nuits is the northern half of the Côte d'Or.

Q-L3-06-03.stem: According to the L3 book, which of these Côte de Beaune villages produces red wine only?

options.a: Meursault
options.b: Pommard
options.c: Beaune
options.d: Puligny-Montrachet

notes.a: Meursault makes red too, but is most famous for its white wines.
notes.b: Correct: with Volnay, the exception among the main Côte de Beaune villages.
notes.c: Beaune produces white wine as well as red.
notes.d: Makes white as well as red; it shares the white grand cru Montrachet.

Q-L3-08-03.stem: Why is organic and biodynamic viticulture widely practised in Alsace?

options.a: Sunny, dry conditions mean low disease pressure.
options.b: Humid, wet summers make chemical sprays useless.
options.c: Alsace Grand Cru rules require organic farming.
options.d: Fertile plain soils need few treatments or inputs.

notes.a: Correct: per the L3 book; the Vosges rain shadow gives sunny summers and dry autumns.
notes.b: Alsace is sheltered from rain-bearing winds; summers are sunny.
notes.c: Not a rule given in the L3 book; the reason is low disease pressure.
notes.d: The plain is for lesser vineyards; the reason given is the dry climate.

Q-L2-09-03.stem: On a bottle of still Vouvray AOC, what does the term 'Demi-Sec' indicate?

options.a: The wine is off-dry or medium in sweetness.
options.b: The wine is fully dry, with fresh apple fruit.
options.c: The wine is lusciously sweet, from botrytis.
options.d: The wine was partly matured in old oak.

notes.a: Correct: the book says off-dry or medium Vouvray is labelled Demi-Sec.
notes.b: Dry Vouvray often has fresh apple, but it is not labelled Demi-Sec.
notes.c: The sweeter styles come from extra-ripe or botrytis grapes; Demi-Sec means off-dry or medium.
notes.d: Demi-Sec is a sweetness term; Vouvray is typically unoaked anyway.

Q-L2-09-04.stem: Which statement about Vouvray AOC is correct?

options.a: Only dry and off-dry still wines may be produced.
options.b: Chenin Blanc is the only grape variety permitted.
options.c: Its sweet wines are typically matured in new oak.
options.d: Sémillon is often blended in to add body and ageing.

notes.a: Medium, sweet and sparkling Vouvray are all made too.
notes.b: Correct: per the book. Even so, styles range from dry to sweet, plus sparkling.
notes.c: Vouvray of every style is typically unoaked, to retain its fresh fruit.
notes.d: That is Sémillon's role in Bordeaux blends; only Chenin Blanc is permitted in Vouvray.

Q-L2-09-06.stem: In Bordeaux, Sémillon is commonly blended with Sauvignon Blanc for dry and sweet wines. What does Sémillon provide to these blends?

options.a: Extra acidity and freshness.
options.b: Herbaceous aromatic intensity.
options.c: Pronounced floral perfume.
options.d: Body and ageing potential.

notes.a: Not what the book gives. (L3: in Sauternes it is Sauvignon Blanc that adds acidity.)
notes.b: Herbaceous aromas are Sauvignon Blanc's hallmark (p. 72); the book credits Sémillon with body and ageing potential.
notes.c: Not given; Sémillon is described with apple, lemon and grass when young.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; very good or outstanding blends are often oak-matured and age for years.

Q-L2-09-08.stem: Why is Sémillon the most important grape variety in Sauternes?

options.a: It has high acidity and thick, rot-resistant skins.
options.b: It dries easily into raisins on the vine.
options.c: It is particularly susceptible to botrytis.
options.d: It ripens early, well before the autumn rains.

notes.a: Sémillon ranges from medium to high acidity, and is prone to botrytis, not resistant.
notes.b: Sauternes relies on noble rot, not on drying the grapes.
notes.c: Correct: Sauternes is made from grapes concentrated by noble rot, and Sémillon is particularly susceptible.
notes.d: Not the book's reason; the key is its susceptibility to botrytis.

Q-L2-09-09.stem: A sweet, full-bodied white wine has high acidity and pronounced apricot, smoke and vanilla flavours. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Vouvray
options.b: Hunter Valley
options.c: Sauternes
options.d: Barossa Valley

notes.a: Sweet Vouvray has stone or tropical fruit, but it is typically unoaked, so no smoke or vanilla.
notes.b: Hunter Semillon is dry, light-bodied and low in alcohol, made in inert vessels.
notes.c: Correct: botrytised and Sémillon-led, with apricot plus oak (smoke, vanilla); very good to outstanding.
notes.d: Some Australian Semillon is botrytised, but the book gives Barossa only dry styles, Hunter-like to full and oaked.

Q-L2-10-07.stem: What does the regional appellation Bourgogne AOC tell you about a white Burgundy?

options.a: It ranks above the village appellations.
options.b: Its grapes must come from the Côte d'Or vineyards only.
options.c: It comes from a single premier cru vineyard.
options.d: Its grapes may come from anywhere in Burgundy.

notes.a: Regional is the lowest level: below village, premier cru and grand cru.
notes.b: Too narrow: the regional appellation covers all of Burgundy.
notes.c: Premier Cru wines carry the village name plus Premier Cru.
notes.d: Correct: usually simple, with apple and lemon and high acidity.

Q-L2-10-08.stem: Why do Chablis Premier Cru and Grand Cru wines tend to be riper and more flavourful than basic Chablis?

options.a: Their flat valley sites are protected from frost.
options.b: They are fermented and matured in new oak barrels instead.
options.c: Their hillsides face south/south-west, giving more sun.
options.d: Their grapes are left on the vine until botrytis develops.

notes.a: The best sites are on hillsides; frost is a key concern across Chablis.
notes.b: With very few exceptions, Chablis shows no detectable oak; inert vessels are preferred.
notes.c: Correct: more sun exposure gives riper grapes and more flavourful, complex wines.
notes.d: Chablis is dry; botrytis plays no part in its style.

Q-L2-10-09.stem: Which two Côte de Beaune villages are famous for very good and outstanding Chardonnay?

options.a: Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges
options.b: Mâcon and Pouilly-Fuissé
options.c: Beaune and Pommard
options.d: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet

notes.a: Côte de Nuits villages, listed for Pinot Noir.
notes.b: Mâconnais appellations in southern Burgundy, not the Côte de Beaune.
notes.c: Côte de Beaune villages, but listed on the spec for Pinot Noir.
notes.d: Correct: their premier and grand crus can develop hazelnut and mushroom for decades.

Q-L2-10-10.stem: How is a Meursault Chardonnay MOST LIKELY to differ from a Chablis?

options.a: It has a lighter body, higher acidity and wet-stone notes.
options.b: It has simpler fruit, as it is made for early drinking.
options.c: It has less oak influence, being fermented in inert vessels.
options.d: It has more body, riper fruit and complexity from oak and lees.

notes.a: That describes Chablis, from the cool north of Burgundy.
notes.b: Meursault's premier and grand crus can develop for decades.
notes.c: Reversed: it is Chablis that is typically fermented in inert vessels.
notes.d: Correct: the moderate climate gives peach and melon; oak and lees add complexity and body.

Q-L2-10-11.stem: Why does Pouilly-Fuissé usually offer more concentrated Chardonnay than basic Mâcon AOC?

options.a: Its vines grow grapes that are affected by botrytis.
options.b: Its vines grow on steep slopes facing east and south-east.
options.c: Its vines grow in the cool north of Burgundy, near Chablis.
options.d: Its vines grow on flat, fertile land on the valley floor.

notes.a: Pouilly-Fuissé is a dry Chardonnay; botrytis plays no part.
notes.b: Correct: these slopes give concentrated stone and tropical fruit; oak is often used too.
notes.c: It is in the Mâconnais, in the south of Burgundy.
notes.d: The book credits steep slopes, not flat land.

Q-L2-10-12.stem: Most Chardonnay from Languedoc-Roussillon is labelled Pays d'Oc IGP. What type of GI is this?

options.a: A PGI: a wide area with less strict rules.
options.b: A PDO: a small area with tightly defined rules.
options.c: A PDO covering the whole of southern France.
options.d: A PGI that permits only Chardonnay grapes.

notes.a: Correct: IGP is the French PGI term; PGIs give producers more flexibility.
notes.b: That describes a PDO (AOC or AOP in France).
notes.c: IGP is a PGI term; the French PDO terms are AOC and AOP.
notes.d: PGI rules are less strict; Pays d'Oc is also a spec GI for Merlot and Syrah.

Q-L3-09-01.stem: Why may pickers need several passes through a Loire Chenin Blanc vineyard at harvest?

options.a: Frost forces early picking of exposed rows.
options.b: Its thick skins need extra time to soften.
options.c: Noble rot only forms on the lowest bunches.
options.d: Grapes in one bunch often ripen unevenly.

notes.a: Not the reason given; passes let pickers choose grapes at the desired ripeness.
notes.b: Not given; the L3 point is uneven ripening within one bunch.
notes.c: Not the reason given; the issue is uneven ripeness within a bunch.
notes.d: Correct: per the L3 book; unripe grapes give green, herbaceous aromas unless excluded.

Q-L3-09-02.stem: Why are Bordeaux's top sweet wine appellations, such as Sauternes, grouped by the Garonne and Ciron rivers?

options.a: The rivers leave warm gravel ideal for Cabernet Sauvignon.
options.b: The rivers protect the vines from spring frost and hail.
options.c: The rivers reflect sunlight, drying grapes into raisins.
options.d: The rivers create misty autumn conditions for noble rot.

notes.a: Sauternes is a sweet white; Sémillon dominates there.
notes.b: Not the reason given; it is the autumn mist for botrytis.
notes.c: Passerillage helps in years with little noble rot; the rivers' role is autumn mist for botrytis.
notes.d: Correct: mist on fully ripened grapes favours noble rot, per the L3 book.

Q-L3-09-03.stem: How does the production of Tokaji Aszú differ from the method used for Sauternes?

options.a: Fermentation is stopped early by adding grape spirit.
options.b: Botrytised bunches are machine-harvested whole.
options.c: Aszú berries are macerated in a base wine, then pressed.
options.d: Aszú grapes are dried on straw mats, rather than rotted.

notes.a: That is fortification, as for Port; Tokaji Aszú is not fortified.
notes.b: Pickers select individual aszú berries by hand, in several passes.
notes.c: Correct: they soak 12-60 hours in a base wine of healthy grapes; Sauternes ferments the botrytised grapes.
notes.d: Aszú berries are botrytised (noble rot), not dried on mats.

Q-L3-10-01.stem: Which two measures does the L3 book say Chablis growers use to protect their vines from frost?

options.a: Low sites and mulching
options.b: Sprinklers and heaters
options.c: Shade cloth and netting
options.d: Leaf removal and pruning

notes.a: Low, flat land is more frost-prone; the L3 book says hillsides are less so.
notes.b: Correct: frost, which can strike as late as May, is the region's major climatic problem.
notes.c: These protect against sun or hail, not frost.
notes.d: Canopy and vine management, not frost protection.

Q-L3-10-02.stem: Within the Côte d'Or, where are all but one of the white grands crus found?

options.a: The Côte de Nuits
options.b: The Côte de Beaune
options.c: The Hautes-Côtes de Nuits
options.d: The Hautes-Côtes de Beaune

notes.a: Home of all but one of the RED grands crus.
notes.b: Correct: and all but one of the red grands crus are in the Côte de Nuits.
notes.c: A regional appellation to the west, at higher altitude; no grands crus.
notes.d: A regional appellation, higher and cooler, giving less body and concentration.

Q-L3-10-03.stem: Besides Pouilly-Fuissé, which Mâconnais village appellation does the L3 book name as one of the region's two most famous?

options.a: Rully
options.b: Meursault
options.c: Montagny
options.d: Saint-Véran

notes.a: A Côte Chalonnaise village, also a centre for sparkling wine.
notes.b: A Côte de Beaune village, not in the Mâconnais.
notes.c: A Côte Chalonnaise village, which makes only white wines.
notes.d: Correct: its best wines show ripe tropical and stone fruit, and most are barrel-matured.

Q-L2-11-07.stem: An unoaked, single-varietal white has high acidity, green apple, grass, asparagus and a hint of wet stones. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Constantia
options.b: Pays d'Oc
options.c: Sancerre
options.d: Pessac-Léognan

notes.a: Constantia Sauvignon Blanc is described with ripe tropical fruit as well as herbaceous aromas (p. 74).
notes.b: Languedoc Sauvignon Blanc shows tropical fruit (passion fruit) alongside grass (p. 73).
notes.c: Correct: the book's Sancerre/Pouilly-Fumé profile is dry, high acid, apple, grass, asparagus, sometimes wet stones.
notes.d: Typically a Sémillon blend, and the best are often oak-matured (p. 73); this stem describes an unoaked varietal.

Q-L2-11-08.stem: Which white grape varieties are permitted in Sancerre AOC and Pouilly-Fumé AOC?

options.a: Only Sauvignon Blanc is permitted in both.
options.b: Their whites are Sauvignon Blanc-Sémillon blends.
options.c: They are sold under the wider Touraine AOC label.
options.d: Both lie side by side on the same bank of the Loire.

notes.a: Correct: both are cool Loire AOCs where Sauvignon Blanc is the only white variety permitted.
notes.b: Sémillon blends are typical of Graves and Pessac-Léognan in Bordeaux, not these Loire AOCs.
notes.c: Touraine AOC is a separate appellation covering the wider sub-region to their west.
notes.d: The book says the two appellations face each other across the Loire River.

Q-L2-11-09.stem: How does Touraine AOC Sauvignon Blanc typically differ from Sancerre?

options.a: It is richer and oak-matured, from a single village to the east.
options.b: It is fruity and inexpensive, from a wider area to the west.
options.c: It is blended with Sémillon to add body and ageing potential.
options.d: It is made sweet from late-harvested, extra-ripe grapes.

notes.a: Wrong on both style and place: Touraine lies to the west and is typically fruity and inexpensive.
notes.b: Correct: grapes come from the wider Touraine sub-region west of Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé (p. 73).
notes.c: Sémillon blends are typical of Bordeaux (Graves, Pessac-Léognan), not Touraine.
notes.d: The book describes Touraine Sauvignon Blanc as fruity and inexpensive, not sweet.

Q-L2-11-10.stem: White Pessac-Léognan is typically a blend. Which grape is blended with Sauvignon Blanc, and what does it add?

options.a: Viognier, which adds floral notes and body
options.b: Chardonnay, which adds body and a creamy texture
options.c: Sémillon, which adds body and helps the wine age
options.d: Sémillon, which adds acidity and herbaceous aromas

notes.a: Viognier is a blending partner elsewhere (p. 80), but not in Bordeaux whites.
notes.b: Chardonnay is not part of the Bordeaux white blend in the book; the partner is Sémillon.
notes.c: Correct: the book says Sémillon adds body to Sauvignon Blanc and helps the wine to age.
notes.d: Right grape, wrong role: high acidity and herbaceous aromas come from Sauvignon Blanc itself.

Q-L2-11-11.stem: An outstanding, oak-matured white Pessac-Léognan has spent ten years in bottle. Which flavours is it MOST LIKELY to have developed?

options.a: Passion fruit and grass
options.b: Banana and candy
options.c: Honey and nuts
options.d: Bread and biscuit

notes.a: These are fresh primary aromas; with age they fade rather than develop.
notes.b: These come from Beaujolais-style red winemaking (p. 94), not aged white Bordeaux.
notes.c: Correct: very good or outstanding Graves and Pessac-Léognan whites develop honey and nuts in bottle (p. 73).
notes.d: These come from contact with dead yeast (lees), as in traditional-method sparkling wine.

Q-L2-11-12.stem: How does a simple white Bordeaux AOC Sauvignon Blanc typically differ from a white Graves AOC?

options.a: It is fresher and simpler, with grass and green apple.
options.b: It must be a blend, while Graves may be single-varietal.
options.c: It is oak-matured, while Graves is usually unoaked.
options.d: It is fuller-bodied, as it contains more Sémillon.

notes.a: Correct: Graves and Pessac-Léognan whites are described as more concentrated and complex (p. 73).
notes.b: Reversed idea: Bordeaux AOC may be varietal Sauvignon Blanc or a blend; Graves is typically a blend.
notes.c: Reversed: it is very good Graves and Pessac-Léognan that are often oak-matured.
notes.d: The book says it is Graves that is the more concentrated, complex wine.

Q-L2-11-13.stem: Much of Languedoc-Roussillon is too warm for Sauvignon Blanc. Where does it make its best wines there, and how are they usually labelled?

options.a: Areas cooled by morning fog; Pays d'Oc IGP
options.b: Areas cooled by altitude; Pays d'Oc AOC
options.c: The warm coastal plains; Pays d'Oc AOC
options.d: Areas cooled by altitude; Pays d'Oc IGP

notes.a: Morning fog (with sea breezes) is the book's explanation for Casablanca, Chile.
notes.b: Right sites, wrong level: Pays d'Oc is an IGP (PGI), not an AOC.
notes.c: The best sites are those cooled by altitude, and Pays d'Oc is an IGP, not an AOC.
notes.d: Correct: both points are in the book (p. 73). Pays d'Oc is a PGI.

Q-L2-12-11.stem: Why does Alsace AOC Pinot Gris typically have only medium acidity?

options.a: The wine is matured for years in new oak.
options.b: The vines are cropped at very high yields.
options.c: The grapes are picked later, when extra-ripe.
options.d: The grapes are picked early to keep them fresh.

notes.a: Not the book's reason; the cause is late picking of extra-ripe grapes.
notes.b: High yields go with the light, simple style, not with Alsace (p. 76).
notes.c: Correct: by then acidity is typically medium, with more sugar ripeness and flavour complexity (p. 77).
notes.d: Early picking retains acidity; it gives the light Italian style (p. 76).

Q-L2-12-12.stem: What does 'Grand Cru' on an Alsace Pinot Gris label tell you?

options.a: The wine is a blend of the region's best grapes.
options.b: The wine was made from late-harvested grapes.
options.c: The grapes came from a specific grand cru vineyard.
options.d: The wine comes from a top-ranked château.

notes.a: Alsace wines are typically labelled by grape variety; grands crus are defined by vineyard.
notes.b: That is Vendanges tardives (VT); both Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru can be VT (p. 78).
notes.c: Correct: Alsace Grand Cru wines must come from specific vineyards, mostly on the Vosges foothills (p. 78).
notes.d: Château rankings are a Bordeaux idea (Grand Cru Classé), not Alsace.

Q-L2-12-13.stem: Why are Alsace grand cru wines typically riper in flavour and fuller in body than wines from the flatter plains?

options.a: Their slopes face north, sheltered from the sun.
options.b: Their flat, fertile sites give higher yields of riper grapes.
options.c: Their grapes are concentrated by noble rot each year.
options.d: Their steep east/south-east slopes get more sunlight.

notes.a: They face east/south-east, which gives more sunlight, not less.
notes.b: The grands crus are on steep slopes; the book contrasts them with the flatter plains.
notes.c: Not the book's reason; it credits the extra sunlight on the steep slopes.
notes.d: Correct: the grand cru sites on the Vosges foothills receive more sunlight (p. 78).

Q-L2-12-14.stem: What does 'Vendanges tardives' (VT) mean on an Alsace label, and what style does it typically denote?

options.a: Late harvest; a medium to sweet wine from extra-ripe grapes
options.b: Old vines; a concentrated dry wine from low yields
options.c: Grand cru vineyard; a dry wine from steep, sunny slopes
options.d: Late harvest; a dry wine with high alcohol from very ripe grapes

notes.a: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 78).
notes.b: Old Vines is a different term with no legal definition; VT means late harvest.
notes.c: That describes Alsace Grand Cru, not VT.
notes.d: VT typically denotes a medium to sweet wine, not a dry one.

Q-L2-12-15.stem: Which statement about Vendanges tardives (VT) in Alsace is correct?

options.a: VT is a separate appellation for the sweet wines of Alsace.
options.b: Alsace AOC and Alsace Grand Cru wines can both be VT.
options.c: VT is reserved for Alsace Grand Cru wines.
options.d: Pinot Gris cannot be labelled VT in Alsace.

notes.a: Wrong: VT is a labelling term used on Alsace or Alsace Grand Cru wines.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 78).
notes.c: Wrong: the book says both Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru wines can be labelled VT.
notes.d: Wrong: Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewurztraminer can all be labelled VT.

Q-L2-12-16.stem: As of the 2021 vintage, what must the label of an Alsace AOC wine indicate?

options.a: The percentage of each grape in the blend
options.b: The name of the grand cru vineyard
options.c: Whether the wine was matured in oak
options.d: Its level of sweetness, on a standardised scale

notes.a: Not the 2021 rule; most Alsace wines are labelled with a single grape variety.
notes.b: Only Alsace Grand Cru wines come from named grand cru vineyards.
notes.c: Not a label requirement given in the book; the 2021 rule concerns sweetness.
notes.d: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 78); Alsace wines are also typically labelled by grape variety.

Q-L2-12-18.stem: A guest orders a strongly flavoured dish. Which of these wines is the BEST match?

options.a: A New World 'Pinot Grigio'
options.b: Veneto IGT Pinot Grigio
options.c: Pinot Grigio delle Venezie DOC
options.d: Alsace Grand Cru Pinot Gris

notes.a: The name signals a lighter, higher-acid style that the dish could overpower.
notes.b: A light, simple style that a strongly flavoured dish would overpower.
notes.c: A light, simple style with a short finish; the dish would overpower it.
notes.d: Correct: riper Pinot Gris pairs well with strongly flavoured food (p. 78); intensities should match (p. 18).

Q-L2-12-19.stem: An off-dry white has medium acidity, a full body, pronounced peach and mango, and notes of honey and ginger. Which wine is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Sancerre
options.b: Alsace Pinot Gris
options.c: Rías Baixas Albariño
options.d: Veneto IGT Pinot Grigio

notes.a: Sancerre is dry with high acidity, green apple and herbaceous notes (p. 73).
notes.b: Correct: medium acidity, medium to full body, peach and mango, with honey and ginger in bottle (p. 77).
notes.c: Albariño is dry with high acidity, citrus and stone fruit (p. 80).
notes.d: Typically dry and light-bodied, with simple pear and lemon (p. 76-77).

Q-L2-13-04.stem: In Alsace, Gewurztraminer makes some of the region's highest-quality grand cru wines alongside which two other grapes?

options.a: Riesling and Pinot Gris
options.b: Pinot Gris and Viognier
options.c: Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris
options.d: Riesling and Chardonnay

notes.a: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 79); these are also the typical grand cru grapes on p. 78.
notes.b: Viognier's classic French home is Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône (p. 80).
notes.c: The book's French homes for Sauvignon Blanc are the Loire, Bordeaux and Languedoc.
notes.d: Chardonnay is not named as an Alsace grand cru grape in the book.

Q-L2-13-05.stem: A dry white has low to medium acidity, high alcohol, a full body, pronounced blossom, peach and apricot, and a light vanilla note. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: delle Venezie
options.b: Rías Baixas
options.c: Sancerre
options.d: Condrieu

notes.a: Typically light, simple Pinot Grigio with pear and lemon (p. 77).
notes.b: Albariño from here has high acidity and a medium body (p. 80).
notes.c: Sancerre has high acidity and herbaceous, green-fruit aromas (p. 73).
notes.d: Correct: Viognier gives blossom, peach and apricot, and light vanilla from oak is common in Condrieu (p. 79-80).

Q-L2-13-06.stem: Unusually for an aromatic grape, Viognier is sometimes oaked. How is oak typically used in Condrieu AOC?

options.a: It is not used, as oak is banned in Condrieu AOC
options.b: To soften the wine's very high natural acidity
options.c: To add strong toast and smoke flavours that dominate
options.d: To add light vanilla without hiding the floral aromas

notes.a: Wrong: the book says light oak flavours are common in Condrieu.
notes.b: Viognier already has low to medium acidity (p. 79).
notes.c: The book stresses care not to overpower the delicate floral aromas.
notes.d: Correct: light oak (vanilla) is common, but winemakers take care not to overpower the floral aromas (p. 80).

Q-L2-13-07.stem: Which statement best describes Condrieu AOC?

options.a: A Northern Rhône AOC for Syrah co-fermented with Viognier
options.b: A Southern Rhône AOC for white blends led by Viognier
options.c: An Alsace AOC for late-harvested, sweet Viognier
options.d: A Northern Rhône AOC for single-varietal Viognier

notes.a: That is the tradition in Côte Rôtie, a red wine AOC (p. 91).
notes.b: Condrieu is in the Northern Rhône and is dedicated to single-varietal Viognier.
notes.c: Condrieu is in the Rhône; Viognier is not an Alsace grape in the book.
notes.d: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 80).

Q-L3-11-02.stem: Why do the best white Pessac-Léognan wines have a rounder body and more toasty notes than most Sauvignon Blanc?

options.a: They are fermented cool in steel and bottled early.
options.b: They are made from grapes affected by noble rot.
options.c: They are blended with Chardonnay for extra body.
options.d: They are fermented and/or matured partly in new oak.

notes.a: That is the aromatic approach (e.g. New Zealand), which keeps fresh, fruity flavours.
notes.b: Noble rot is for the sweet wines of Sauternes, not the dry whites of Pessac-Léognan.
notes.c: The blending partner is Sémillon, not Chardonnay.
notes.d: Correct: per the L3 book, often with lees ageing and MLF; Sémillon adds further body.

Q-L3-11-03.stem: Why might a Sancerre producer encourage malolactic conversion (MLF) in a cooler vintage?

options.a: To protect the wine from oxidation in barrel.
options.b: To raise the alcohol of under-ripe grapes.
options.c: To add herbaceous aromas of grass and asparagus.
options.d: To lower the wine's high acidity.

notes.a: Not the role of MLF; SO2 is the winemaker's antioxidant.
notes.b: MLF converts malic acid to softer lactic acid; it does not raise alcohol.
notes.c: MLF can add buttery notes, not herbaceous ones; those come from the grape.
notes.d: Correct: per the L3 book, MLF is most likely to be encouraged in cooler vintages to lower acidity.

Q-L2-14-08.stem: Why does Bordeaux have high levels of rainfall?

options.a: It lies close to the Mediterranean Sea.
options.b: It lies close to the Atlantic Ocean.
options.c: It is cooled by the Gironde's morning fogs.
options.d: It sits in the shelter of high mountains.

notes.a: That is Languedoc-Roussillon, which is warm with less variable weather.
notes.b: Correct: the book links Bordeaux's moderate climate and high rainfall to the nearby Atlantic.
notes.c: Not the book's explanation; the Gironde is the estuary that divides the region.
notes.d: Mountain shelter reduces rainfall; it does not cause high rainfall.

Q-L2-14-09.stem: Which of these Bordeaux appellations is on the Right Bank?

options.a: Margaux
options.b: Pauillac
options.c: Pomerol
options.d: Pessac-Léognan

notes.a: Left Bank: within the Haut-Médoc.
notes.b: Left Bank: within the Haut-Médoc, north of the city of Bordeaux.
notes.c: Correct: Pomerol and Saint-Émilion are the most important Right Bank appellations.
notes.d: Left Bank: within Graves, south of the city of Bordeaux.

Q-L2-14-10.stem: Which two rivers meet to form Bordeaux's Gironde Estuary?

options.a: The Garonne and Dordogne
options.b: The Loire and the Garonne
options.c: The Rhône and the Dordogne
options.d: The Loire and the Rhône

notes.a: Correct: the book says the Gironde Estuary is where the Garonne and Dordogne Rivers meet.
notes.b: The Loire is a separate river and wine region to the north.
notes.c: The Rhône flows south to the Mediterranean, far from Bordeaux.
notes.d: Neither river flows through Bordeaux.

Q-L2-14-11.stem: Which statement best describes a typical red wine labelled Bordeaux AOC?

options.a: A Merlot-led blend from anywhere in Bordeaux
options.b: A classified wine from one of the region's best châteaux
options.c: A Cabernet-led blend from the Left Bank's gravel soils
options.d: A single-varietal Merlot from the Right Bank only

notes.a: Correct: Bordeaux AOC reds are typically Merlot-dominated and can come from anywhere in the region.
notes.b: That is Grand Cru Classé / Cru Classé, not the regional appellation.
notes.c: That fits Left Bank AOCs such as Haut-Médoc; Bordeaux AOC is regional and Merlot-led.
notes.d: Grapes can come from anywhere in Bordeaux, and the wines are typically blends.

Q-L2-14-12.stem: How does Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC relate to Saint-Émilion AOC?

options.a: It is a more prestigious AOC within Saint-Émilion.
options.b: It is a term any Bordeaux château may apply to use.
options.c: It is a lower-level appellation covering a wider area.
options.d: It is a ranking of Médoc châteaux, not an appellation.

notes.a: Correct: the book says Saint-Émilion AOC includes the more prestigious Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC.
notes.b: That resembles Cru Bourgeois, which unclassified Médoc wines can apply to use.
notes.c: Reversed: it lies within Saint-Émilion AOC and is the more prestigious.
notes.d: It is a Right Bank AOC, not a Médoc ranking.

Q-L2-14-16.stem: A single-varietal Merlot from Languedoc-Roussillon is typically labelled with which GI?

options.a: Bordeaux AOC
options.b: Minervois AOC
options.c: Pays d'Oc IGP
options.d: Côtes du Rhône AOC

notes.a: Bordeaux AOC grapes must come from the Bordeaux region, not Languedoc.
notes.b: A Languedoc AOC given for blends with Syrah (and a Grenache GI), not single-varietal Merlot.
notes.c: Correct: the book says Languedoc-Roussillon Merlot is typically labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.
notes.d: A Rhône Valley appellation, not Languedoc-Roussillon.

Q-L2-14-18.stem: Which is the most widely planted grape variety in Bordeaux?

options.a: Sémillon
options.b: Cabernet Sauvignon
options.c: Merlot
options.d: Sauvignon Blanc

notes.a: The key grape of Sauternes, but not the region's most widely planted variety.
notes.b: Typically dominant on the Left Bank, but not the most widely planted overall.
notes.c: Correct: the book says Merlot is the most widely planted variety in the region.
notes.d: A white grape for dry whites and sweet blends; not the most widely planted.

Q-L2-15-05.stem: In a cool year on Bordeaux's Left Bank, why might a producer raise the proportion of Merlot in the blend?

options.a: Appellation rules require more Merlot in cool years.
options.b: Cabernet may not ripen; Merlot softens the blend.
options.c: Merlot needs a longer, warmer season than Cabernet.
options.d: Merlot adds tannin and acidity that cool years lack.

notes.a: No such rule is given; the choice is driven by how well Cabernet ripened.
notes.b: Correct: Merlot's share may rise when Cabernet struggles to ripen; blending softens tannin and acidity.
notes.c: Reversed: it is late-ripening Cabernet that needs a long, warm season.
notes.d: Reversed: Merlot softens; cool years leave Cabernet with harsh tannin and acid.

Q-L2-15-07.stem: Which two AOCs named in the Level 2 book lie within the Haut-Médoc?

options.a: Margaux and Pauillac
options.b: Graves and Pessac-Léognan
options.c: Pauillac and Pessac-Léognan
options.d: Margaux and Saint-Émilion

notes.a: Correct: the Haut-Médoc, north of the city of Bordeaux, includes Margaux and Pauillac.
notes.b: Both lie south of the city; Pessac-Léognan is within Graves.
notes.c: Pessac-Léognan lies within Graves, south of the city.
notes.d: Saint-Émilion is on the Right Bank.

Q-L2-15-08.stem: Which statement about Pessac-Léognan AOC is correct?

options.a: It lies on the Right Bank, close to Saint-Émilion and Pomerol.
options.b: It lies within the Haut-Médoc, north of Bordeaux city.
options.c: It lies within Graves; its reds are typically Merlot-led.
options.d: It lies within Graves; its reds are typically Cabernet-led.

notes.a: It is a Left Bank appellation within Graves.
notes.b: Graves, which includes Pessac-Léognan, is SOUTH of the city.
notes.c: Right location, wrong grape: Left Bank reds are typically Cabernet-dominated.
notes.d: Correct: Graves (incl. Pessac-Léognan) is Left Bank, where Cabernet Sauvignon typically dominates.

Q-L2-15-09.stem: What does the term 'Château' indicate on a Bordeaux label?

options.a: The wine meets slightly stricter rules on yields and alcohol.
options.b: The wine was made in a grand historic building.
options.c: The grapes were grown on the producer's own land.
options.d: The wine has been ranked in an official classification.

notes.a: That describes Bordeaux Supérieur.
notes.b: The book says the term does not necessarily refer to a grand building.
notes.c: Correct: it refers to an estate or producer, not bought-in grapes, and not necessarily a grand building.
notes.d: That is Grand Cru Classé / Cru Classé.

Q-L2-15-10.stem: What do the terms Grand Cru Classé and Cru Classé on a Bordeaux label indicate?

options.a: The wine has been aged for a minimum period in new oak.
options.b: The wine comes from an unclassified Médoc château that applied.
options.c: The wine was made from grapes grown anywhere in Bordeaux.
options.d: The château is ranked in a sub-region's classification.

notes.a: No ageing rule is given; the terms reflect a classification ranking.
notes.b: That is Cru Bourgeois.
notes.c: That describes the regional Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur AOCs.
notes.d: Correct: some sub-regions classify the best wines from the best châteaux; widely seen as a strong quality sign.

Q-L2-15-11.stem: Wines from the Médoc that are not classified as Grand Cru Classé can apply to use which term on their labels?

options.a: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru
options.b: Bordeaux Supérieur
options.c: Cru Bourgeois
options.d: Cru Classé

notes.a: A Right Bank appellation; a Médoc wine cannot use it.
notes.b: A regional AOC with slightly stricter rules, not a status term for Médoc châteaux.
notes.c: Correct: the book says Médoc wines not classified as Grand Cru Classé can apply to use Cru Bourgeois.
notes.d: Only for wines ranked in a classification, which this château is not.

Q-L2-15-12.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Bordeaux Supérieur from Cru Bourgeois?

options.a: Supérieur covers all Bordeaux; Cru Bourgeois is a Médoc term.
options.b: Supérieur is Right Bank only; Cru Bourgeois is Left Bank only.
options.c: Each is used only by châteaux ranked as Cru Classé.
options.d: Supérieur is a Médoc term; Cru Bourgeois is a region-wide AOC.

notes.a: Correct: Supérieur can come from anywhere in Bordeaux; Cru Bourgeois is for unclassified Médoc wines that apply.
notes.b: Supérieur can come from anywhere in Bordeaux, not only the Right Bank.
notes.c: Neither: Cru Classé is the ranked term; Cru Bourgeois is for UNclassified Médoc wines.
notes.d: Reversed.

Q-L2-15-13.stem: Why can Cabernet Sauvignon ripen more reliably in Languedoc-Roussillon than in Bordeaux?

options.a: Its high-altitude vineyards have cool nights.
options.b: It is warm, with less variable weather from year to year.
options.c: It is moderate, with cooling breezes from the Atlantic.
options.d: Its gravel soils drain quickly after heavy autumn rain.

notes.a: Not the book's explanation; it credits the warm, reliable climate.
notes.b: Correct: the book says the climate is warm and annual weather is less variable than in Bordeaux.
notes.c: Languedoc is warm; it is Bordeaux whose moderate, rainy climate comes from the Atlantic.
notes.d: Gravel is the book's explanation for the Bordeaux Left Bank, not Languedoc.

Q-L2-16-04.stem: Outside France and Australia, a producer labels its red 'Syrah' rather than 'Shiraz'. Which style does this MOST likely suggest?

options.a: Full-bodied and high in alcohol, with cooked black fruit
options.b: Medium-bodied, with fresh black fruit and black pepper
options.c: Light-bodied, with red cherry and banana aromas
options.d: Sweet and fortified, with dried-fruit flavours

notes.a: That is the warm-climate style the name 'Shiraz' suggests.
notes.b: Correct: 'Syrah' points to the moderate-climate style, as in the Northern Rhône.
notes.c: Closer to Beaujolais (Gamay).
notes.d: Not linked to the Syrah/Shiraz name choice.

Q-L2-16-06.stem: What does Syrah typically contribute to a 'Rhône Blend', and which grape is it most commonly blended with?

options.a: Acidity and floral aromas; Viognier
options.b: Colour, black fruit and tannin; Grenache
options.c: Softness and red fruit; Cabernet Sauvignon
options.d: Colour, black fruit and tannin; Merlot

notes.a: Viognier is co-fermented in some Côte Rôtie, but that is not a 'Rhône Blend'.
notes.b: Correct: it is most commonly blended with Southern Rhône grapes such as Grenache.
notes.c: That is Merlot's role with Cabernet; Rhône Blends are Syrah with Grenache.
notes.d: Right contribution, wrong partner: the book names Grenache.

Q-L2-16-08.stem: Why are the AOC wines of the Northern Rhône expensive to produce?

options.a: Steep slopes mean the vines must be worked by hand.
options.b: The grapes must be dried before fermentation.
options.c: Frequent spring frosts destroy much of each year's crop.
options.d: Strict rules require all wines to be aged in new oak.

notes.a: Correct: many vineyards are so steep that machinery cannot be used.
notes.b: That is appassimento (e.g. Amarone), not Northern Rhône practice.
notes.c: Not given in the book; the cost is hand labour on steep slopes.
notes.d: No such rule is given; the cost comes from hand-working steep slopes.

Q-L2-16-09.stem: Some Côte Rôtie producers co-ferment a small amount of a white grape with Syrah. Which grape is it, and what can it add?

options.a: Viognier, which can add floral aromas
options.b: Chardonnay, which can add buttery notes
options.c: Sauvignon Blanc, which adds herbaceous notes
options.d: Viognier, which adds tannin and deep colour

notes.a: Correct: a tradition, though not practised by all producers.
notes.b: Not the Côte Rôtie tradition, which uses Viognier.
notes.c: Not the Côte Rôtie tradition, which uses Viognier.
notes.d: Right grape, wrong effect: the book says it can add floral aromas.

Q-L2-16-10.stem: Which Northern Rhône AOC, with exceptionally steep and stony slopes, marks the northern limit for successfully ripening Syrah?

options.a: Hermitage
options.b: Côte Rôtie
options.c: Crozes-Hermitage
options.d: Minervois

notes.a: Further south: a single steep, south-facing hill.
notes.b: Correct: in the far north of the Northern Rhône; complex, peppery Syrah that can age for years.
notes.c: A larger, flatter appellation surrounding Hermitage.
notes.d: In Languedoc-Roussillon, not the Northern Rhône.

Q-L2-16-11.stem: What makes up the entire Hermitage AOC?

options.a: Several north-facing terraces
options.b: Stony slopes at Syrah's northern limit
options.c: One steep, south-facing slope
options.d: A large, flat plain around a hill

notes.a: The Hermitage slope faces south, which aids ripening.
notes.b: That is Côte Rôtie, in the far north of the Northern Rhône.
notes.c: Correct: one steep, south-facing slope (the hill of Hermitage) forms the whole appellation.
notes.d: That describes Crozes-Hermitage, which surrounds the hill.

Q-L2-16-12.stem: Why are Crozes-Hermitage wines typically less expensive than those of Hermitage?

options.a: Its cooler sites often fail to ripen
options.b: It blends Syrah with cheaper Grenache
options.c: Higher yields and easier mechanisation
options.d: It is aged in stainless steel, not oak

notes.a: Not the reason given; it is yields and mechanisation.
notes.b: Syrah is the only black grape permitted in Northern Rhône AOC wines.
notes.c: Correct: Crozes is larger and flatter, so yields are higher and vineyards easier to mechanise.
notes.d: No such rule; the book explains price by yields and mechanisation.

Q-L2-16-13.stem: A Syrah with fresh black cherry and blackberry, herbal notes and black pepper, from a moderate climate, is MOST LIKELY from:

options.a: South Eastern Australia
