options.b: Pays d'Oc
options.c: Crozes-Hermitage
options.d: Barossa Valley

notes.a: Warm inland fruit for inexpensive, high-volume Shiraz.
notes.b: Warm Languedoc-Roussillon, where Syrah ripens reliably to a riper style.
notes.c: Correct: the moderate-climate Northern Rhône style described in the book.
notes.d: Warm: full body, cooked black fruit, often vanilla or coconut oak.

Q-L2-16-14.stem: In Languedoc-Roussillon, Syrah is often blended with other grapes in which appellation (AOC) named in the Level 2 book?

options.a: Côtes de Provence
options.b: Pays d'Oc
options.c: Minervois
options.d: Crozes-Hermitage

notes.a: A Provence AOC (a Grenache GI), not in Languedoc-Roussillon.
notes.b: Pays d'Oc is a PGI (IGP), not an AOC; the book mentions it for single-varietal Syrah.
notes.c: Correct: per the book; single-varietal Syrah there is often labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.
notes.d: A Northern Rhône AOC.

Q-L3-14-02.stem: According to the L3 book, why does Bordeaux's weather make blending several grape varieties a sensible strategy?

options.a: Their flowering and ripening dates differ, spreading risk.
options.b: They all ripen together, so the harvest can be done at once.
options.c: Single-varietal wines of any colour are banned in Bordeaux.
options.d: The warm, dry climate gives every variety excess sugar.

notes.a: Correct: one bad frost or heavy shower is unlikely to ruin the entire crop.
notes.b: The reverse: the varieties flower and ripen at different times.
notes.c: Not the reason; L3 notes varietal dry white Sauvignon Blanc is made.
notes.d: Bordeaux is moderate maritime with high rainfall, not warm and dry.

Q-L3-14-03.stem: According to the L3 book, what effect does the Gulf Stream have on Bordeaux's vineyards?

options.a: It brings cold air that makes spring frost a major risk.
options.b: It shelters the vineyards from Atlantic storms.
options.c: It removes rain, giving dry and reliable vintages.
options.d: It extends the season; ripening can run into October.

notes.a: The reverse: it is a warming current; spring frosts are rarely a problem.
notes.b: That is the Landes forest and coastal sand dunes to the west.
notes.c: The Atlantic brings high rainfall and humidity, so vintage variation matters.
notes.d: Correct: a warming current, so spring frosts are rarely a problem and ripening continues well into October.

Q-L3-14-04.stem: According to the L3 book, how does the Saint-Émilion classification differ from Bordeaux's other classifications?

options.a: It is part of the appellation system and is revised.
options.b: It ranks individual vineyards rather than châteaux.
options.c: It ranks red and white wines in separate lists.
options.d: It was drawn up in 1855 alongside the Médoc ranking.

notes.a: Correct: it sits within Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC and is revised at least once every ten years.
notes.b: All Bordeaux classifications rank estates (châteaux), not vineyards.
notes.c: Separate red and white lists describe the Graves classification.
notes.d: 1855 covered Médoc reds and Sauternes, not Saint-Émilion.

Q-L3-15-01.stem: According to the L3 book, what do Bordeaux's classifications actually rank?

options.a: Appellations, from regional up to commune level
options.b: Communes, ranked by the price of their wines
options.c: Estates (châteaux); a name acts like a brand
options.d: Individual vineyard plots, as in Burgundy

notes.a: Classifications rank estates, not appellations.
notes.b: No: classifications rank estates; L3 says the AOCs form no neat quality hierarchy.
notes.c: Correct: estates can buy or sell plots, so the land behind a name can change.
notes.d: Not in Bordeaux: classifications rank estates, not vineyards.

Q-L3-15-02.stem: According to the L3 book, how do the finest red wines of Pessac-Léognan generally compare with those of the Haut-Médoc?

options.a: Softer and richer, with red berry and plum
options.b: Lighter, because they are mostly Merlot-based
options.c: Fuller-bodied, with more Merlot in the blend
options.d: A little lighter in body and more fragrant

notes.a: This is the L3 description of Saint-Émilion's Right Bank style.
notes.b: Pessac-Léognan's gravel suits Cabernet Sauvignon; its reds are Cabernet-led.
notes.c: No: lighter. It is Graves further south that usually has more Merlot.
notes.d: Correct: gravel suits Cabernet in both, but Pessac-Léognan reds are a little lighter and more fragrant.

Q-L3-16-01.stem: According to the L3 book, why are the best Northern Rhône Syrah sites on steep, south-facing slopes, often in side valleys?

options.a: The slopes shade the vines from intense Mediterranean heat.
options.b: Syrah is at its limit; side valleys block the cold mistral.
options.c: Flat valley floors are reserved for white grapes by law.
options.d: Side valleys funnel warm, humid sea air up from the coast.

notes.a: Reversed: the north is moderate; south-facing slopes add heat, not shade.
notes.b: Correct: latitude plus the cold mistral wind leave Syrah needing maximum sun and shelter.
notes.c: No such rule; slopes are chosen for aspect and shelter.
notes.d: Not in the L3 book; the side valleys protect against the cold mistral.

Q-L3-16-03.stem: According to the L3 book, where in Crozes-Hermitage do the more concentrated, complex and tannic red wines usually come from?

options.a: The hill of Hermitage itself
options.b: Irrigated vineyards near the river
options.c: The flat plain south of Hermitage
options.d: The steeper slopes north of Hermitage

notes.a: That hill is the separate Hermitage AOC, not Crozes-Hermitage.
notes.b: Not in the L3 account, which contrasts northern slopes with the flat southern plain.
notes.c: This is where the lighter, higher-yielding wines come from.
notes.d: Correct: lighter wines come from the higher-yielding flat sites to the south.

Q-L2-17-03.stem: Why are wines labelled Beaujolais AOC typically the lightest-bodied and simplest wines of the region?

options.a: Most come from high-yielding vines on flat, fertile land.
options.b: Most are matured briefly in large, old oak vessels.
options.c: Most come from cool, north-facing slopes that ripen slowly.
options.d: Most are blended with a share of white grape varieties.

notes.a: Correct: mostly from the flat, fertile south, where high-yielding vines give the lightest, simplest wines.
notes.b: Gamay is usually made in inert vessels; the book links the style to high yields.
notes.c: Not the book's reason. The slopes are in the north (Villages) and they aid ripening.
notes.d: No such blending is described; the book's reason is high yields on flat, fertile land.

Q-L2-17-04.stem: What helps Beaujolais Villages wines achieve greater flavour intensity and body than basic Beaujolais?

options.a: Flat, fertile vineyards that allow the vines to crop heavily
options.b: Sloped vineyards with more sun and warm, well-drained soils
options.c: Maturation in small new-oak barrels for several months
options.d: Cool sea breezes that slow ripening and preserve acidity

notes.a: That describes the south, the main source of the lightest Beaujolais AOC wines.
notes.b: Correct: the book says these aid grape ripening in the northern villages.
notes.c: Gamay is usually made in inert vessels and rarely shows oak.
notes.d: No sea influence is given; the book credits slopes and warm, well-drained soils.

Q-L2-17-05.stem: Which list shows these Beaujolais appellations in order, from the base of the hierarchy to the top?

options.a: Fleurie, Beaujolais Villages, Beaujolais
options.b: Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages, Fleurie
options.c: Beaujolais Villages, Beaujolais, Fleurie
options.d: Beaujolais, Fleurie, Beaujolais Villages

notes.a: This is the reverse order: the crus are at the top.
notes.b: Correct: Beaujolais AOC at the base, then Beaujolais Villages AOC, then the ten crus such as Fleurie AOC.
notes.c: Beaujolais AOC is the base; Beaujolais Villages is the step above it.
notes.d: The crus, such as Fleurie, sit above Beaujolais Villages, within its area.

Q-L2-17-06.stem: A red wine has high acidity, low to medium tannins, medium to pronounced red cherry and raspberry aromas and a medium to long finish. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
options.b: Fleurie
options.c: Beaujolais
options.d: Côtes du Rhône

notes.a: Full-bodied and high in alcohol; ripe Grenache is low in acidity.
notes.b: Correct: crus are the region's most concentrated wines; very good ones show medium to pronounced red fruit and a medium to long finish.
notes.c: Same grape, but the lightest and simplest wines; the intensity and finish point to a cru.
notes.d: Simple and medium-bodied with red fruit and white pepper; Grenache-based, so not usually high in acidity.

Q-L2-17-07.stem: Why are Beaujolais wines sometimes served lightly chilled?

options.a: To emphasise the freshness of their delicate red fruit
options.b: To reduce the burning sensation of their high alcohol levels
options.c: To hide the banana and candy aromas from winemaking
options.d: To soften the effect of their high levels of tannin

notes.a: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 95).
notes.b: Beaujolais is light- to medium-bodied; the book gives freshness of fruit as the reason.
notes.c: These aromas are part of the style; the book gives freshness of fruit as the reason.
notes.d: Beaujolais is only low to medium in tannin, so this is not the reason.

Q-L2-17-08.stem: Which of these is NOT typical of most Beaujolais wines?

options.a: Pronounced vanilla and toast from new oak
options.b: Best drunk young, while the fruit is fresh
options.c: Low to medium tannins and red-fruit flavours
options.d: Light to medium body and high acidity

notes.a: Correct: Gamay is usually made in inert vessels and rarely displays aromas from oak.
notes.b: Typical: most are for immediate drinking and quickly lose fresh fruit in bottle.
notes.c: Typical: this is the book's description of Beaujolais.
notes.d: Typical: light- to medium-bodied, and Gamay gives high acidity.

Q-L2-18-03.stem: In Minervois AOC, what does Grenache mainly contribute to blends with Syrah and other local grapes?

options.a: Colour, acidity and tannin
options.b: Herbaceous and floral aromas
options.c: Red-fruit flavours and body
options.d: Freshness from high acidity

notes.a: These are what Syrah adds to Grenache-based blends (p. 96).
notes.b: Not given; Grenache gives red fruit (strawberry, red plum, red cherry) and sometimes spice.
notes.c: Correct: Grenache ripens well in this warm climate and gives red fruit and body.
notes.d: Ripe Grenache is typically low in acidity.

Q-L2-18-06.stem: How do the large, round stones in many Châteauneuf-du-Pape vineyards help Grenache?

options.a: They absorb heat by day and radiate it at night.
options.b: They reflect sunlight away to keep the grapes cool.
options.c: They shelter the vines from cold northerly winds.
options.d: They shade the soil and keep the roots cool.

notes.a: Correct: this helps Grenache achieve full ripeness.
notes.b: The reverse: the stones store heat and release it at night, helping ripening.
notes.c: Not the book's explanation; the book credits stored heat.
notes.d: The stones add warmth; their role is to help ripening.

Q-L2-18-07.stem: An inexpensive, simple, medium-bodied red blend has red-fruit and white pepper flavours. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Priorat
options.b: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
options.c: Côtes du Rhône
options.d: Ribera del Duero

notes.a: Spain's most powerful and full-bodied Garnacha-based wines.
notes.b: Full-bodied and high in alcohol; not simple or inexpensive.
notes.c: Correct: the book's description of the least expensive Southern Rhône reds.
notes.d: Very full-bodied Tempranillo with fresh black fruit.

Q-L2-18-08.stem: Which list shows these Rhône appellations in hierarchy order, from the broadest to the most prestigious?

options.a: Côtes du Rhône Villages, Côtes du Rhône, Châteauneuf-du-Pape
options.b: Côtes du Rhône, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Côtes du Rhône Villages
options.c: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Côtes du Rhône Villages, Côtes du Rhône
options.d: Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages, Châteauneuf-du-Pape

notes.a: Côtes du Rhône is the broadest regional AOC, so it comes first.
notes.b: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is a cru, above Côtes du Rhône Villages.
notes.c: This is the reverse: the crus are at the top.
notes.d: Correct: regional AOC, then Villages (more intensity and complexity), then the crus.

Q-L2-18-11.stem: A dry, pale-coloured rosé in which Grenache is a key part of the blend is MOST LIKELY from which GI?

options.a: Barossa Valley
options.b: Priorat
options.c: Côtes de Provence
options.d: Châteauneuf-du-Pape

notes.a: Known for concentrated old-vine Grenache reds and Shiraz blends.
notes.b: Known for Spain's most powerful, full-bodied Garnacha-based reds.
notes.c: Correct: Provence is best known for dry, pale rosé, mostly from Côtes de Provence AOC.
notes.d: Known for full-bodied, high-alcohol reds.

Q-L3-17-01.stem: According to the L3 book, why are the best Beaujolais wines made from grapes grown on granite soils?

options.a: Granite soils are flat, which allows machine harvesting.
options.b: Granite holds water, protecting the vines in drought.
options.c: Granite is very fertile, so the vines ripen more fruit.
options.d: Low nutrients limit yields, concentrating the flavours.

notes.a: The granite is on rolling hills in the north and west; the flat alluvial plain is south and east.
notes.b: Not the reason given; the L3 book links granite to low nutrients and yields.
notes.c: The reverse: these granite soils are low in nutrients, which limits yields.
notes.d: Correct: Gamay can crop heavily; poor granite soils keep yields down.

Q-L3-17-02.stem: According to the L3 book, which quality levels may be sold as Beaujolais Nouveau?

options.a: Beaujolais, Villages or any of the crus
options.b: Beaujolais or Beaujolais Villages
options.c: Only Beaujolais Villages from the north
options.d: Only wines from the ten Beaujolais crus

notes.a: The L3 book says the crus cannot be sold as Nouveau.
notes.b: Correct: the ten crus cannot be sold in this way.
notes.c: Beaujolais AOC qualifies too; the alluvial south is Nouveau's major source.
notes.d: The crus are excluded; Nouveau is Beaujolais or Villages quality.

Q-L3-18-01.stem: Why is Grenache usually bush-trained low to the ground in the Southern Rhône?

options.a: To shade the grapes so that they keep high acidity.
options.b: To raise yields on the region's flat, fertile soils.
options.c: To make machine harvesting easier on the flat land.
options.d: To shelter from the mistral and gain soil warmth.

notes.a: Not the reason given; the L3 book cites wind protection and soil warmth.
notes.b: Not the reason given; the L3 book cites wind protection and soil warmth.
notes.c: Bush vines hinder machines; the L3 book links wire training to mechanisation.
notes.d: Correct: per the L3 book; the mistral gains speed in the flatter south.

Q-L2-24-11.stem: Which of these grape varieties is NOT one of the three typically blended to make Champagne?

options.a: Pinot Noir
options.b: Chardonnay
options.c: Meunier
options.d: Chenin Blanc

notes.a: One of the three Champagne varieties.
notes.b: One of the three Champagne varieties.
notes.c: One of the three Champagne varieties, with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
notes.d: Correct: the book mentions it for some South African Cap Classique, not Champagne.

Q-L2-24-12.stem: Why is the Champagne region well suited to making base wines for sparkling wine?

options.a: Its warm climate gives very ripe grapes with high levels of sugar.
options.b: Its cool climate gives base wines with high alcohol and full body.
options.c: Its cool climate gives base wines low in alcohol and high in acidity.
options.d: Its cool climate gives grapes with low acidity and soft, ripe fruit.

notes.a: Sparkling base wines should be low in alcohol, so very ripe grapes are not wanted.
notes.b: Cool climates give modest sugar, so the base wine is low in alcohol.
notes.c: Correct: the book says this provides ideal conditions for the base wine.
notes.d: Cool climates retain acidity; the base wine should be high in acid.

Q-L2-24-14.stem: What does 'Vintage' on a bottle of Champagne indicate?

options.a: The wine was aged for a stated time on its lees.
options.b: The wine is a blend of the producer's best recent years.
options.c: The wine is made every year from the best grapes.
options.d: The grapes all come from a single exceptional year.

notes.a: Vintage refers to the harvest year, not lees time (though these wines do age long on lees).
notes.b: A blend of several vintages is non-vintage, the style of most Champagne.
notes.c: No: Vintage Champagne is made only in exceptional years (p. 113).
notes.d: Correct: best grapes of an exceptional year (p. 113); 'vintage' is the year the grapes were harvested (p. 38).

Q-L2-24-15.stem: A traditional-method sparkling wine shows pronounced apple, citrus and toasted-bread notes, with nuts and honey. Which is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: A high-volume non-vintage Cava
options.b: An inexpensive non-vintage Champagne
options.c: A very good non-vintage Champagne
options.d: A Vintage Champagne

notes.a: Simple, high-volume Cava has light apple and lemon with very subtle autolytic notes.
notes.b: These have apple and only light autolytic notes, after the 12-month legal minimum on lees.
notes.c: Apple, lemon, toast and biscuit, but the book links nuts and honey to Vintage bottle age.
notes.d: Correct: long lees ageing gives pronounced autolytic notes; extended bottle age after disgorgement adds nuts and honey.

Q-L2-24-16.stem: What is the legal minimum time that Champagne must spend ageing on its lees?

options.a: 24 months
options.b: 12 months
options.c: 5 years
options.d: 6 months

notes.a: Longer than the legal minimum; many better wines do age for longer.
notes.b: Correct: the least expensive Champagnes usually spend this legal minimum.
notes.c: Far longer than the legal minimum, though top wines may age this long.
notes.d: Too short; the book gives a legal minimum of 12 months.

Q-L2-24-19.stem: Which pair of sparkling wines is exempt from having to state its PDO status on the label?

options.a: Cava and Asti
options.b: Champagne and Cava
options.c: Champagne and Prosecco
options.d: Prosecco and Asti

notes.a: Cava is exempt, but the book does not name Asti.
notes.b: Correct: the book names Champagne as exempt and Cava as another notable exemption.
notes.c: Champagne is exempt, but the book does not name Prosecco.
notes.d: Neither is named as exempt in the book.

Q-L2-24-20.stem: Compared with Champagne, how do the best traditional-method wines from South Africa, the USA, Australia and New Zealand typically differ?

options.a: Stronger autolytic notes, from a longer legal lees time.
options.b: Higher acidity, from a much cooler growing season.
options.c: Slightly riper fruit, from extra sunlight and warmth.
options.d: Lower alcohol, from grapes picked at lower sugar levels.

notes.a: No lees rule is given for them; the book's difference is riper fruit.
notes.b: Champagne is the cooler region; these wines show riper fruit.
notes.c: Correct: per the book; the best come from the coolest regions and are intense with a long finish.
notes.d: Not the book's comparison; extra warmth gives riper fruit.

Q-L2-24-21.stem: Which statement about South African Cap Classique is correct?

options.a: It is tank-method wine, made mainly from Moscato for sweetness.
options.b: It is traditional-method wine, made only from Champagne grapes.
options.c: It is traditional-method wine, sometimes made from Chenin Blanc.
options.d: It is tank-method wine, made mainly from Pinotage for colour.

notes.a: Cap Classique signifies the traditional method; sweet Moscato suggests the Asti method.
notes.b: Too narrow: other varieties such as Chenin Blanc may also be used.
notes.c: Correct: sometimes the Champagne grapes are used, other times varieties such as Chenin Blanc.
notes.d: Cap Classique signifies the traditional method (second fermentation in bottle).

Q-L3-24-01.stem: How does the meaning of 'Vintage' on a Champagne label compare with its meaning in some other sparkling wine regions?

options.a: Champagne: one year only; some regions allow a little from other years.
options.b: Both require 100% from one year, so the term means the same everywhere.
options.c: Neither has a rule: 'Vintage' simply means the best wine of the house.
options.d: Champagne allows a little from other years; some regions require one only.

notes.a: Correct: as stated on L3 p. 178.
notes.b: L3 says some other appellations allow a small percentage of other years.
notes.c: That is closer to Prestige Cuvée, which L3 says is not a labelling term.
notes.d: Reversed: in Champagne the wine must come from a single year.

Q-L3-24-02.stem: Why does Meunier predominate in Champagne's Vallée de la Marne?

options.a: It buds late, so it avoids the area's frequent spring frosts.
options.b: It gives the most body, the backbone of most Champagne blends.
options.c: It thrives on chalk, which is found only in this sub-region.
options.d: It buds early, so it makes the most of a short season.

notes.a: Correct: L3 p. 180; it also gives fruity flavours, useful for wines made to drink young.
notes.b: That is Pinot Noir's role (Montagne de Reims, Côte des Bar).
notes.c: Chalk dominates the whole region; Chardonnay leads in the Côte des Blancs.
notes.d: The reverse: L3 says it buds LATE, avoiding spring frosts.

Q-L2-01-21.stem: What are the two important features of a tasting glass such as the ISO glass, and why do they matter?

options.a: A rounded bowl to aid swirling, and inward walls to trap aromas.
options.b: A long stem to hold, and a wide rim to let aromas escape.
options.c: A thick base for stability, and a large bowl for a big sample.
options.d: Thin, light glass, and straight walls so the wine can breathe.

notes.a: Correct: per the book (p. 7); other good tasting glasses share both features.
notes.b: The walls slope inward to capture aromas at the top, not release them.
notes.c: Good tasting glasses are small enough for a tasting sample.
notes.d: The book's features are a rounded bowl and inward-sloping walls.

Q-L2-01-01.stem: On the L2 SAT, what can a 'hazy' appearance indicate about a wine?

options.a: That it has been aged for many years in bottle.
options.b: That it is high in alcohol and full in body.
options.c: That it has been matured in new oak barrels.
options.d: A possible fault, or that it was not clarified.

notes.a: Age shows in the colour (e.g. garnet, tawny), not clarity; haze is suspended particles.
notes.b: Alcohol and body are judged on the palate; haze is caused by suspended particles.
notes.c: Oak shows as secondary aromas such as vanilla and smoke, not as haze.
notes.d: Correct: the book gives both; the precise fault is normally found on the nose and palate.

Q-L2-01-02.stem: Tilted at 45°, a white wine shows a broad watery rim and a colour with a hint of orange. How should its appearance be described on the L2 SAT?

options.a: Pale lemon
options.b: Pale amber
options.c: Deep gold
options.d: Pale gold

notes.a: Lemon has no hint of orange or brown; that hint makes it gold.
notes.b: Amber is for a very noticeable level of browning, not just a hint.
notes.c: Deep means the pigment reaches almost to the rim; a broad watery rim means pale.
notes.d: Correct: a broad watery rim = pale; a hint of orange or brown = gold.

Q-L2-01-03.stem: A red wine shows a noticeable orange or brown colour but is still more red than brown. Which L2 SAT colour term fits?

options.a: Ruby
options.b: Tawny
options.c: Brown
options.d: Garnet

notes.a: Ruby is the most common red colour, without garnet's noticeable orange or brown.
notes.b: Tawny is for a wine that is more brown than red.
notes.c: Brown is only for wines where no redness remains.
notes.d: Correct: noticeable orange/brown, but still more red than brown.

Q-L2-01-04.stem: Which L2 SAT term describes a pink rosé that shows a hint of orange?

options.a: Pink-orange
options.b: Orange
options.c: Onion-skin
options.d: Salmon

notes.a: Correct: the L2 rosé scale is pink - pink-orange - orange.
notes.b: Orange is for a rosé where orange is the dominant colour; very rare.
notes.c: Not an SAT term; the L2 rosé scale is pink - pink-orange - orange.
notes.d: Not on the L2 SAT: it is the 2016 L3 term. For the L2 exam say pink-orange.

Q-L2-01-12.stem: On the L2 SAT, which sweetness term describes a wine with a distinct presence of sugar that is generally not sweet enough to partner most desserts?

options.a: Sweet
options.b: Medium-sweet
options.c: Off-dry
options.d: Medium

notes.a: Sweet is where sugar is the prominent feature, e.g. Sauternes and Port.
notes.b: Not an L2 term: the L2 scale is dry - off-dry - medium - sweet.
notes.c: Off-dry is only a tiny amount of detectable sugar.
notes.d: Correct: as defined in the book.

Q-L2-01-05.stem: A taster finds honey, caramel and coffee on the nose. When should this be treated as a likely sign of a fault?

options.a: Only when the aromas are of pronounced intensity.
options.b: When these are not the expected style of the wine.
options.c: Only when the wine also looks hazy in the glass.
options.d: Whenever they appear, whatever the wine's style or age.

notes.a: Intensity is a separate line; the issue is whether the aromas fit the style.
notes.b: Correct: the book flags them as a likely fault only when that is not the expected style.
notes.c: Haze is a separate clue; the nose alone can signal a fault.
notes.d: No: deliberately oxidised wines list coffee and caramel among their aromas.

Q-L2-01-06.stem: Even after swirling, a red wine's aromas are faint and hard to detect, but they include leather, earth and mushroom. How should the nose be recorded?

options.a: Light intensity, with secondary aromas
options.b: Light intensity, with tertiary aromas
options.c: Medium intensity, with primary aromas
options.d: Pronounced intensity, with tertiary aromas

notes.a: Secondary aromas come from winemaking (yeast, MLF, oak); these come from maturation.
notes.b: Correct: faint even after swirling = light; leather, earth, mushroom are red-wine tertiary aromas.
notes.c: Faint after swirling is light, and these are not grape or fermentation aromas.
notes.d: Confuses age with strength: tertiary aromas do not make a nose pronounced.

Q-L2-01-07.stem: A white wine smells of butter and cream. Which winemaking process is the MOST LIKELY source of these aromas?

options.a: Maturation in new oak
options.b: Long ageing in bottle
options.c: Autolysis of dead yeast
options.d: Malolactic conversion

notes.a: Oak gives vanilla, cloves, coconut, cedar, smoke and the like, not butter or cream.
notes.b: Bottle ageing gives tertiary aromas such as petrol, honey and mushroom.
notes.c: Autolysis gives biscuit, bread and toasted-bread aromas.
notes.d: Correct: the Wine-Lexicon lists butter, cheese and cream under malolactic conversion (secondary).

Q-L2-01-08.stem: Which of these aromas is NOT classed as tertiary in the L2 Wine-Lexicon?

options.a: Forest floor
options.b: Orange marmalade
options.c: Hazelnut
options.d: Toasted bread

notes.a: This IS tertiary: listed for red wines.
notes.b: This IS tertiary: listed for white wines.
notes.c: This IS tertiary: listed for white wines and for deliberately oxidised wines.
notes.d: Correct: secondary, from yeast (lees, autolysis), e.g. in sparkling wines.

Q-L2-01-09.stem: Which tertiary aromas does the book link with ageing protected from oxygen, such as a long period in bottle?

options.a: Petrol, honey and mushroom
options.b: Biscuit, pastry and toasted bread
options.c: Vanilla, smoke and cloves
options.d: Coffee and caramel

notes.a: Correct: as given in the book. In both kinds of ageing, fruit becomes less fresh.
notes.b: These are secondary aromas from autolysis in sparkling wines.
notes.c: These are secondary aromas from oak.
notes.d: These come from oxidative ageing, e.g. a long period in oak.

Q-L2-01-11.stem: In the L2 Wine-Lexicon, what are primary aromas and flavours?

options.a: Those of maturation in barrel or bottle
options.b: Those of the grape alone, before it is fermented
options.c: Those of post-fermentation winemaking
options.d: Those of the grape and alcoholic fermentation

notes.a: That is tertiary, e.g. leather, petrol, honey, caramel.
notes.b: Too narrow: aromas created during fermentation are also primary.
notes.c: That is secondary: yeast (lees, autolysis, flor), MLF and oak.
notes.d: Correct: e.g. the fruit, floral, herbaceous, herbal and spice clusters.

Q-L2-01-13.stem: Sugar can mask acidity, and alcohol can burn like acidity. What does the book give as the reliable guide to a wine's acidity?

options.a: How sweet the wine tastes on the tongue
options.b: How much and how long the mouth waters
options.c: How dry and rough the gums feel
options.d: How hot the wine feels after spitting

notes.a: Sugar masks acidity, so sweetness is no guide to it.
notes.b: Correct: the mouth-watering effect remains whatever the sugar level.
notes.c: Drying and roughness come from tannin binding to saliva.
notes.d: That burning sensation is alcohol, which can be mistaken for acidity.

Q-L2-01-14.stem: Which sensation on the palate is caused mainly by tannin?

options.a: The mouth watering for a long time
options.b: A hot, burning feeling after swallowing
options.c: The mouth drying up and feeling rough
options.d: A taste of sugar on the tongue

notes.a: That is acidity.
notes.b: That is high alcohol triggering pain receptors.
notes.c: Correct: tannins bind to saliva; they can also taste bitter.
notes.d: That is sweetness.

Q-L2-01-15.stem: Which of these would be described as HIGH in alcohol on the L2 SAT?

options.a: A fortified wine at 16% abv
options.b: A fortified wine at 17% abv
options.c: A still wine at 13.5% abv
options.d: A still wine at 14% abv

notes.a: Low: the fortified low band is 15-16.4% abv.
notes.b: Medium: the fortified medium band is 16.5-18.4% abv.
notes.c: Medium: the still-wine medium band is 11-13.9% abv.
notes.d: Correct: for still wines, high is 14% abv and above.

Q-L2-01-16.stem: On the L2 SAT, what creates a wine's body?

options.a: Sugar, acidity, tannin and alcohol together
options.b: The intensity of the fruit flavours
options.c: Alcohol alone, so body simply mirrors abv
options.d: Acidity, with higher acid giving a fuller body

notes.a: Correct: body is not a single component; alcohol is the main factor for most wines.
notes.b: Body is felt by touch, not taste; flavour intensity is a separate line.
notes.c: Alcohol is the main factor, but sugar, acidity and tannin also play a part.
notes.d: Reversed: high acidity makes a wine feel lighter in body.

Q-L2-01-17.stem: According to the book, why might a wine's flavour intensity on the palate differ from its aroma intensity on the nose?

options.a: Alcohol in the mouth hides all spice characteristics
options.b: Floral aromas become much stronger on the palate
options.c: Tannin coats the tongue and masks the fruit flavours
options.d: Warming in the mouth can bring out some flavours

notes.a: Reversed: some spice characteristics tend to be MORE prominent on the palate.
notes.b: Reversed: floral characteristics are sometimes LESS prominent on the palate.
notes.c: Not the book's reason; it cites the wine warming in the mouth.
notes.d: Correct: e.g. some spice is more prominent on the palate; floral can be less so.

Q-L2-01-18.stem: After spitting, a wine's fruit flavours vanish quickly but a bitter taste lingers for a long time. How should its finish be described?

options.a: Short
options.b: Pronounced
options.c: Medium
options.d: Long

notes.a: Correct: only desirable sensations count; the lingering bitterness is a bitter aftertaste.
notes.b: Pronounced is an intensity term; the finish scale is short - medium - long.
notes.c: The pleasant flavours disappear quickly, so the finish is short.
notes.d: Bitterness is not counted, so its long linger does not make the finish long.

Q-L2-01-19.stem: A wine is well balanced, with a range of flavours of medium intensity, but has a short finish. Which quality level fits BEST?

options.a: Good
options.b: Very good
options.c: Acceptable
options.d: Outstanding

notes.a: Good is positive on two criteria and short on two.
notes.b: Correct: positive on three criteria, short on one (length). This is the book's own example.
notes.c: Acceptable is positive on only one criterion and short on three.
notes.d: Outstanding must show positively on all four criteria.

Q-L2-01-20.stem: Which statement about assessing quality is correct, according to the L2 book?

options.a: A long-lingering bitter aftertaste counts as a long finish.
options.b: A wine out of balance is rarely more than acceptable.
options.c: The more intense a wine's flavours, the higher its quality.
options.d: Every premium wine must show a complex range of flavours.

notes.a: Only desirable sensations count towards length.
notes.b: Correct: stated under Balance.
notes.c: Only up to a point: beyond a certain level, more intensity is not necessarily better.
notes.d: No: some, e.g. ice wines, are great through purity and definition.

Q-L2-01-10.stem: Which of these descriptors is NOT in the 'Herbal' cluster of the L2 Wine-Lexicon?

options.a: Eucalyptus
options.b: Mint
options.c: Dill
options.d: Tomato leaf

notes.a: This IS herbal: listed with mint, fennel, dill and dried herbs.
notes.b: This IS herbal: listed with eucalyptus, fennel, dill and dried herbs.
notes.c: This IS herbal: listed with eucalyptus, mint, fennel and dried herbs.
notes.d: Correct: it is in the separate 'Herbaceous' cluster, with green bell pepper, grass and asparagus.

Q-L2-02-02.stem: A dry, tannic red wine is served with a sweet dessert. How is the wine MOST LIKELY to taste?

options.a: More drying and bitter, more acidic and less fruity
options.b: Softer, sweeter and fruitier than on its own
options.c: Fuller-bodied, with noticeably softer tannins
options.d: Unchanged, because sweet food does not affect tannin at all

notes.a: Correct: sweetness in food makes wine taste 'harder'.
notes.b: That is the effect of acid (and partly salt) in food.
notes.c: That is the effect of salty food.
notes.d: Sweet food makes a wine seem more drying and bitter, so tannin is affected.

Q-L2-02-04.stem: Which two components in food tend to make a wine taste 'softer'?

options.a: Salt and acid
options.b: Sweetness and umami
options.c: Salt and umami
options.d: Acid and sweetness

notes.a: Correct: they make wine less drying, bitter and acidic, and sweeter and fruitier.
notes.b: These two make wine taste 'harder'.
notes.c: Salt softens, but umami hardens.
notes.d: Acid softens, but sweetness hardens.

Q-L2-02-13.stem: Which statement about food and wine interactions is correct, according to the book?

options.a: Food usually affects the wine more than the reverse.
options.b: Food's impact on wine is usually more positive than negative.
options.c: Mouth-coating foods such as chocolate sharpen the sense of taste.
options.d: Wine usually affects the food more than the reverse.

notes.a: Correct: and the impact is more likely to be negative than positive.
notes.b: The book says the impact is more likely to be negative.
notes.c: Chocolate and thick creamy dishes coat the mouth and can impair taste.
notes.d: Reversed: food generally has more impact on the wine.

Q-L2-02-14.stem: Why might a food and wine pairing that seems perfect to one person seem ordinary to another?

options.a: The basic food and wine interactions are essentially random.
options.b: Some tasters have not been trained in the SAT.
options.c: People differ in their sensitivities and preferences.
options.d: Wine served too cold hides the effects of food.

notes.a: No: the book sets out clear basic interactions; it is people who vary.
notes.b: Not the book's reason; it cites individual sensitivities and preferences.
notes.c: Correct: pairings should consider the individual as well as the basic interactions.
notes.d: Not the book's reason; it cites individual sensitivities and preferences.

Q-L2-02-01.stem: How will a dish high in umami usually make a wine taste?

options.a: Fuller-bodied and fruitier, with noticeably softer tannins.
options.b: Less bitter and drying, with softer and rounder acidity.
options.c: Sweeter, fruitier and less acidic than on its own.
options.d: More drying and bitter, more acidic, less sweet and fruity.

notes.a: That is the effect of salt.
notes.b: That is the softening effect of salt or acid in food.
notes.c: That is the effect of acid in food (and partly salt).
notes.d: Correct: umami (like sweetness) makes wine taste 'harder'.

Q-L2-02-03.stem: What general rule does the book give for choosing a wine to drink with a sweet dish?

options.a: Choose a wine slightly less sweet than the dish.
options.b: Choose a wine that is sweeter than the dish.
options.c: Choose a high-tannin red to balance the sugar.
options.d: Choose a dry wine with high acid to cut the sugar.

notes.a: The rule is a wine with a HIGHER level of sweetness than the dish.
notes.b: Correct: otherwise a dry wine seems less fruity and unpleasantly acidic.
notes.c: Sweetness makes wine more drying and bitter, so the tannin is emphasised.
notes.d: Sweet food makes a dry wine taste unpleasantly acidic and less fruity.

Q-L2-02-05.stem: Which of these foods does the book give as an example of a food with umami taste?

options.a: Fresh chilli
options.b: Fresh lemon
options.c: Aged cheese
options.d: Clear honey

notes.a: Chilli adds heat, not umami.
notes.b: Lemon is acidic, a 'softening' component.
notes.c: Correct: listed with cooked or dried mushrooms, air-dried meats and miso.
notes.d: Honey is sweet, the other 'hardening' component.

Q-L2-02-06.stem: Why can umami be difficult to isolate in food, according to the book?

options.a: It is the same taste as salt, so the two are confused.
options.b: It disappears when food is cooked, so it is rarely tasted.
options.c: It usually comes with tastes such as salt that offset it.
options.d: It is only found in foods that also contain a lot of sugar.

notes.a: No: the book calls umami a taste distinct from the other primary tastes.
notes.b: No: cooked mushrooms are one of the book's umami examples.
notes.c: Correct: the salt balances umami's negative effects on wine.
notes.d: No: the examples (mushrooms, air-dried meats, aged cheeses, miso) are not sugary.

Q-L2-02-07.stem: Salty food tends to change how a wine tastes. Which of these is NOT one of those effects?

options.a: The wine seems more fruity.
options.b: Tannins in red wine seem softer.
options.c: The wine seems more acidic.
options.d: The wine seems fuller in body.

notes.a: This IS an effect of salt.
notes.b: This IS an effect: salt softens the tannin in red wines.
notes.c: Correct: salt makes a wine seem LESS acidic.
notes.d: This IS an effect: the book's table says 'more body'.

Q-L2-02-08.stem: A very high-acid white wine is paired with a dish dressed with lemon juice. How is the wine MOST LIKELY to taste?

options.a: Hotter and more alcoholic
options.b: Less acidic and more fruity
options.c: More bitter and more drying
options.d: More acidic and much less fruity

notes.a: That is the effect of chilli heat.
notes.b: Correct: acid in food can balance a very high-acid wine and enhance its fruit.
notes.c: Acid in food makes wine LESS drying and bitter.
notes.d: That is the effect of sweet or umami food.

Q-L2-02-09.stem: A dish high in acidity is served with a wine that is LOW in acidity. According to the book, how may the wine seem?

options.a: Higher in alcohol
options.b: Less fruity than on its own
options.c: More drying and tannic
options.d: Sweeter and fruitier

notes.a: That is the effect of chilli heat.
notes.b: Correct: the book's exception: high-acid food can make a low-acid wine seem less fruity.
notes.c: Acid in food makes wine less drying and bitter.
notes.d: That is the usual effect with a wine of very high acidity, not low.

Q-L2-02-10.stem: Which of these wines would be LEAST suitable for a guest eating a dish with strong chilli heat?

options.a: A light rosé at 12% abv
options.b: A full-bodied red at 15% abv
options.c: An off-dry white at 11% abv
options.d: A light-bodied white at 11.5% abv

notes.a: Moderate alcohol, so chilli has less effect than in a 15% wine.
notes.b: Correct: chilli effects are greater in high-alcohol wines, and alcohol increases the chilli burn.
notes.c: Lower alcohol than 15%, so chilli heat has less effect.
notes.d: Lower alcohol than 15%, so chilli heat has less effect.

Q-L2-02-11.stem: Why do many people enjoy acidic wines with fatty or oily foods?

options.a: Acidic wines add body to otherwise light dishes.
options.b: Fat makes the wine seem more acidic and more refreshing.
options.c: Acid seems to cut through the fat and cleanse the palate.
options.d: Fat softens the tannins and adds fruit to the wine.

notes.a: Not in the book; it describes the acid 'cutting through' the fattiness.
notes.b: Reversed: fatty or oily food makes wine seem LESS acidic.
notes.c: Correct: though the book notes this effect is very subjective.
notes.d: Softer tannin and more fruit are effects of salt.

Q-L2-02-12.stem: A delicate, lightly flavoured white wine is served with a very highly flavoured dish. What is the MOST LIKELY result?

options.a: The wine's flavours seem more intense and vivid.
options.b: The wine's alcohol seems much hotter.
options.c: The food's flavours seem lighter.
options.d: The wine is overwhelmed by the food's flavours.

notes.a: A highly flavoured dish overwhelms a lighter wine; it does not intensify it.
notes.b: That is the effect of chilli heat.
notes.c: The reverse: the food's flavours overpower the wine.
notes.d: Correct: the book advises matching flavour intensities so one does not overpower the other.

Q-L2-03-02.stem: Why should a bottle sealed with a cork be stored on its side?

options.a: It reduces the risk of cork taint (TCA) developing.
options.b: It protects the wine from strong light and heat.
options.c: It lets any deposit settle along the length of the bottle.
options.d: It keeps the cork moist so that it does not let air in.

notes.a: TCA comes mainly from contaminated cork; storage position is about keeping the cork moist.
notes.b: Light and heat are avoided by where you store wine, not by its position.
notes.c: Not the book's reason; it is about keeping the cork moist.
notes.d: Correct: a dried-out cork can let in air, which oxidises the wine and dulls its fruit.

Q-L2-03-03.stem: Which of these storage conditions is MOST LIKELY to damage wine kept for the long term?

options.a: A cool, dark cellar at a constant temperature
options.b: Screwcapped bottles stored standing upright
options.c: Cork-sealed bottles stored lying down on their side
options.d: A sunny window where the temperature swings daily

notes.a: This is the ideal: cool, constant and away from light.
notes.b: Fine: screwcapped wines can be stored standing up.
notes.c: Good practice: it keeps the cork moist.
notes.d: Correct: strong sunshine and big temperature changes can both damage wine.

Q-L2-03-18.stem: A young white has spent months in a hot, brightly lit shop window. It is not browned, but has lost its freshness and fruit. Which fault is MOST LIKELY?

options.a: Failure of closure
options.b: Cork taint (TCA)
options.c: Heat damage
options.d: Lack of clarification

notes.a: Oxidation would show as a browner colour, with honey, caramel or coffee.
notes.b: TCA gives damp cardboard aromas, mainly from contaminated cork.
notes.c: Correct: too hot, direct sunlight or bright artificial light -> loses freshness and fruit.
notes.d: Not clarifying shows as haze, not loss of fruit; and the cause here is heat.

Q-L2-03-04.stem: Which of these wines should NOT be served well chilled?

options.a: An oaked Chardonnay
options.b: A sweet Sauternes
options.c: A non-vintage Champagne
options.d: A sweet Tokaji Aszú

notes.a: Correct: full-bodied whites are served lightly chilled, 10-13°C.
notes.b: Sweet wines: well chilled, 6-8°C.
notes.c: Sparkling wines: well chilled, 6-10°C.
notes.d: Sweet wines: well chilled, 6-8°C.

Q-L2-03-06.stem: A guest prefers their red wine cooler than the recommended temperature. What does the book advise the host to do?

options.a: Offer a white wine instead of the red.
options.b: Serve it cooler, as the guest prefers.
options.c: Serve it at the recommended temperature.
options.d: Explain that cool red wine is a fault.

notes.a: Not the book's advice; it says to respect the guest's preference.
notes.b: Correct: recommended temperatures should not override personal preference.
notes.c: The book says the guidance should not override a guest's preference.
notes.d: Temperature preference is not a fault; the book says respect it.

Q-L2-03-08.stem: How should an ice bucket be prepared to keep a bottle of white wine chilled?

options.a: Fill it with cold water only, no ice.
options.b: Fill it with ice and cold water.
options.c: Fill it with ice only, and no water.
options.d: Fill it with ice and a little warm water.

notes.a: The book says to use cold water AS WELL AS ice.
notes.b: Correct: the book says a bucket filled only with ice will not work as efficiently.
notes.c: Ice alone works less efficiently; add cold water as well.
notes.d: The book says COLD water as well as ice; warm water would warm the wine.

Q-L2-03-09.stem: A bottle of red wine is too cold to serve. What does the book advise?

options.a: Put it in the serving room to warm naturally.
options.b: Stand it beside a radiator to warm it quickly.
options.c: Stand it in a bowl of hot water for a few minutes.
options.d: Leave it in a sunny window for a short while.

notes.a: Correct: let the temperature rise naturally in the room.
notes.b: The book warns against heating wine this way; it can damage the flavours.
notes.c: This heats the wine, which the book says can damage its flavours.
notes.d: Sunshine (its light and heat) can make a wine lose its fruit character.

Q-L2-03-10.stem: What feature do all of the best wine glasses share, and why?

options.a: The bowl narrows at the rim, concentrating the aromas.
options.b: The glass is tinted, to hide any slight haze.
options.c: The bowl widens at the rim, releasing more aroma.
options.d: The bowl is thick-walled, to keep the wine cool for longer.

notes.a: Correct: aromas are concentrated inside the glass and better appreciated.
notes.b: You should be able to check appearance: haze can signal a fault.
notes.c: Reversed: the bowl narrows at the rim to concentrate the aromas.
notes.d: Not in the book; the shared feature is a bowl that narrows at the rim.

Q-L2-03-15.stem: How do inert gas systems help to keep an opened bottle of wine fresh?

options.a: The gas reacts with the wine to preserve its fruit.
options.b: A pump removes the air from inside the bottle.
options.c: The gas chills the wine to slow its reaction with air.
options.d: Gases such as argon keep air away from the wine.

notes.a: 'Inert' means they do NOT react with the wine.
notes.b: That is how vacuum systems work.
notes.c: Not how they work; chilling is what the fridge does.
notes.d: Correct: inert gases (nitrogen, argon) do not react with the wine and stop it contacting air.

Q-L2-03-16.stem: Checking a wine before service, you find aromas of damp cardboard and muted, less fresh fruit. Which fault is MOST LIKELY?

options.a: Heat damage
options.b: Failure of closure
options.c: Cork taint (TCA)
options.d: A heavy deposit

notes.a: Heat damage dulls freshness and fruit, but damp cardboard points to TCA.
notes.b: Oxidation shows as a browner colour with honey, caramel or coffee.
notes.c: Correct: TCA, mainly from contaminated cork, gives damp cardboard and muted fruit.
notes.d: A deposit is natural in some aged reds and is not a fault.

Q-L2-03-19.stem: How does a vacuum system help to keep an opened bottle of still wine fresh?

options.a: An inert gas forms a layer over the wine.
options.b: Sulfur dioxide is added through the closure.
options.c: A pump removes the air from inside the bottle.
options.d: The bottle is chilled to stop all oxidation.

notes.a: That is an inert gas system (e.g. nitrogen, argon).
notes.b: Not a method the book describes for keeping wine fresh.
notes.c: Correct: per the book (p. 20); less air means the wine goes stale more slowly.
notes.d: A fridge slows the changes but does not stop them; this is not a vacuum system.

Q-L2-03-20.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the checks the book recommends before serving a wine?

options.a: Check that the wine is clear and not hazy.
options.b: Check that the colour is deep rather than pale.
options.c: Check that there are no bits floating in the wine.
options.d: Check that there are no aromas of wet cardboard or vinegar.

notes.a: A check: a hazy wine may be faulty.
notes.b: Correct: not a check; colour depth varies with style and is not a sign of a fault.
notes.c: A check given in the book.
notes.d: A check: these aromas suggest a faulty wine.

Q-L2-03-01.stem: When opening a bottle of sparkling wine, what is the correct technique once the cage is loosened?

options.a: Hold the bottle upright and ease the cork out with a waiter's friend.
options.b: Hold the cork, tilt the bottle and turn the bottle, not the cork.
options.c: Remove the cage fully, then let the gas pressure push the cork out.
options.d: Hold the bottle still and steadily twist the cork until it comes free.

notes.a: Corkscrews are for still wines; sparkling bottles are held at an angle.
notes.b: Correct: releases the pressure with a quiet 'phut'.
notes.c: Dangerous: from loosening the cage the cork must stay in your hand.
notes.d: The book says hold the cork and turn the bottle.

Q-L2-03-11.stem: Which sequence gives the correct order for opening a bottle of still wine sealed with a cork?

options.a: Remove capsule top, clean neck, draw cork, wipe neck
options.b: Draw cork, remove capsule top, clean neck, wipe neck
options.c: Remove capsule top, draw cork, clean neck, wipe neck
options.d: Clean neck, remove capsule top, draw cork, wipe neck

notes.a: Correct: cut the capsule, clean the neck, draw the cork, then wipe inside and out.
notes.b: The capsule top is removed first, before the corkscrew goes in.
notes.c: The neck is cleaned BEFORE the cork is drawn, then wiped again after.
notes.d: The capsule top comes off first; then the neck is cleaned.

Q-L2-03-12.stem: Why must the cork of a sparkling wine be kept covered by hand from the moment the wire cage is loosened?

options.a: Warmth from the hand helps the cork come out smoothly.
options.b: The pressure can force the cork out and injure someone.
options.c: It keeps the cork moist so that it does not crumble.
options.d: It stops the wine losing its bubbles before it is poured.

notes.a: No: it is about controlling the pressure; chilling, not warmth, reduces it.
notes.b: Correct: even when the wine is chilled, the cork can easily fly out.
notes.c: Keeping the cork moist is why still wines are stored on their side.
notes.d: Not the reason given; the risk is the cork flying out.

Q-L2-03-13.stem: According to the L2 book, which wines need to be decanted?

options.a: Wines that smell of damp cardboard
options.b: All sparkling wines before serving
options.c: Wines with a heavy natural deposit
options.d: Wines that look hazy in the glass

notes.a: That is cork taint (TCA), a fault; the book decants wines with a heavy deposit.
notes.b: Not in the book; it decants wines with a heavy deposit.
notes.c: Correct: the deposit is natural, formed during bottle ageing of some red wines.
notes.d: Haze may indicate a fault; the book decants wines with a heavy deposit.

Q-L2-03-14.stem: When decanting, how do you know when to stop pouring?

options.a: When the deposit shows near the neck.
options.b: When the wine in the decanter starts to look hazy.
options.c: When the bottle is completely empty.
options.d: When half of the wine has been poured.

notes.a: Correct: pour in front of a light and stop when the deposit can be seen near the neck.
notes.b: Too late: the aim is to stop before any deposit enters the decanter.
notes.c: That would pour the deposit into the decanter.
notes.d: No set amount: you watch for the deposit against a light.

Q-L2-03-17.stem: Which of these is NOT a sign of a wine oxidised by failure of its closure?

options.a: Aromas of honey, caramel or coffee
options.b: A lack of freshness and fruit
options.c: Aromas of damp cardboard
options.d: A browner colour than expected

notes.a: This IS a sign (unless it is an oxidative style or a very old wine).
notes.b: This IS a sign of oxidation.
notes.c: Correct: damp cardboard is cork taint (TCA).
notes.d: This IS a sign: oxidised wines look browner than they should.

Q-L2-04-04.stem: Which part of the grape gives a red wine its colour?

options.a: The skins of black grapes
options.b: The pulp of black grapes
options.c: The seeds of black grapes
options.d: The stems of black grapes

notes.a: Correct: the skin holds colour, tannins and flavours; colour and tannin are much higher in black grapes.
notes.b: With a tiny number of exceptions, the pulp of white and black grapes has the same pale colour.
notes.c: Seeds contain high levels of tannin, which can taste bitter, but they do not colour the wine.
notes.d: Stems contain high levels of tannin, not the colour that red wine takes from the grape.

Q-L2-04-05.stem: Which part or parts of the grape contain high levels of tannins that can make a wine taste very bitter if handled roughly in winemaking?

options.a: The area just below the skin
options.b: The pulp
options.c: The skins of white grapes
options.d: The seeds and stems

notes.a: The book says this area holds high levels of flavour, not the bitter tannins in question.
notes.b: The pulp is mainly water and sugar, with acids and flavours; the book gives it no tannin.
notes.c: Tannin levels are much higher in black grapes; the bitterness warning is for seeds and stems.
notes.d: Correct: the book says these parts can make a wine taste very bitter if handled roughly in winemaking.

Q-L2-04-06.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the five things a vine needs in order to grow and thrive?

options.a: Warmth
options.b: Nutrients
options.c: Carbon dioxide
options.d: Oxygen

notes.a: Needed: without enough heat a vine cannot grow, which is why it is dormant in winter.
notes.b: Needed in small amounts, taken up by the roots, to grow healthy shoots, leaves and roots.
notes.c: Needed: it is taken in by the leaves and used in photosynthesis to make sugars.
notes.d: Correct: not on the list. The five needs are warmth, sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and nutrients.

Q-L2-04-07.stem: Which sequence shows the stages of grape formation and ripening in the correct order?

options.a: Flowering, fruit set, véraison, ripening
options.b: Flowering, véraison, fruit set, ripening
options.c: Véraison, flowering, fruit set, ripening
options.d: Fruit set, flowering, véraison, ripening

notes.a: Correct: flowers are pollinated, become small hard green grapes, then start ripening at véraison.
notes.b: Véraison comes after fruit set, in mid-summer, once the grapes are big enough.
notes.c: Véraison marks the start of ripening, so it cannot come before flowering.
notes.d: Fruit set follows flowering: once pollinated, the flower swells and becomes a grape.

Q-L2-04-08.stem: Which changes take place in a grape as it ripens?

options.a: Acidity falls, sugar rises and black-grape tannins ripen.
options.b: Acidity falls, sugar rises and herbaceous flavours increase.
options.c: Acidity rises, sugar falls and black-grape tannins ripen.
options.d: Acidity falls, sugar falls and the grapes become harder.

notes.a: Correct: grapes also swell with water and soften. Unripe tannins can taste bitter.
notes.b: Herbaceous flavours DECREASE as the signature flavours develop.
notes.c: Reversed: unripe grapes start with very high acid and hardly any sugar.
notes.d: Sugar rises, and the grapes become soft and fleshy as they swell with water.

Q-L2-04-09.stem: Which statement about how grape aromas and flavours change during ripening is correct?

options.a: Some white grapes move from green fruit towards tropical fruit.
options.b: Some white grapes move from tropical fruit towards green fruit.
options.c: Black grapes move from cooked fruit towards fresh fruit.
options.d: Black grapes develop more herbaceous flavours as they ripen.

notes.a: Correct: green fruit, then stone fruit, then tropical fruit as ripeness increases.
notes.b: Reversed: green fruit is the less-ripe end of the scale.
notes.c: Reversed: black grapes go from fresh fruit to cooked fruit as they ripen.
notes.d: Herbaceous flavours decrease in all grapes as they ripen.

Q-L2-04-10.stem: Grapes are left on the vine long after the normal harvest, and the weather stays dry and warm. After a long period, what happens to them?

options.a: Water evaporates, concentrating sugar and acid; dried-fruit aromas develop.
options.b: Sugar falls and acidity rises, giving fresher, more herbaceous flavours.
options.c: A fungus pierces the skins, concentrating sugars, acids and flavours.
options.d: The water freezes and is left behind as ice when the grapes are pressed.

notes.a: Correct: such grapes can be so sweet that they are commonly used for sweet wines.
notes.b: The reverse: sugars concentrate and dried-fruit aromas develop.
notes.c: That is botrytis/noble rot, which also needs damp, misty mornings.
notes.d: That is how frozen grapes for icewine are concentrated.

Q-L2-04-13.stem: How is the concentrated juice for an Icewine/Eiswein obtained?

options.a: Frozen grapes are allowed to thaw, then pressed for maximum juice.
options.b: Grapes are left to turn into raisins on the vine, then pressed.
options.c: Frozen grapes are pressed before they thaw, leaving the ice behind.
options.d: Grapes with noble rot are left on the vine and pressed in winter.

notes.a: They are pressed BEFORE they thaw, so the ice can be separated out.
notes.b: That is extra ripening; icewine grapes are frozen, not raisined.
notes.c: Correct: ice crystals and skins are separated from a little concentrated liquid.
notes.d: Icewine uses HEALTHY grapes, left on the vine into winter until frozen.

Q-L2-04-17.stem: Two vineyards lie at the same latitude, but one is much higher. Compared with the lower site, the higher site's grapes are MOST LIKELY to have:

options.a: more sugar, because the cooler air speeds up ripening.
options.b: higher acidity, because the cooler climate slows ripening.
options.c: lower acidity, because the higher site gets more heat.
options.d: riper flavours, because mountains keep autumn rain away.

notes.a: Cooler conditions slow ripening, so sugar is likely to be lower.
notes.b: Correct: altitude means a cooler site (p. 32); less ripening leaves more acid (p. 29, 33).
notes.c: Temperatures drop with altitude, so the higher site is cooler.
notes.d: Shelter from rain is what mountains do as a barrier, not altitude itself.

Q-L2-04-20.stem: Which moderating influence does the Level 2 book link to some warmer Australian regions?

options.a: Mist, which forms near rivers on autumn mornings
options.b: Cloud, which blocks sunlight and slows photosynthesis
options.c: Fog, which forms at ground level and cools the vines
options.d: Cold currents, which cool vineyards from the sea

notes.a: River mists are linked to botrytis, not to Australia.
notes.b: Correct: grapes take longer to ripen; a very important factor in some warmer Australian regions.
notes.c: The book links fog to coastal California and Chile.
notes.d: The book's example of cold currents is the Cape, South Africa.

Q-L2-04-46.stem: At véraison, how do the colours of white and black grapes change?

options.a: White grapes become pink; black grapes turn brown, then black.
options.b: White grapes become golden; black grapes turn red, then purple.
options.c: White grapes turn green; black grapes turn purple, then red.
options.d: Both stay green until harvest, then darken in the sun.

notes.a: Not the book's description.
notes.b: Correct: véraison is when grapes start to lose their green colour (p. 28).
notes.c: Grapes LOSE their green at véraison, and black grapes go red, then purple.
notes.d: Colour change marks the start of ripening, by mid-summer.

Q-L2-04-01.stem: Why does a vineyard on a slope facing the equator usually produce riper grapes than one on flat land at the same latitude?

options.a: Its soils are deeper and more fertile.
options.b: It receives more heat and sunlight.
options.c: It is sheltered from rain-bearing winds.
options.d: Its cooler nights help the grapes keep their acidity.

notes.a: No: the book links slopes to heat and light, not fertility. (L3, on Burgundy: hillside soils tend to be shallower.)
notes.b: Correct: the book says slopes facing the equator receive more heat and light, so they produce riper grapes than flat land or slopes facing away.
notes.c: That is the effect of mountains acting as a barrier, not of slope and aspect.
notes.d: Cooler nights are a diurnal-range effect, not what aspect does; aspect adds warmth.

Q-L2-04-11.stem: Which vineyard conditions are ideal for botrytis to develop as noble rot, rather than destroying the grapes?

options.a: Warm, dry mornings, then damp, misty afternoons
options.b: Damp, misty mornings, then warm, dry afternoons
options.c: Long spells of dry, warm weather with no mist
options.d: Heavy autumn rain followed by freezing nights

notes.a: Reversed: the book gives misty mornings followed by warm, dry afternoons.
notes.b: Correct: mist lets the fungus grow and spread; dry afternoons limit it. It must grow on ripe grapes.
notes.c: This suits extra ripening (raisining); botrytis needs damp, misty mornings.
notes.d: Rain spreads harmful fungal disease; freezing is the icewine method.

Q-L2-04-14.stem: What is the difference between climate and weather?

options.a: Climate is the long-term average; weather is the day-to-day.
options.b: Weather is the long-term average; climate is the day-to-day.
options.c: Climate covers temperature only; weather covers rain and sun.
options.d: Climate changes yearly; weather stays the same for decades.

notes.a: Correct: climate = average temperature, sunlight and rainfall a region can expect.
notes.b: Reversed.
notes.c: Climate covers average temperature, sunlight AND rainfall.
notes.d: Reversed: climate does not change yearly, though it can shift over decades.

Q-L2-04-15.stem: A region has an average growing season temperature of 19.5°C. How is its climate classified in the Level 2 book?

options.a: Cool
options.b: Warm
options.c: Moderate
options.d: Hot

notes.a: Cool = 16.5°C or below.
notes.b: Correct: warm = 18.5°C to 21°C.
notes.c: Moderate = 16.5°C to 18.5°C.
notes.d: Not one of the L2 book's three bands; 19.5°C falls within warm (18.5°C to 21°C).

Q-L2-04-16.stem: Which factor does the Level 2 book describe as the most important influence on a wine region's climate?

options.a: Ocean currents
options.b: Altitude
options.c: Latitude
options.d: Soil

notes.a: Seas moderate climate (e.g. cooling the Cape) but come after latitude.
notes.b: Important (higher = cooler), but the book names latitude as the most important factor.
notes.c: Correct: the closer to the equator, the hotter. Most vineyards lie between 30° and 50° north or south.
notes.d: Soil supplies water and nutrients, and stones can add warmth, but it is not the main factor.

Q-L2-04-18.stem: Which influence does the Level 2 book say cools the climate of the grape-growing regions of the Cape in South Africa?

options.a: Autumn river mists
options.b: Cold ocean currents
options.c: Warm ocean currents
options.d: Heavy cloud cover

notes.a: Mists near rivers matter for botrytis, not for cooling the Cape.
notes.b: Correct: the Cape is a warm region close to the sea, moderated by cold ocean currents.
notes.c: Warm currents are what WARM the vineyards of northern Europe.
notes.d: The book links cloud to some warmer Australian regions, not the Cape.

Q-L2-04-19.stem: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of rivers described in the Level 2 book?

options.a: Helping to protect vineyards against frost
options.b: Extending the period warm enough to ripen grapes
options.c: Reflecting sunlight on to the vineyards
options.d: Sheltering vineyards from rain and cold winds

notes.a: A benefit: rivers stay warmer than the land in autumn.
notes.b: A benefit: their stored warmth lengthens the ripening period.
notes.c: A benefit: this helps grapes ripen further from the equator.
notes.d: Correct: this barrier effect is what mountains provide (p. 33).

Q-L2-04-21.stem: According to the Level 2 book, how can a mountain range benefit nearby vineyards?

options.a: They block cloud, rain and cold winds, giving dry autumns.
options.b: Their height makes the sheltered vineyards much warmer.
options.c: They reflect sunlight on to the vines, helping them ripen.
options.d: They bring autumn mists that encourage the growth of botrytis.

notes.a: Correct: the result is sunny summers, dry autumns and an extended growing season.
notes.b: Altitude makes vineyards cooler, not warmer.
notes.c: Reflecting sunlight is a benefit the book gives for rivers.
notes.d: Autumn morning mists that encourage botrytis form near rivers.

Q-L2-04-22.stem: How can many stones on the surface of a vineyard's soil help the grapes to ripen?

options.a: They push cold air away from the vines at night.
options.b: They store extra water for the vine in summer.
options.c: They absorb heat and make the vineyard warmer.
options.d: They add extra nutrients for the vine's roots.

notes.a: Not in the book; the stones help by absorbing heat.
notes.b: The book credits the stones with absorbing heat, not with storing water.
notes.c: Correct: the book says this extra heat can help with grape ripening.
notes.d: Nutrients come from the soil itself; the stones' role here is heat.

Q-L2-04-41.stem: How can air moving from nearby mountains or cold seas help vineyards in a warm area?

options.a: It warms them, stopping spring frost on the valley floor.
options.b: It brings rain, so irrigation is not needed.
options.c: It concentrates sugars by drying out the grapes on the vine.
options.d: It cools them, e.g. cold mountain air flowing down at night.

notes.a: The book's point is that air from seas and mountains cools warm areas, not warms them.
notes.b: The book's point is cooling, not rainfall.
notes.c: Grapes shrivel when left long on the vine; this air cools vineyards instead.
notes.d: Correct: onshore winds from cold seas and night-time mountain air moderate warm areas (p. 32).

Q-L2-04-42.stem: What effect does fog have on vineyards in coastal California and Chile?

options.a: It warms them by trapping the day's heat close to the ground.
options.b: It protects the vines from spring frost and hail.
options.c: It cools the vineyards, a very important moderating influence.
options.d: It encourages noble rot, essential for their sweet wines.

notes.a: Fog cools a vineyard rather than warming it.
notes.b: Not the book's explanation; fog's role is cooling.
notes.c: Correct: fog forms at ground level and cools a vineyard (p. 33).
notes.d: That is autumn mist near rivers (e.g. Sauternes), not coastal fog.

Q-L2-04-23.stem: In an unusually cool growing season with less bright sunlight, which problems are the grapes MOST LIKELY to have?

options.a: Swollen grapes with diluted flavours
options.b: Acid too high, sugar too low, weak signature aromas
options.c: Acid too low, sugar too high and few signature aromas
options.d: Dried-fruit aromas and damage from sunburn

notes.a: Caused by heavy rain close to harvest, not by cool temperatures.
notes.b: Correct: the vines may struggle to ripen their grapes.
notes.c: Reversed: less heat and light means less ripening.
notes.d: These are problems of HOT vintages with untypically bright sun.

Q-L2-04-24.stem: Why can heavy rain shortly before harvest reduce the quality of the grapes?

options.a: The grapes lose water, so their sugar becomes too concentrated.
options.b: The vines shut down and stop ripening the grapes.
options.c: The grapes swell with water, which dilutes their flavours.
options.d: The cold rain freezes the grapes on the vine.

notes.a: Rain adds water; losing water is what happens in raisining.
notes.b: Vines shut down when SHORT of water in hot, dry conditions.
notes.c: Correct: high moisture also helps fungal diseases to spread.
notes.d: Frozen grapes come from winter temperatures and are used for icewine.

Q-L2-04-25.stem: Which weather hazard is a particular risk in spring because it can damage and kill the vine's new growth?

options.a: Hail
options.b: Drought
options.c: Frost
options.d: Fog

notes.a: Hail can destroy a vineyard's entire crop, but the book ties the spring risk to frost.
notes.b: Prolonged low rainfall stops the grapes ripening and can kill vines; not this spring risk.
notes.c: Correct: this reduces the number of grapes that can be grown that year.
notes.d: Fog cools coastal vineyards; the book treats it as a moderating influence, not a hazard.

Q-L2-04-26.stem: Which statement about managing vines is NOT correct, according to the Level 2 book?

options.a: In regions short of rainfall, growers may normally irrigate.
options.b: Water is increasingly limited, so most growers use it sparingly.
options.c: The majority of vines are trained on trellises.
options.d: Vines are typically pruned in summer, while they are in leaf.

notes.a: True: growers in dry regions are normally allowed to irrigate.
notes.b: True: water is an increasingly limited and expensive resource.
notes.c: True: as stated in the book.
notes.d: Correct: the book says vines are typically pruned in winter, while they are dormant.

Q-L2-04-27.stem: What is the main risk to grape quality if a vineyard's yields are too high?

options.a: Higher sugar levels and much riper flavours
options.b: Diluted flavours and lower sugar levels
options.c: Over-concentrated, raisined flavours
options.d: A crop too small to be commercially viable

notes.a: The reverse: high yields can lower sugar and dilute flavour.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book.
notes.c: Raisining comes from leaving grapes long on the vine, not from high yields.
notes.d: That is the risk of yields that are too LOW.

Q-L2-04-28.stem: A producer wants a crisp, high-acid white wine with less-ripe fruit flavours. When should the grapes be picked?

options.a: Once frozen on the vine in winter
options.b: Later in the ripening process
options.c: Earlier in the ripening process
options.d: After the grapes have shrivelled

notes.a: Frozen grapes are used for sweet icewine.
notes.b: Later picking gives more sugar, less acid and riper flavours.
notes.c: Correct: earlier picking gives lower sugar, higher acid and less-ripe flavours.
notes.d: Shrivelled grapes are very sweet, with raisin and dried-fruit flavours.

Q-L2-04-29.stem: Which statement about harvesting grapes by hand or by machine is correct?

options.a: Machine harvesters work best on steep, terraced slopes.
options.b: Neither method is fundamentally better for wine quality.
options.c: Hand harvesting gives higher-quality wine in every case.
options.d: The method is normally set down by law in each region.

notes.a: The reverse: machine harvesters cannot be used on steep slopes.
notes.b: Correct: the choice normally depends on the style of wine being made.
notes.c: The book says neither approach is fundamentally better.
notes.d: The book says the choice normally depends on the style of wine.

Q-L2-04-30.stem: What does it mean if a vineyard is certified as organic?

options.a: The vines may not be irrigated or trained on trellises.
options.b: Most chemicals are not used, though some sprays are allowed.
options.c: Only herbicides are banned; fungicides and insecticides are fine.
options.d: No chemical sprays of any kind may be used on the vines.

notes.a: Organic status concerns chemicals, not irrigation or training.
notes.b: Correct: some sprays are still permitted to control the worst fungal diseases.
notes.c: Most chemicals are not used, not just herbicides.
notes.d: Some sprays are still permitted against the worst fungal diseases.

Q-L2-04-43.stem: Why is hail a serious hazard for grape growers?

options.a: It freezes the grapes, so they can only make icewine.
options.b: It cools the vineyard air at night, so grapes ripen slowly.
options.c: Heavy storms can destroy a vineyard's entire annual crop.
options.d: It spreads fungal disease, which causes noble rot.

notes.a: Icewine comes from healthy grapes frozen in winter, not hail.
notes.b: Cold night air from mountains does that; hail physically damages the vines.
notes.c: Correct: hail can badly damage vines and grapes (p. 34).
notes.d: Noble rot needs misty mornings and warm, dry afternoons.

Q-L2-04-44.stem: What happens to a vine in drought, and why can't irrigation always solve it?

options.a: It produces more sugar, and irrigation would dilute it.
options.b: It ripens its grapes faster, and irrigation is banned in PDOs.
options.c: Its grapes swell and dilute, and irrigation spreads disease.
options.d: It cannot ripen its grapes, and water may not be available.

notes.a: Without water the vine cannot ripen its grapes at all.
notes.b: Drought stops ripening; the book gives lack of water as the limit.
notes.c: Swelling and dilution come from heavy rain near harvest, not drought.
notes.d: Correct: in the worst cases the vine may die; irrigation needs water (p. 34).

Q-L2-04-45.stem: Which pairing of vineyard spray and target is correct?

options.a: Fungicide: birds and animals
options.b: Insecticide: weed growth
options.c: Herbicide: insect pests
options.d: Fungicide: fungal disease

notes.a: Birds and larger animals are kept out with nets and fences.
notes.b: Insecticides kill insects; herbicides control weeds.
notes.c: Herbicides control weeds; insecticides kill insects.
notes.d: Correct: fungicides kill fungi; insecticides kill insects; herbicides control weeds (p. 35).

Q-L2-04-31.stem: Why do consumers buying wine from a GI outside the European Union often need the grape variety to predict its style?

options.a: Those GIs set strict rules on which grapes may be planted.
options.b: Their labels need not state any origin, so the GI is vague.
options.c: Those GIs always cover whole countries, not small regions.
options.d: Growers there face minimal rules on grapes and winemaking.

notes.a: Reversed: that is true of GIs INSIDE the EU, making them a guide to style.
notes.b: Some statement of origin, such as the country, is legally required.
notes.c: GIs anywhere can range from a whole country down to one vineyard.
notes.d: Correct: they can grow whatever they think will succeed, so styles vary widely.

Q-L2-04-02.stem: Which of the following is NOT a labelling term for a PGI wine?

options.a: Vino de la Tierra
options.b: Qualitätswein
options.c: Indicazione Geografica Tipica (IGT)
options.d: Landwein

notes.a: This IS a PGI term (Spain).
notes.b: Correct: Qualitätswein is a German PDO term (with Prädikatswein). The German PGI term is Landwein.
notes.c: This IS a PGI term (Italy).
notes.d: This IS a PGI term (Germany).

Q-L2-04-33.stem: Which Spanish labelling term indicates a PGI wine?

options.a: Vino de la Tierra
options.b: Denominación de Origen Calificada (DOCa)
options.c: Denominación de Origen (DO)
options.d: Indicazione Geografica Tipica (IGT)

notes.a: Correct: Spain's PGI term.
notes.b: A Spanish PDO term (e.g. Rioja DOCa).
notes.c: A Spanish PDO term.
notes.d: This IS a PGI term, but it is Italian, not Spanish.

Q-L2-04-34.stem: A German wine is labelled 'Landwein'. What does this term tell you?

options.a: It is a PDO wine with higher minimum sugar
options.b: It is a sweet wine from grapes frozen on the vine
options.c: It is a PDO wine from one of 13 wine areas
options.d: It is a PGI wine, Germany's version of IGP

notes.a: That describes Prädikatswein.
notes.b: That describes Eiswein.
notes.c: That describes Qualitätswein (p. 60).
notes.d: Correct: Landwein is Germany's PGI term; typically light-bodied, dry to off-dry (p. 60).

Q-L2-04-35.stem: On a wine label, what does the term IGT indicate?

options.a: A PGI wine from Italy
options.b: A PDO wine from Spain
options.c: A PGI wine from France
options.d: A PDO wine from Italy

notes.a: Correct: Indicazione Geografica Tipica is Italy's PGI term.
notes.b: Spain's PDO terms are DO and DOCa.
notes.c: France's PGI term is IGP, not IGT.
notes.d: Italy's PDO terms are DOC and DOCG.

Q-L2-04-36.stem: Which group contains ONLY PDO labelling terms?

options.a: AOP, DOCG, DOCa
options.b: AOP, DO, Landwein
options.c: AOC, IGT, DO
options.d: IGP, DOC, Qualitätswein

notes.a: Correct: PDO terms from France, Italy and Spain.
notes.b: Landwein is Germany's PGI term; AOP and DO are PDO.
notes.c: IGT is Italy's PGI term; AOC and DO are PDO.
notes.d: IGP is France's PGI term; DOC and Qualitätswein are PDO.

Q-L2-04-40.stem: Why are wines labelled 'Old Vine' or 'Vieilles vignes' often thought to be of higher quality?

options.a: Older vines give more grapes, so yields are commercially viable.
options.b: Older vines give fewer grapes, with more concentrated aromas.
options.c: Older vines are picked later, giving riper, sweeter grapes.
options.d: Older vines must be grown organically, without most chemicals.

notes.a: Reversed: older vines typically produce smaller numbers of grapes.
notes.b: Correct: the smaller crop can give more complex aromas and higher-quality wines (p. 38).
notes.c: That describes Late Harvest; vine age is about crop size.
notes.d: Organic status concerns chemical use, not vine age.

Q-L2-04-03.stem: Which statement about the term 'Old Vine' (vieilles vignes) on a label is correct?

options.a: It may only be used on PDO wines.
options.b: It shows the grapes were picked later than normal.
options.c: The vines must be at least 35 years old.
options.d: It is not legally defined, so its use can be disputed.

notes.a: No such restriction is given; the book says the term is not legally defined.
notes.b: That describes Late Harvest / Vendanges tardives, not Old Vine.
notes.c: No minimum age is set; the book says the term is not legally defined.
notes.d: Correct: the book says it is not a legally defined concept, so there can be disagreement over its use.

Q-L2-04-12.stem: A wine labelled 'Botrytis Semillon' is made from grapes affected by noble rot. How does noble rot change the grapes?

options.a: It turns the acids in the pulp into extra sugar.
options.b: It freezes the water inside the grapes on the vine.
options.c: It thickens the skins, so the grapes resist rain.
options.d: It makes tiny holes in the skins, so water evaporates.

notes.a: No: sugar AND acid both become very highly concentrated.
notes.b: That is icewine/Eiswein, which needs healthy grapes.
notes.c: No: it pierces the skins, and the fungus can easily destroy grapes.
notes.d: Correct: this concentrates the acids, sugars and flavours of the grape.

Q-L2-04-38.stem: An Australian wine and a Californian wine are both labelled 2022. How do their ages compare?

options.a: They are exactly the same age, as both say 2022.
options.b: The Australian wine is about half a year older.
options.c: It depends on when each producer bottled the wine.
options.d: The Californian wine is about half a year older.

notes.a: Same year, but the southern hemisphere harvest comes earlier in it.
notes.b: Correct: the southern growing season ends around April, the northern one around October.
notes.c: The vintage is the year the grapes were HARVESTED, not bottled.
notes.d: Reversed: the southern hemisphere harvests about half a year earlier.
