Q-L2-04-39.stem: Which statement about wines labelled 'Late Harvest' is correct?

options.a: They must be made from grapes affected by noble rot.
options.b: They are lighter in body than wines from a normal harvest.
options.c: They may be dry, off-dry, medium or sweet.
options.d: They must be made from grapes frozen on the vine.

notes.a: Botrytis/Noble Rot is a separate term; these grapes are just picked much later.
notes.b: The reverse: riper grapes and more sugar give fuller-bodied wines.
notes.c: Correct: riper grapes give fuller-bodied, more concentrated wines in any of these styles.
notes.d: That is Icewine/Eiswein.

Q-L2-05-03.stem: During alcoholic fermentation, what do yeast produce as they feed on the sugars in grape juice?

options.a: Alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat
options.b: Alcohol, oxygen and heat
options.c: Carbon dioxide, colour and acidity
options.d: Alcohol, acid and tannin

notes.a: Correct: the book says yeast produce alcohol, CO2 (which escapes) and heat.
notes.b: Yeast produce carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
notes.c: Colour comes from black-grape skins; alcohol is the key product.
notes.d: Acid and tannin come from the grapes, not from yeast feeding on sugar.

Q-L2-05-04.stem: In winemaking, what is the purpose of crushing the grapes?

options.a: To split the skins and release some juice.
options.b: To separate the new wine from the skins.
options.c: To push the floating cap down into the juice.
options.d: To squeeze out as much liquid as possible.

notes.a: Correct: as defined in the book.
notes.b: That is draining, which in red winemaking follows fermentation.
notes.c: That is punching down, a red-wine extraction technique.
notes.d: That is pressing, done in a machine called a press.

Q-L2-05-05.stem: Which of these shows the typical order of the stages in making a dry red wine?

options.a: Crushing, fermentation, pressing, draining, maturation, packaging
options.b: Crushing, pressing, fermentation, draining, maturation, packaging
options.c: Crushing, fermentation, draining, pressing, maturation, packaging
options.d: Pressing, crushing, fermentation, draining, maturation, packaging

notes.a: Draining comes before pressing: the free wine is drained, then the rest is pressed out.
notes.b: Pressing before fermentation is the white-wine order; reds need the skins in the ferment.
notes.c: Correct: the book's order; reds ferment with the skins, then are drained and pressed.
notes.d: Crushing comes first in the book's order for red wine.

Q-L2-05-06.stem: How can a winemaker make a white wine from black grapes?

options.a: Ferment on the skins, but at cool white-wine temperatures.
options.b: Drain the fermenting juice off the skins after a few hours.
options.c: Ferment it as a red, then blend it with a larger amount of white.
options.d: Press them very gently and ferment the juice without the skins.

notes.a: The colour is in the skins; fermenting with them extracts colour, giving a red or rosé.
notes.b: That is short maceration, which makes a rosé, not a white.
notes.c: Blending red and white wine is a method for making rosé.
notes.d: Correct: colour in black grapes is only in the skins, so very gentle pressing gives white juice.

Q-L2-05-07.stem: Why do red winemakers use punching down or pumping over during fermentation?

options.a: Skins left floating in the cap give up little colour and tannin.
options.b: They add oxygen, which creates nutty and caramel flavours.
options.c: They remove the skins before too much tannin is extracted.
options.d: They help the bacteria begin malolactic conversion much sooner.

notes.a: Correct: the skins rise to form a cap; they must be mixed with the liquid to extract colour and tannin.
notes.b: Nutty, caramel notes come from oxygen during oak maturation.
notes.c: The reverse: they keep the skins in contact with the liquid.
notes.d: MLF is done by bacteria after fermentation; cap management is for colour and tannin.

Q-L2-05-08.stem: Most wines are stored for less than a year before bottling. How do their flavours change in that time?

options.a: They gain vanilla and coconut notes.
options.b: Their fruit fades into vegetal notes.
options.c: They change very little, if at all.
options.d: They move from primary to tertiary.

notes.a: These come from new oak, not from a short storage period.
notes.b: That is what happens to most wines kept too long in bottle.
notes.c: Correct: the book says flavours change very little, if at all, in a short storage period.
notes.d: That happens during maturation, an extended period of storage.

Q-L2-05-09.stem: When a rosé is made by short maceration, how does its production differ from that of a red wine?

options.a: It is fermented on the skins at hotter temperatures.
options.b: It is made from white grapes rather than black.
options.c: It is drained off the skins after a few hours.
options.d: It is pressed and blended with a white wine.

notes.a: After draining it ferments at white-wine temperatures, which are cooler than red.
notes.b: Short-maceration rosés are made from black grapes.
notes.c: Correct: it starts like a red but is drained after a few hours; fermentation goes on without the skins.
notes.d: Blending red with white is the other rosé method, not short maceration.

Q-L2-05-10.stem: Which of these statements about dry rosé winemaking is NOT correct?

options.a: Most rosés are matured for a time in new oak barrels.
options.b: Once drained, short-maceration rosé ferments cool.
options.c: Short-maceration rosés are made from black grapes.
options.d: Rosé can be made by blending red and white wine.

notes.a: Correct (the false statement): the book says rosés are rarely stored or matured in oak.
notes.b: True: it continues at white-wine temperatures (12-22°C).
notes.c: True: they start like a red wine, then are drained off the skins.
notes.d: True, though not permitted in many parts of Europe.

Q-L2-05-11.stem: Why does fermentation stop naturally, leaving residual sugar, in a sweet wine such as Tokaji Aszú?

options.a: Sweet grape juice is added after the wine is fermented dry.
options.b: Grape spirit is added, raising the alcohol and killing the yeast.
options.c: Very fine filters remove the yeast while sugar still remains.
options.d: The juice has so much sugar that the yeast cannot eat it all.

notes.a: That is adding sweetness to a dry wine; it does not stop a fermentation.
notes.b: That is fortification, as used for Port; the stem says it stops naturally.
notes.c: Removing the yeast is the book's method for White Zinfandel.
notes.d: Correct: juice from botrytised, extra-ripe or frozen grapes is too sugary for the yeast to finish.

Q-L2-05-12.stem: A winemaker wants to stop a pink wine's fermentation while sugar remains, without adding alcohol. Which technique is MOST appropriate?

options.a: Remove the yeast from the juice using very fine filters.
options.b: Ferment it at the cooler end of the white range.
options.c: Add grape spirit to kill the yeast before they finish.
options.d: Keep the wine in contact with its lees and stir them.

notes.a: Correct: the book's example is White Zinfandel from California.
notes.b: Cool fermentation can give fruity aromas; it does not stop the fermentation.
notes.c: Fortification raises the alcohol to 15-20% abv, which the winemaker wants to avoid.
notes.d: Lees stirring adds body and bread or biscuit flavours; it does not stop fermentation.

Q-L2-05-13.stem: Why is there no risk that a fortified wine such as Port will start fermenting again in the bottle?

options.a: All of its sugar has been fermented out before it is bottled.
options.b: Its yeast are removed with fine filters before fortification.
options.c: Its alcohol, at 15-20% abv, is high enough to kill the yeast.
options.d: It is stored in airtight steel tanks that keep oxygen away.

notes.a: Port is sweet: fortification kills the yeast before all the sugar is fermented.
notes.b: Filtering out yeast is the White Zinfandel method; Port relies on added alcohol.
notes.c: Correct: the book says the high alcohol means there is no risk of further fermentation.
notes.d: Keeping out oxygen protects flavour; the book credits the high alcohol.

Q-L2-05-14.stem: A producer wants an off-dry white with exactly the same level of sweetness every year. Which method gives the MOST precise control?

options.a: Add sugar to the juice before fermentation.
options.b: Ferment it dry, then add sweetness from grapes.
options.c: Wait for noble rot to concentrate the sugars.
options.d: Encourage full malolactic conversion.

notes.a: That raises the alcohol; the yeast ferment the extra sugar.
notes.b: Correct: the book says this lets winemakers precisely control the sweetness.
notes.c: Fermentation just stops when the yeast can eat no more; the book credits ADDING sweetness with precise control.
notes.d: MLF lowers acidity and can add buttery notes; it adds no sweetness.

Q-L2-05-01.stem: A winemaker wants to give an inexpensive white wine some oak flavour at low cost. Which option is MOST appropriate?

options.a: Mature it for several months in new, small oak barrels.
options.b: Add oak chips or staves to wine in a steel tank.
options.c: Encourage full malolactic conversion after fermentation.
options.d: Mature it in large, old oak vessels for a long period.

notes.a: This adds oak flavour, but barrels are expensive, so it is not the low-cost option.
notes.b: Correct: the book says staves or chips are much cheaper than barrels and add oak flavour to wine in inert vessels.
notes.c: MLF can add buttery flavours and lowers acidity, but it adds no oak flavour.
notes.d: Large vessels are rarely used to give oak flavour, and old oak has little flavour left.

Q-L2-05-15.stem: In a cool vintage, why might a winemaker increase the level of sugar in the grape juice?

options.a: To balance the low acidity of grapes from a cool vintage.
options.b: To leave the finished wine noticeably sweeter on the palate.
options.c: To raise the alcohol of a wine that would be thin and light.
options.d: To help the yeast extract more colour from the black grape skins.

notes.a: Cool vintages give HIGH acidity; low acidity is a warm-climate problem.
notes.b: The yeast ferment the added sugar, so it raises alcohol, not sweetness.
notes.c: Correct: low-sugar grapes give low-alcohol wines lacking body; added sugar becomes alcohol.
notes.d: Colour extraction depends on skin contact and heat, not added sugar.

Q-L2-05-16.stem: Which of these correctly matches a climate with the acid adjustment the book links to it?

options.a: Warm climate: neutralise some of the acid
options.b: Cool climate: add acid to the grape juice
options.c: Cool climate: neutralise some of the acid
options.d: Warm climate: add sugar to raise acidity

notes.a: Warm-climate grapes are LOW in acid, so acid is added, not neutralised.
notes.b: Cool-climate grapes already have high acid; adding more would unbalance the wine.
notes.c: Correct: cool-climate grapes can be too high in acid, so some is neutralised.
notes.d: Adding sugar raises alcohol, not acidity; warm climates add acid.

Q-L2-05-17.stem: Why are red wines usually fermented at higher temperatures than white wines?

options.a: To stop the fermentation while sugar remains.
options.b: To produce more notable fruity aromas in the wine.
options.c: To raise the final alcohol level of the wine.
options.d: To help extract colour and tannin from the skins.

notes.a: Higher temperatures are used for extraction, not to stop fermentation.
notes.b: Fruity aromas are linked to the COOLER end of the white range.
notes.c: Alcohol depends on how much sugar is in the grapes.
notes.d: Correct: reds ferment at 20-32°C to help extraction from the skins.

Q-L2-05-18.stem: What is the typical fermentation temperature range for white wines, and what can fermenting at the cooler end produce?

options.a: 20-32°C; notable fruity aromas
options.b: 12-22°C; notable fruity aromas
options.c: 12-22°C; deeper colour and tannin
options.d: 20-32°C; buttery, toasty flavours

notes.a: 20-32°C is the red-wine range.
notes.b: Correct: as given in the book.
notes.c: Colour and tannin extraction is the reason reds ferment warmer.
notes.d: Wrong range; buttery notes come from MLF and toast from oak.

Q-L2-05-19.stem: Which statement about stainless steel and concrete winery vessels is correct?

options.a: Concrete adds flavour; stainless steel does not.
options.b: They are inert and can also be made airtight.
options.c: They let in oxygen, which softens tannins.
options.d: They are used for storage but not fermentation.

notes.a: Both are inert: neither adds any flavour.
notes.b: Correct: neither adds flavour, and made airtight they stop oxygen changing the flavours.
notes.c: That describes oak, which is watertight but not airtight.
notes.d: The book says both can be used for fermentation and storage.

Q-L2-05-20.stem: In barrel-making, what is meant by the 'level of toasting'?

options.a: How long and how hot the staves are heated.
options.b: How many times the barrel has been used.
options.c: How long the wine is matured in the barrel.
options.d: How much oxygen the barrel lets into the wine.

notes.a: Correct: staves are heated over a flame to bend them; time and heat set the toast level.
notes.b: That is the barrel's age (new oak vs old oak).
notes.c: That is the length of maturation, not toasting.
notes.d: Oxygen passes through all oak barrels; toast is about heating the staves.

Q-L2-05-21.stem: During oak maturation, which flavours develop from the wine's interaction with oxygen?

options.a: Biscuit, bread and fuller body
options.b: Caramel, dried fruit and nuts
options.c: Vanilla, coconut and charred wood
options.d: Butter and softer acidity

notes.a: These come from stirring the lees.
notes.b: Correct: oxygen entering the barrel can develop caramel, dried fruit and nut (hazelnut, almond, walnut).
notes.c: These are flavours added directly by new oak.
notes.d: These come from malolactic conversion (bacteria).

Q-L2-05-22.stem: Why do oxygen-related changes happen more quickly in small barrels than in large oak vessels?

options.a: More of the wine is in contact with the wood.
options.b: Small barrels are airtight but not watertight.
options.c: Small barrels are normally made of newer oak.
options.d: Small barrels are usually given a heavier toast.

notes.a: Correct: the book says more of the wine's surface area is in contact with the barrel.
notes.b: Reversed: oak is watertight but not airtight.
notes.c: Barrel age affects oak flavour; size affects how fast changes happen.
notes.d: Toast affects flavour, not the rate of the oxygen changes.

Q-L2-05-23.stem: A winemaker wants a red's tannins to soften slowly through gentle contact with oxygen, with little added oak flavour. Which vessel is MOST suitable?

options.a: An airtight concrete tank
options.b: A large, old oak vessel
options.c: A steel tank with oak chips
options.d: A small, new oak barrel

notes.a: Airtight inert vessels prevent oxygen interacting with the wine.
notes.b: Correct: oak lets oxygen in; large vessels are rarely used for oak flavour, and old oak has little left.
notes.c: Chips are used to ADD oak flavour; an airtight steel tank lets no oxygen in.
notes.d: New oak adds a great deal of flavour, and small barrels change the wine faster.

Q-L2-05-24.stem: Which microorganisms carry out malolactic conversion, and when does it take place?

options.a: Yeast, after the alcoholic fermentation
options.b: Bacteria, after the alcoholic fermentation
options.c: Bacteria, before alcoholic fermentation
options.d: Yeast, during the alcoholic fermentation

notes.a: Yeast carry out the alcoholic fermentation; MLF is done by bacteria.
notes.b: Correct: it is not carried out by yeast but by bacteria, once fermentation has finished.
notes.c: The book says it takes place after the alcoholic fermentation has finished.
notes.d: Wrong on both counts: bacteria, and afterwards.

Q-L2-05-25.stem: A Chardonnay has softer acidity than expected and noticeable buttery flavours. Which winemaking step MOST LIKELY caused this?

options.a: Malolactic conversion
options.b: Maturing in new oak
options.c: A cool fermentation
options.d: Stirring the lees

notes.a: Correct: bacteria lower acidity and can give buttery flavours; it suits certain Chardonnay styles.
notes.b: New oak adds vanilla, coconut, charred wood and spice.
notes.c: Cool fermentation is linked to notable fruity aromas.
notes.d: Lees stirring adds body and biscuit or bread flavours, not lower acidity.

Q-L2-05-26.stem: A winemaker making a dry Riesling wants to keep its high acidity and pure fruit. What should they do about malolactic conversion?

options.a: Carry it out in new oak barrels.
options.b: Encourage it to run to completion.
options.c: Prevent it from taking place at all.
options.d: Carry it out before fermentation.

notes.a: New oak would add oak flavours and MLF would still lower acidity.
notes.b: MLF lowers acidity and can add buttery notes, the opposite of the aim.
notes.c: Correct: the book says preventing MLF is a common choice for aromatic varieties such as Riesling.
notes.d: MLF follows the alcoholic fermentation; it would still lower acidity.

Q-L2-05-27.stem: What are lees, and what can stirring them through a white wine during maturation add?

options.a: Bacteria; lower acidity and buttery flavours
options.b: Grape skins; deeper colour and more tannin
options.c: Dead yeast; more body and biscuit or bread notes
options.d: Oak chips; vanilla, toast and sweet-spice flavours

notes.a: That describes malolactic conversion.
notes.b: Lees are dead yeast cells, not skins; white grapes are pressed before fermentation.
notes.c: Correct: as described in the book.
notes.d: Oak chips are an oak alternative, not lees.

Q-L2-05-28.stem: Which of these is NOT a reason for blending given in the Level 2 book?

options.a: To define and maintain a style
options.b: To make the wine more complex
options.c: To keep a brand tasting the same each year
options.d: To add biscuit and bread flavours

notes.a: A reason: the book says blending defines and maintains a wine's style.
notes.b: A reason: blending varieties, sites or techniques adds complexity.
notes.c: A reason: consumers expect some brands to taste the same each year (consistency).
notes.d: Correct (not a reason): biscuit and bread flavours come from stirring the lees, not from blending.

Q-L2-05-29.stem: A premium red is slightly hazy in the glass but smells clean, with fresh fruit. Which explanation is MOST LIKELY?

options.a: It has oxidised through a faulty closure.
options.b: It has been damaged by too much heat.
options.c: The winemaker chose not to filter it.
options.d: It is affected by TCA cork taint.

notes.a: Oxidation shows browner colour, caramel notes and a lack of fresh fruit.
notes.b: Heat damage makes a wine lose freshness and fruit character.
notes.c: Correct: some winemakers skip filtration, so the wine may be less than perfectly clear.
notes.d: TCA gives damp-cardboard aromas and muted fruit, which the stem rules out.

Q-L2-05-02.stem: Which change typically happens to a red wine as it matures in bottle?

options.a: Its tannins become firmer and more drying.
options.b: Its fresh fruit flavours become more pronounced.
options.c: Its colour becomes deeper and moves from ruby towards purple.
options.d: Its colour becomes paler and moves from ruby towards garnet.

notes.a: The opposite: tannins become softer and smoother.
notes.b: Fresh fruit gives way to dried fruit and tertiary notes such as fig, prune, meat and wet leaves.
notes.c: Reversed: purple is youthful. Deepening colour with age is what happens to WHITE wines.
notes.d: Correct: reds go ruby -> garnet -> tawny -> brown and typically become paler; tannins soften.

Q-L2-05-30.stem: Wines that can improve in bottle often have all of the following EXCEPT:

options.a: high tannin (in reds)
options.b: high sugar (in sweet wines)
options.c: concentrated flavours
options.d: low levels of acidity

notes.a: They do: high tannin helps preserve red wines.
notes.b: They do: high residual sugar helps preserve sweet wines.
notes.c: They do: the book says enough flavour concentration to evolve positively matters above all.
notes.d: Correct (the exception): ageworthy wines often have HIGH acidity, which helps preserve them.

Q-L2-05-31.stem: How does a white wine typically change as it matures in bottle?

options.a: Its colour stays the same; vanilla and coconut notes develop.
options.b: Its colour moves towards garnet; fig and prune notes develop.
options.c: Its colour pales towards lemon; citrus and green apple develop.
options.d: Its colour deepens towards amber; honey and nut notes develop.

notes.a: Colour changes with age; vanilla and coconut come from new oak.
notes.b: Garnet, fig and prune describe an ageing RED wine.
notes.c: Reversed: whites deepen with age, and fresh fruit gives way to tertiary notes.
notes.d: Correct: lemon -> gold -> amber and deeper; dried apricot, honey, nut and spice develop.

Q-L2-05-32.stem: A red wine is pale garnet, with soft tannins and aromas of fig, prune, meat and wet leaves. Which explanation is MOST LIKELY?

options.a: It was made by short maceration.
options.b: It is a young wine matured in new oak barrels.
options.c: It was fermented at a cool temperature.
options.d: It has matured for many years in bottle.

notes.a: Short maceration makes rosé, not red; it does not explain tertiary notes.
notes.b: New oak adds vanilla, coconut, charred wood and spice; young reds are ruby or purple.
notes.c: Cooler fermentation is linked to fruity aromas in whites, not tertiary notes.
notes.d: Correct: garnet colour, softer tannins and fig, prune, meat and wet leaves are bottle-age signs.

Q-L2-06-02.stem: A red wine is pale ruby, with high acidity, low tannin, fresh strawberry and raspberry fruit and subtle smoke and clove. Which grape is it MOST LIKELY made from?

options.a: Syrah
options.b: Cabernet Sauvignon
options.c: Zinfandel
options.d: Pinot Noir

notes.a: Syrah is known for black fruit and black pepper aromas, not fresh strawberry and raspberry (L2 book p. 90).
notes.b: Cabernet is deeply coloured and high in tannin, with black fruit, not a pale, low-tannin red.
notes.c: Red Zinfandel is full-bodied and high in alcohol with medium to high tannin, not pale and low-tannin (L2 book p. 56).
notes.d: Correct: pale to medium colour, high acid, low to medium tannin, red fruit; the best show subtle oak (smoke, cloves, vanilla).

Q-L2-06-03.stem: What is the MOST LIKELY result of growing Pinot Noir in a climate that is too warm for it?

options.a: Cooked fruit flavours and too much alcohol
options.b: Higher acidity and green, herbal flavours
options.c: Botrytis that makes it suited to sweet wines
options.d: Deeper colour and much firmer tannins

notes.a: Correct: it loses fresh fruit and tastes cooked (p. 51); too-warm sites give overly alcoholic wines (p. 55).
notes.b: These are signs of under-ripeness in cool conditions, not of too much heat.
notes.c: Botrytis is not mentioned for Pinot Noir; heat causes cooked flavours.
notes.d: Pinot Noir is pale to medium with low to medium tannin; warmth does not give it firm tannins.

Q-L2-06-04.stem: Why do many producers mature Pinot Noir in older and/or larger oak barrels?

options.a: They add tannin to balance the high acidity.
options.b: They give stronger smoke and vanilla aromas.
options.c: They extract more colour from the thin Pinot skins.
options.d: They give less flavour, so the fruit is not masked.

notes.a: Not the reason given; the aim is to avoid strong oak flavour, not to add tannin.
notes.b: The reverse: older and larger barrels give LESS oak flavour than small new ones.
notes.c: Colour is extracted during fermentation on the skins, not in maturation barrels.
notes.d: Correct: strong flavours from small new-oak barrels can easily overwhelm delicate Pinot Noir.

Q-L2-06-13.stem: Which of these correctly matches a Pinot Noir region with the cooling influence the book describes for it?

options.a: Santa Barbara County: sea breezes from west and south
options.b: Oregon: morning fogs drifting in from San Pablo Bay
options.c: Western Sonoma: a ring of mountains blocking the sea
options.d: Los Carneros: cool breezes blowing from the Southern Ocean

notes.a: Correct: in California's Central Coast, cooled by sea breezes from the west and south.
notes.b: Oregon is cooler due to its northerly latitude and Pacific exposure.
notes.c: Western Sonoma is cooled by Pacific Ocean breezes; the ring of mountains is Central Otago.
notes.d: Los Carneros is cooled by morning fogs from the San Pablo Bay.

Q-L2-06-14.stem: Why is Oregon generally cooler than California, with a mostly moderate climate ideal for Pinot Noir?

options.a: Its morning fogs drawn in from the San Pablo Bay
options.b: Its cooling breezes blowing off the Southern Ocean
options.c: Its northerly latitude and Pacific Ocean exposure
options.d: Its ring of mountains blocking rain and sea breezes

notes.a: That describes Los Carneros in California.
notes.b: That describes Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula in Australia.
notes.c: Correct: as the book states; best wines show complex fresh red fruit and subtle oak.
notes.d: That describes Central Otago in New Zealand.

Q-L2-06-15.stem: A Pinot Noir with strawberry fruit and sometimes herbal notes comes from a coastal region cooled by Pacific sea breezes and morning fogs, and offers excellent value. Where is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Mornington Peninsula
options.b: Central Otago
options.c: Casablanca Valley
options.d: Walker Bay

notes.a: Cooled by breezes from the Southern Ocean, not the Pacific.
notes.b: Protected FROM sea breezes by mountains; New Zealand's ripest, most powerful Pinot.
notes.c: Correct: Chile's coastal Casablanca Valley; red fruit, sometimes herbal, excellent value.
notes.d: Walker Bay is cooled by strong southerly sea breezes, not Pacific fogs; vibrant red fruit.

Q-L2-06-16.stem: Which South African GI is listed for Pinot Noir in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Constantia
options.b: Walker Bay
options.c: Stellenbosch
options.d: Elgin

notes.a: Constantia is listed for Sauvignon Blanc (Southern Ocean breezes).
notes.b: Correct: strong southerly sea breezes encourage vibrant red fruit; very good to outstanding wines.
notes.c: Stellenbosch is listed for Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
notes.d: Elgin is listed for Sauvignon Blanc (cooled by altitude).

Q-L2-06-17.stem: Which two Australian regions are listed for Pinot Noir in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Eden Valley and Hunter Valley
options.b: Barossa Valley and Clare Valley
options.c: Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula
options.d: Coonawarra and Margaret River

notes.a: Eden is a Riesling region; Hunter is listed for Semillon and Shiraz.
notes.b: Barossa is warm (Shiraz); Clare is a Riesling region in South Australia.
notes.c: Correct: in Victoria, among the few Australian regions cool enough for Pinot Noir, thanks to Southern Ocean breezes.
notes.d: Both are listed for Cabernet Sauvignon, not Pinot Noir.

Q-L2-06-18.stem: Despite its southerly latitude, Central Otago makes New Zealand's ripest Pinot Noir. Which conditions explain this?

options.a: A ring of mountains, very sunny days and cool nights
options.b: Morning fogs from the Pacific and gravel soils
options.c: Low altitude near the coast and high rainfall
options.d: Warm sea breezes and mild, cloudy nights throughout the year

notes.a: Correct: mountains block sea breezes and rain; intense sun ripens, cool nights keep freshness.
notes.b: Fogs are a feature of Casablanca and Los Carneros, not Central Otago.
notes.c: It is shielded from rain; low coastal sites are not the explanation.
notes.d: The mountains PROTECT it from sea breezes; nights are cool.

Q-L2-06-19.stem: Which of these New Zealand GIs is NOT listed for Pinot Noir in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Martinborough
options.b: Hawke's Bay
options.c: Central Otago
options.d: Marlborough

notes.a: Listed: a cool climate producing very good and outstanding Pinot Noir.
notes.b: Correct: Hawke's Bay is listed for Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
notes.c: Listed: New Zealand's ripest, most powerfully flavoured Pinot Noir.
notes.d: Listed: cool climate; also listed for Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.

Q-L2-07-01.stem: Zinfandel/Primitivo needs a warm climate to ripen. How do its fruit flavours change as the grapes ripen?

options.a: From red fruit to black fruit
options.b: From black fruit to red fruit
options.c: From red fruit to herbal notes
options.d: From black fruit to forest floor

notes.a: Correct: from strawberry and raspberry to black plum, blackberry and blueberry.
notes.b: Reversed: red fruit comes first, black fruit with more ripeness.
notes.c: Herbal notes are not described for Zinfandel; ripening moves to black fruit.
notes.d: Forest floor is a tertiary note from bottle age (typical of Pinot Noir).

Q-L2-07-02.stem: Why can Zinfandel grapes reach high sugar levels and give wines dried-fruit flavours such as prune and raisin?

options.a: Noble rot shrivels the berries late in the season.
options.b: Some grapes raisin before the rest of the bunch ripens.
options.c: The grapes are dried on mats for months after they are harvested.
options.d: The grapes freeze on the vine before being picked.

notes.a: Botrytis is not part of the Zinfandel story; the cause is uneven ripening.
notes.b: Correct: uneven ripening within the bunch gives high sugar and dried-fruit flavours.
notes.c: Drying after harvest is the Amarone method (appassimento), not the book's explanation.
notes.d: Freezing on the vine is how icewine/Eiswein is made.

Q-L2-07-03.stem: How are the low alcohol and medium sweetness of a typical White Zinfandel achieved?

options.a: The yeasts are removed before fermentation finishes.
options.b: Grape spirit is added to stop the fermentation.
options.c: The grapes are left hanging on the vine until they freeze.
options.d: The juice stays on the skins for several weeks.

notes.a: Correct: leaves residual sugar and low alcohol, typically 8-10%; made by short maceration.
notes.b: Adding spirit is fortification, which would RAISE the alcohol.
notes.c: That is how icewine is made, not White Zinfandel.
notes.d: Long skin contact is red winemaking; White Zinfandel uses short maceration.

Q-L2-07-04.stem: Two Californian Zinfandels are on a shelf: one is labelled 8.5% abv, the other 15.5% abv. What is MOST LIKELY true?

options.a: Each is a dry red; the 15.5% is from much older vines.
options.b: The 8.5% is a medium-sweet rosé; the 15.5% is a dry red.
options.c: The 8.5% is a dry red; the 15.5% is a medium-sweet rosé.
options.d: The 8.5% is a light, dry red; the 15.5% is fortified.

notes.a: An 8.5% Zinfandel signals a rosé; the book does not link alcohol on the label to vine age.
notes.b: Correct: rosé (White) Zinfandels have low abv; red Zinfandels typically have high abv.
notes.c: Reversed: White Zinfandel is low in alcohol, red Zinfandel high.
notes.d: Low abv here signals White Zinfandel; 15.5% is a normal unfortified red Zinfandel.

Q-L2-07-05.stem: A dry, full-bodied red has high alcohol, medium to high tannin, pronounced blackberry and raspberry, raisin and prune, and vanilla and coffee. Which is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: A red Zinfandel from California
options.b: A Bourgogne AOC Pinot Noir
options.c: A Pinot Noir from Sonoma
options.d: A White Zinfandel from California

notes.a: Correct: matches the book's typical red Zinfandel, commonly matured in oak.
notes.b: Light to medium body, low tannin, fresh red fruit - the opposite of this wine.
notes.c: Californian Pinot has ripe red fruit (strawberry, red cherry) and low to medium tannin, not raisin and prune.
notes.d: White Zinfandel is a medium-sweet, low-alcohol rosé.

Q-L2-07-06.stem: In which Italian region is Zinfandel known as Primitivo, and what does it mainly produce there?

options.a: Piemonte: tannic, long-lived reds for ageing
options.b: Puglia: soft, fruity, dry reds for volume brands
options.c: Veneto: reds made from partially dried grapes
options.d: Tuscany: high-acid reds labelled as Riserva

notes.a: Piemonte is home to Nebbiolo (Barolo, Barbaresco), not Primitivo.
notes.b: Correct: warm southern Puglia; top examples from controlled yields can be excellent value.
notes.c: That is Corvina in Valpolicella (Amarone, Recioto).
notes.d: Tuscany is Sangiovese country (Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino).

Q-L2-08-01.stem: Why is Riesling well suited to producing outstanding sweet wines?

options.a: Its high acidity balances sweetness and it is prone to botrytis.
options.b: Its thick skins resist noble rot, keeping the grapes healthy.
options.c: It ripens quickly, building high sugar levels in hot climates.
options.d: Its low acidity makes the sweetness taste richer and rounder.

notes.a: Correct: both reasons are given in the book; it also builds sugar slowly while keeping acid, so it suits late harvesting.
notes.b: The book says Riesling is susceptible to botrytis, which is an advantage for sweet wines.
notes.c: It prefers cool to moderate climates and builds sugar and flavour slowly.
notes.d: Riesling is high in acidity; low acid would leave a sweet wine unbalanced.

Q-L2-08-02.stem: A Riesling is made from grapes picked when just ripe. Which flavours is it MOST LIKELY to show?

options.a: Dried apricot, mango and peach
options.b: Green apple, lime and blossom
options.c: Peach, mango and pineapple
options.d: Honey, petrol and dried apricot

notes.a: Dried fruit can appear with extra-ripe grapes, not just-ripe ones.
notes.b: Correct: just-ripe grapes give green fruit, citrus and floral notes.
notes.c: Stone and tropical fruit come from EXTRA-ripe grapes.
notes.d: Honey and petrol are tertiary notes that develop with bottle age.

Q-L2-08-03.stem: Some off-dry and medium Rieslings are made using Süssreserve. What is Süssreserve?

options.a: Unfermented grape juice added to the wine
options.b: Grape spirit added to stop the fermentation
options.c: Yeast removed to stop fermentation early
options.d: Grapes left on the vine to concentrate sugar

notes.a: Correct: the alternative is to interrupt fermentation by removing the yeast.
notes.b: That is fortification, used for Port, not for Riesling.
notes.c: This is the OTHER method for off-dry styles, not Süssreserve itself.
notes.d: That is late harvesting, used for sweeter styles.

Q-L2-08-04.stem: Why do winemakers typically ferment Riesling in inert vessels such as stainless-steel tanks?

options.a: To develop nutty, oxidative notes
options.b: To preserve its floral aromas
options.c: To add smoke and vanilla flavours
options.d: To soften its naturally high acidity

notes.a: Inert, airtight vessels protect the wine from oxygen.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book.
notes.c: Those come from oak; stainless steel is inert and adds no flavour.
notes.d: Inert vessels do not lower acidity; Riesling keeps high acid.

Q-L2-08-05.stem: A light-bodied Riesling has medium sweetness balancing very high acidity. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Clare Valley
options.b: Alsace
options.c: Pfalz
options.d: Mosel

notes.a: Clare Valley Riesling is dry, with pronounced lime and lemon.
notes.b: A typical Alsace Riesling is dry and medium-bodied with pronounced flavour.
notes.c: Pfalz is dry and sunny; typical Riesling is dry and medium-bodied.
notes.d: Correct: one of Germany's most northerly regions, so lighter body; medium sweetness balances very high acid.

Q-L2-08-06.stem: Compared with a typical Mosel Riesling, a typical Rheingau Riesling is:

options.a: drier in style, with less body.
options.b: sweeter in style, with less body.
options.c: sweeter in style, with more body.
options.d: drier in style, with more body.

notes.a: Half right: Rheingau is drier, but it has MORE body than Mosel.
notes.b: Reversed: Mosel is the lighter and commonly sweeter style.
notes.c: Half right: Rheingau has more body, but it is typically DRIER than Mosel.
notes.d: Correct: steep south-facing slopes on the Rhine's north bank maximise sun and warmth.

Q-L2-08-09.stem: Why do the Clare Valley and Eden Valley have moderate climates, unlike the nearby warm Barossa Valley?

options.a: Their southerly latitude
options.b: Their morning sea fogs
options.c: Their higher altitude
options.d: Their ring of mountains

notes.a: Not the reason given; the book credits altitude.
notes.b: Fogs are given for Casablanca and Los Carneros, not these regions.
notes.c: Correct: giving refreshing dry Rieslings with pronounced lime, lemon and sometimes petrol.
notes.d: A ring of mountains is the Central Otago explanation (blocking sea breezes).

Q-L2-08-10.stem: Which of these GIs is NOT listed for Riesling in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Pfalz
options.b: Rheingau
options.c: Clare Valley
options.d: Barossa Valley

notes.a: Listed: a dry, sunny German region giving dry, medium-bodied Riesling.
notes.b: Listed: steep south-facing slopes on the north bank of the Rhine.
notes.c: Listed: with Eden Valley, South Australia's premium Riesling centre.
notes.d: Correct: Barossa is warm; the book contrasts it with the moderate, higher-altitude Eden and Clare Valleys.

Q-L2-08-11.stem: What is the key requirement that sets Prädikatswein above Qualitätswein?

options.a: Grapes affected by noble rot in every category
options.b: Grapes grown only in classified grand cru sites
options.c: A minimum period of ageing in oak before release
options.d: A higher minimum level of sugar in the grapes

notes.a: Only some Prädikats (BA, TBA) rely on botrytis; Kabinett does not.
notes.b: German categories are ripeness-based, not vineyard-based.
notes.c: No oak ageing rule is given; the categories are based on grape sugar.
notes.d: Correct: Prädikatswein also needs grapes from a single winegrowing area.

Q-L2-08-12.stem: Which of these lists Prädikats in ASCENDING order of the minimum sugar level required at harvest?

options.a: Spätlese, Kabinett, Auslese, TBA
options.b: TBA, Auslese, Spätlese, Kabinett
options.c: Kabinett, Auslese, Spätlese, TBA
options.d: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, TBA

notes.a: Kabinett is the lowest Prädikat, below Spätlese.
notes.b: This is DESCENDING order - the right sequence, wrong direction.
notes.c: Spätlese (late harvest) comes before Auslese (selected harvest).
notes.d: Correct: Kabinett is the lowest (lightest); TBA the highest.

Q-L2-08-13.stem: Which Prädikat category requires the highest minimum sugar level in the grapes at harvest?

options.a: Spätlese (late harvest)
options.b: Beerenauslese (BA)
options.c: Auslese (selected harvest)
options.d: Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)

notes.a: Spätlese is second lowest, just above Kabinett.
notes.b: BA shares its minimum with Eiswein, below TBA.
notes.c: Auslese is third of six, below BA, Eiswein and TBA.
notes.d: Correct: individually selected berries dried by botrytis; rare and concentrated. (Kabinett is the lowest end.)

Q-L2-08-17.stem: A German Riesling is made from carefully selected extra-ripe bunches and tastes of apricot, mango and dried fruit. Most such wines have some sweetness. Which Prädikat is it?

options.a: Spätlese
options.b: Eiswein
options.c: Auslese
options.d: Kabinett

notes.a: Riper than Kabinett, but with citrus and some peach, not selected extra-ripe bunches.
notes.b: Made from grapes frozen on the vine, not selected extra-ripe bunches.
notes.c: Correct: 'selected harvest'; it can be trocken, but most have some sweetness.
notes.d: The lightest Prädikat: delicate green apple, lime and blossom.

Q-L2-08-14.stem: How does the minimum sugar level required for Eiswein compare with the other Prädikat categories?

options.a: It is the same as for Beerenauslese.
options.b: It is the same as for Spätlese.
options.c: It is higher than for Trockenbeerenauslese.
options.d: It is lower than for Auslese.

notes.a: Correct: the one exception to the ascending order of the six Prädikats.
notes.b: Spätlese is second lowest; Eiswein matches BA, much higher.
notes.c: TBA has the highest requirement of all.
notes.d: Eiswein needs MORE sugar than Auslese; it equals BA.

Q-L2-08-15.stem: Which statement about German Eiswein is NOT correct?

options.a: Its yields are very small.
options.b: It cannot be made in every year.
options.c: Its grapes have frozen on the vine.
options.d: Its grapes are concentrated by botrytis.

notes.a: True: labour-intensive with tiny yields, so prices are high.
notes.b: True: the weather it needs does not occur every year.
notes.c: True: Eiswein is made from grapes frozen on the vine.
notes.d: Correct (the false statement): botrytis plays no part in Eiswein.

Q-L2-08-16.stem: How does a Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) differ from a Beerenauslese (BA)?

options.a: It needs a lower minimum sugar level at harvest.
options.b: It uses individually selected botrytis-dried berries.
options.c: It is made from grapes that froze on the vine.
options.d: It is fermented fully dry, as 'trocken' suggests.

notes.a: TBA needs the HIGHEST minimum sugar level of all.
notes.b: Correct: TBA is rarer and more concentrated, with flavours like BA but more intense.
notes.c: That is Eiswein; TBA relies on botrytis.
notes.d: Here 'trocken' refers to berries dried by botrytis; TBA is sweet.

Q-L2-08-18.stem: Three dry (trocken) Rieslings from the same German region are labelled Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese. Which is MOST LIKELY to be highest in alcohol?

options.a: The Spätlese
options.b: They will all be the same
options.c: The Auslese
options.d: The Kabinett

notes.a: A dry Spätlese is above a dry Kabinett but below a dry Auslese.
notes.b: Prädikats need different sugar levels, so dry versions differ in alcohol.
notes.c: Correct: it needs the most sugar in the grapes, so fermented dry it has the most alcohol.
notes.d: The reverse: Kabinett needs the least sugar, so a dry Kabinett is lowest in alcohol.

Q-L2-08-19.stem: On a German wine label, what does 'Halbtrocken' indicate?

options.a: A wine with some sweetness
options.b: A wine from botrytised grapes
options.c: A wine from frozen grapes
options.d: A completely dry wine

notes.a: Correct: Trocken = dry; Halbtrocken = some sweetness.
notes.b: Botrytis is signalled by BA or TBA, not Halbtrocken.
notes.c: Frozen grapes are signalled by Eiswein.
notes.d: That is Trocken.

Q-L2-09-02.stem: Which two features of Chenin Blanc allow it to make wines ranging from dry right through to sweet?

options.a: Low acidity that softens the sweetness, and botrytis-resistant skins.
options.b: High acidity that suits late harvest, and susceptibility to botrytis.
options.c: An aromatic, floral character, and a habit of ripening very early.
options.d: Thin skins that dry easily in the sun, and a resistance to frost.

notes.a: Chenin has naturally high acidity and is susceptible to botrytis, not resistant to it.
notes.b: Correct: the book gives both features as the reason Chenin is made in a very broad range of styles, dry to sweet.
notes.c: Not the book's reasons. The floral style comes from blending with Viognier.
notes.d: Drying grapes is not mentioned for Chenin; the book's reasons are high acidity and botrytis.

Q-L2-09-05.stem: Why is Chenin Blanc particularly prized in South Africa?

options.a: It keeps high acidity in a warm climate.
options.b: It ripens fully in a very cool climate.
options.c: It reliably develops noble rot each year.
options.d: It gives low yields of very sweet grapes.

notes.a: Correct: the reason the book gives. It is also South Africa's most planted white grape.
notes.b: The book stresses a warm climate; the prized trait is keeping acidity there.
notes.c: Chenin can get botrytis, but the book prizes SA Chenin for its acidity in the heat.
notes.d: High-volume Western Cape brands are common; low yields come from old vines.

Q-L2-09-01.stem: Which description best fits a typical Hunter Valley Semillon?

options.a: Dry and light-bodied from early-picked grapes; gains honey and nuts with age.
options.b: Off-dry and rich, from extra-ripe grapes picked late in the season.
options.c: Full-bodied and oak-matured, with ripe tropical fruit flavours.
options.d: Sweet and full-bodied, from grapes concentrated by noble rot.

notes.a: Correct: picked early because the climate is warm; neutral when young, complex with age.
notes.b: Hunter Semillon is picked early, not late.
notes.c: Closer to some Barossa Valley styles; Hunter Semillon uses inert vessels.
notes.d: That describes Sauternes, not Hunter Valley.

Q-L2-09-10.stem: Which statement BEST compares Barossa Valley Semillon with Hunter Valley Semillon?

options.a: Barossa ranges from Hunter-like styles to full, oaked wines.
options.b: Barossa is sweet and botrytised; Hunter is dry and oaked.
options.c: Barossa is picked early; Hunter is picked late for extra richness.
options.d: Each is blended with Sauvignon Blanc before it is bottled.

notes.a: Correct: the book says Barossa styles range from very like Hunter to full-bodied and oak-matured.
notes.b: Hunter is dry but made in inert vessels; the book gives no sweet Barossa style.
notes.c: Wrong for Hunter: it is harvested early, while sugar is low and acidity high.
notes.d: Hunter is single-varietal. Australian blends with Sauvignon exist but define neither GI.

Q-L2-09-11.stem: On a bottle of Tokaji Aszú, what does '6 Puttonyos' indicate compared with '5 Puttonyos'?

options.a: More Furmint.
options.b: More sweetness.
options.c: Higher alcohol.
options.d: Longer oak ageing.

notes.a: Furmint is the principal grape, but Puttonyos say nothing about the blend.
notes.b: Correct: the number of Puttonyos is a good guide to sweetness; 6 is sweeter than 5.
notes.c: Puttonyos are a guide to sweetness, not alcohol.
notes.d: Tokaji Aszú does age in oak, but Puttonyos indicate sweetness.

Q-L2-09-12.stem: Which statement about Tokaji Aszú is NOT correct?

options.a: It can be dry or sweet, depending on the vintage.
options.b: It is amber in colour, from its long ageing in oak.
options.c: Its sweetness is balanced by high acidity.
options.d: Furmint is its principal grape, often with others.

notes.a: Correct (the false one): the book says Tokaji Aszú is always sweet. Tokaj's dry and medium wines are not Aszú.
notes.b: True: it traditionally spends a significant time ageing in oak.
notes.c: True: sweet and full-bodied, with high acidity and a long, intense finish.
notes.d: True: blended with other local grapes for greater aroma complexity.

Q-L2-09-13.stem: Which two natural features of Furmint make it ideal for the sweet wines of Tokaj?

options.a: High acidity and high susceptibility to botrytis
options.b: Thick skins and strong resistance to botrytis
options.c: Low acidity and a habit of ripening early
options.d: Pronounced floral aromas and a deep colour

notes.a: Correct: the book gives both, making Furmint ideal for sweet wines (p. 66).
notes.b: The reverse: Furmint is very susceptible to botrytis.
notes.c: Furmint has naturally high acidity, which balances the sweetness.
notes.d: Not the book's reasons; Furmint is often blended with local grapes for more aroma.

Q-L2-09-07.stem: Which of these grapes is NOT listed for the Western Cape GI in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Sauvignon Blanc
options.b: Chenin Blanc
options.c: Chardonnay
options.d: Pinotage

notes.a: Correct: the spec's South African Sauvignon Blanc GIs are Elgin and Constantia.
notes.b: Listed: Western Cape (high-volume wines from the warmer inland areas).
notes.c: Listed: Western Cape and Walker Bay.
notes.d: Listed: Western Cape, with the labelling term Cape Blend.

Q-L2-10-02.stem: How would you describe a typical moderate-climate Chardonnay?

options.a: Medium acid, full body; peach, pineapple and banana.
options.b: High acid, light to medium body; apple, pear, lemon, wet stones.
options.c: Medium to high acid, medium to full body; lemon, peach, melon.
options.d: Low acid, light body; simple pear and floral notes.

notes.a: That is the typical warm-climate style (for example, Pays d'Oc).
notes.b: That is the typical cool-climate style (for example, Chablis).
notes.c: Correct: as described in the book (for example, the Côte d'Or).
notes.d: Not one of the book's Chardonnay climate styles.

Q-L2-10-03.stem: Why is acidification commonplace for many warm-climate Chardonnays?

options.a: To lower the alcohol after a late harvest.
options.b: To balance the wine's alcohol and body.
options.c: To add buttery flavours and soften acid.
options.d: To give flavours of bread and biscuit.

notes.a: Adding acid does not lower alcohol; it balances it.
notes.b: Correct: warm climates give full body and only medium acidity, so added acid restores balance.
notes.c: That is malolactic conversion, which lowers acidity rather than adding it.
notes.d: Those come from lees contact, not from adding acid.

Q-L2-10-04.stem: Which of these flavours in a Chardonnay is LEAST likely to come from oak?

options.a: Vanilla
options.b: Coconut
options.c: Butter
options.d: Smoke

notes.a: Oak adds vanilla; chips or staves can give it more cheaply.
notes.b: Oak adds coconut, along with smoke and vanilla.
notes.c: Correct: butter and cream come from malolactic conversion, which also softens harsh acids.
notes.d: Oak barrel fermentation or maturation adds smoke.

Q-L2-10-05.stem: A producer has lightly flavoured Chardonnay grapes from a cool site. Which winemaking approach is BEST?

options.a: Add oak chips and use extended contact with the lees.
options.b: Ferment and mature in new oak barrels for more complexity.
options.c: Use full malolactic conversion for buttery richness.
options.d: Use inert vessels and avoid strong secondary flavours.

notes.a: Chips and lees add secondary flavours that could overwhelm delicate fruit.
notes.b: Only wines of enough flavour intensity benefit; new oak would swamp delicate fruit.
notes.c: Buttery MLF flavours could swamp delicate fruit; such producers may avoid MLF.
notes.d: Correct: the book says strong secondary flavours can easily overwhelm lightly flavoured wines.

Q-L2-10-06.stem: Which tertiary flavours does a very good or outstanding Chardonnay gather with bottle age?

options.a: Butter and cream
options.b: Bread and biscuit
options.c: Vanilla and coconut
options.d: Hazelnut and mushroom

notes.a: Secondary flavours from malolactic conversion, not tertiary.
notes.b: Secondary flavours from lees contact.
notes.c: Secondary flavours from oak.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; top Côte d'Or crus develop these for decades.

Q-L2-10-13.stem: Why can coastal regions such as Sonoma make more intensely flavoured, balanced Chardonnay than California's Central Valley?

options.a: Coastal sites are warmer, so the grapes ripen more fully.
options.b: Sea influences slow ripening, so grapes keep acidity.
options.c: Higher yields give more concentrated grape flavours.
options.d: Mountains shield the coastal vines from the ocean.

notes.a: Reversed: coastal influences cool the vineyards and slow ripening.
notes.b: Correct: coastal influences moderate the climate; the Central Valley is cut off from the sea by mountains.
notes.c: High, irrigated yields are a Central Valley feature and do not concentrate flavour.
notes.d: Reversed: mountains cut the inland Central Valley off from sea influence.

Q-L2-10-14.stem: Which statement about Chardonnay GIs in coastal California is NOT correct?

options.a: Napa Valley grows cooler and cloudier further north.
options.b: Sonoma's coastal vineyards get Pacific sea breezes.
options.c: Santa Barbara County gets breezes funnelled inland.
options.d: Los Carneros is cooled by fogs from San Pablo Bay.

notes.a: Correct (the false one): Napa gets warmer and sunnier further north; full body, tropical fruit, new oak.
notes.b: True: these help grapes keep acidity while building complex flavours.
notes.c: True: lateral valleys funnel sea breezes; styles range from Côte de Beaune-like to tropical.
notes.d: True: morning fogs come in from San Pablo Bay.

Q-L2-10-15.stem: A Chardonnay from a generally moderate region, made in relatively small quantities, has refreshingly high acidity and flavours from lemon to melon. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Pays d'Oc
options.b: California
options.c: Oregon
options.d: Napa Valley

notes.a: Warm Languedoc-Roussillon gives high volumes of peach, pineapple and banana.
notes.b: Central Valley wines labelled California have medium acidity, peach and pineapple, high volume.
notes.c: Correct: moderate climate, high acidity, lemon to melon; small production next to California.
notes.d: Napa Chardonnay is full-bodied, with pronounced tropical fruit and new-oak vanilla and spice.

Q-L2-10-16.stem: Which Australian Chardonnay region is cooled by ocean currents from the south?

options.a: South Eastern Australia
options.b: Margaret River
options.c: Adelaide Hills
options.d: Yarra Valley

notes.a: High-volume wines, with fruit often from warm, irrigated inland vineyards.
notes.b: Warm, but moderated by cooling sea breezes; smaller volume, consistently high quality.
notes.c: Adelaide Hills is cooled by altitude, not ocean currents.
notes.d: Correct: the longer growing season gives ripe peach, medium to high acid and balanced oak.

Q-L2-10-17.stem: Which two New Zealand regions are listed for Chardonnay in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Marlborough and Hawke's Bay
options.b: Marlborough and Central Otago
options.c: Hawke's Bay and Martinborough
options.d: Central Otago and Martinborough

notes.a: Correct: Marlborough (cool, sunny) and Hawke's Bay (moderate; Chardonnay is its most planted white).
notes.b: Central Otago is listed for Pinot Noir only.
notes.c: Martinborough is listed for Pinot Noir only.
notes.d: Both are Pinot Noir GIs on the spec.

Q-L2-10-18.stem: Why does Chile's Casablanca Valley produce fresher Chardonnay than much of the larger, warmer Central Valley?

options.a: Pacific sea breezes and morning fogs slow the ripening.
options.b: Its inland position shelters it from the Pacific Ocean.
options.c: Its heavy summer rainfall keeps the grapes cool.
options.d: Its vineyards are cooled mainly by their high altitude.

notes.a: Correct: these cooling influences give refreshing wines with lemon and peach flavours.
notes.b: Casablanca is coastal and exposed to the Pacific Ocean.
notes.c: Not given; the book credits sea breezes and morning fogs.
notes.d: Altitude moderates the best Central Valley vineyards, not Casablanca.

Q-L2-10-19.stem: Why does Walker Bay Chardonnay typically have higher acidity than high-volume Western Cape Chardonnay?

options.a: Walker Bay Chardonnay is blended with Chenin.
options.b: Strong southerly sea breezes keep Walker Bay cool.
options.c: Walker Bay grapes are picked late for richness.
options.d: Walker Bay vineyards are high and far inland.

notes.a: The book links Chenin blends to the hot inland, high-volume wines.
notes.b: Correct: among South Africa's coolest regions; high acid, peach, pineapple and oak.
notes.c: Not given, and late picking lowers acidity; the cause is cooling sea breezes.
notes.d: It is coastal; the hot inland areas supply high-volume Western Cape wines.

Q-L2-10-20.stem: Why are high-volume Chardonnays labelled South Eastern Australia sometimes blended with Semillon or with wine from cooler vineyards?

options.a: To raise the alcohol of grapes from cool coastal sites.
options.b: To meet a legal minimum of two grape varieties in the blend.
options.c: To achieve better balance in fruit from warm inland sites.
options.d: To add oak flavours without the cost of barrels.

notes.a: The fruit often comes from WARM inland vineyards, not cool coastal ones.
notes.b: No such rule is given; blending is a choice made for balance.
notes.c: Correct: the book says blending can help achieve better balance (p. 70).
notes.d: Blending adds no oak; chips and staves are the low-cost oak option.

Q-L2-10-21.stem: A medium- to full-bodied Chardonnay with ripe peach and pineapple comes from a warm, sea-breeze-cooled region of modest output and consistently high quality. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Adelaide Hills
options.b: Margaret River
options.c: South Eastern Australia
options.d: Chablis

notes.a: Cooled by altitude, not sea breezes.
notes.b: Correct: Western Australia; warm, but sea breezes moderate temperatures and slow ripening (p. 70).
notes.c: High volume, often from warm irrigated inland vineyards; not small volume.
notes.d: Cool; light to medium body with green apple, lemon and wet stones.

Q-L2-11-02.stem: Which group of herbaceous aromas is typical of Sauvignon Blanc?

options.a: White blossom, ripe peach and apricot
options.b: Pear, lemon and ripe banana
options.c: Grass, bell pepper and asparagus
options.d: Rose, lychee and ripe apricot

notes.a: This is Viognier's floral and stone-fruit profile (p. 79), not herbaceous.
notes.b: These are fruit flavours of Pinot Grigio/Gris styles (p. 76), not herbaceous aromas.
notes.c: Correct: the book lists grass, green bell pepper (capsicum) and asparagus as its pronounced herbaceous aromas.
notes.d: These are Gewurztraminer's floral and fruit aromas (p. 79), not herbaceous ones.

Q-L2-11-03.stem: A Sauvignon Blanc is made from grapes picked at a low level of ripeness. Which flavour is it LEAST likely to show?

options.a: Crisp green apple
options.b: Passion fruit
options.c: Grapefruit
options.d: Gooseberry

notes.a: Likely: green fruit is at the less ripe end of the book's range.
notes.b: Correct: tropical fruit (passion fruit) comes with riper grapes; less ripe grapes give green fruit and citrus.
notes.c: Likely: citrus (grapefruit) sits with green fruit and wet stones at the less ripe end.
notes.d: Likely: green fruit (apple, gooseberry) is at the less ripe end of the book's range.

Q-L2-11-04.stem: Why are most single-varietal Sauvignon Blancs made in inert vessels rather than new oak?

options.a: New oak can easily overwhelm its herbaceous character.
options.b: Inert vessels add the flavours of grass and asparagus.
options.c: New oak would raise its acidity to quite unpleasant levels.
options.d: Inert vessels allow the wine to age for many years.

notes.a: Correct: the book says its distinctive herbaceous characters may be easily overwhelmed by new oak.
notes.b: Inert vessels add no flavour; grass and asparagus come from the grape itself.
notes.c: Oak does not raise acidity; the book's reason is that oak flavours mask the herbaceous character.
notes.d: No: the book says Sauvignon Blanc is usually best drunk young.

Q-L2-11-05.stem: A Sauvignon Blanc label says 'barrel aged'. What does this tell you about the wine?

options.a: It was aged in bottle before release.
options.b: It was made from late-picked grapes.
options.c: Oak was used during winemaking.
options.d: It was made from very old vines.

notes.a: 'Barrel' refers to oak vessels, not to bottle ageing.
notes.b: That would be 'Late Harvest' or, in Alsace, Vendanges tardives (p. 78).
notes.c: Correct: the book says oak use is typically shown by terms such as 'barrel aged'.
notes.d: That would be 'Old Vines' (vieilles vignes), which has no legal definition (p. 38).

Q-L2-11-06.stem: Why is Sauvignon Blanc usually best drunk young?

options.a: Its oak flavours fade quickly and leave the wine thin.
options.b: Its firm tannins become harsh and drying with bottle age.
options.c: Its low acidity leaves it flat and dull after a short time.
options.d: Its fresh aromas can fade and turn vegetal quite quickly.

notes.a: Most are unoaked (inert vessels); the problem the book gives is loss of fresh aroma.
notes.b: Tannin is not the issue: it is a white wine, mostly made in inert vessels.
notes.c: It has high acidity (p. 72); the problem the book gives is loss of fresh aroma.
notes.d: Correct: even outstanding examples can lose fresh aromas within a couple of years and develop vegetal notes.

Q-L2-11-01.stem: Which of the following GIs is NOT listed for Sauvignon Blanc in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Pessac-Léognan
options.b: Walker Bay
options.c: Elgin
options.d: Constantia

notes.a: Listed: blends of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon.
notes.b: Correct: Walker Bay is listed for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, not Sauvignon Blanc.
notes.c: Listed: the book describes Elgin Sauvignon Blanc (cooled by altitude; green apple, wet stones).
notes.d: Listed: cooled by Southern Ocean breezes; tropical and herbaceous Sauvignon Blanc.

Q-L2-11-14.stem: Why do many Marlborough Sauvignon Blancs show a broad range of fruit, from grapefruit to passion fruit?

options.a: Grapes from different sites or ripeness levels are blended.
options.b: The wine is blended with Semillon, which adds tropical fruit.
options.c: It is matured in new oak, which adds riper fruit flavours.
options.d: Its warm climate ripens every grape fully to tropical fruit.

notes.a: Correct: the book says blending across sites or ripeness levels gives grapefruit, peach and passion fruit.
notes.b: Semillon blends are typical of Margaret River and Bordeaux, and Sémillon adds body, not tropical fruit.
notes.c: Oak does not add fruit flavours; oak is an experiment beyond the classic style (p. 73).
notes.d: Marlborough has a cool climate (p. 73).

Q-L2-11-15.stem: California is mostly too warm for fresh, herbaceous Sauvignon Blanc. How do producers of very good examples in the Napa Valley achieve this style?

options.a: They delay harvest to build herbaceous flavours.
options.b: They use cooler areas and may harvest early.
options.c: They blend in Sémillon to add acidity and freshness.
options.d: They ferment in new oak to add herbaceous aromas.

notes.a: Picking late would lose acidity and herbaceous aromas; the book says pick early.
notes.b: Correct: early picking retains the grape's acidity and herbaceous aromas (p. 74).
notes.c: Sémillon adds body (p. 73); the book's answer is cooler sites and early picking.
notes.d: When oak is used in Napa it adds body and smoke (p. 74), not herbaceous aromas.

Q-L2-11-16.stem: Which statement about Sauvignon Blanc in Australia is correct?

options.a: Adelaide Hills vineyards are cooled by morning fog.
options.b: In Margaret River it is rarely blended with Semillon.
options.c: Margaret River is in South Australia, near Adelaide.
options.d: It is the most planted grape in Adelaide Hills.

notes.a: Wrong: they are cooled by altitude. Fog and sea breezes cool Casablanca, Chile.
notes.b: Wrong: Margaret River is known for it most commonly as a blend with Semillon.
notes.c: Wrong: Margaret River is in Western Australia; Adelaide Hills is in South Australia.
notes.d: Correct: and the Adelaide Hills vineyards are cooled by altitude (p. 74).

Q-L2-11-17.stem: Why does Chile's Casablanca Valley have a reputation for very good-quality Sauvignon Blanc?

options.a: It is a large valley making mostly high-volume brands.
options.b: It is cooled by sea breezes and morning fogs.
options.c: It is cooled by its high altitude in the Andes.
options.d: It is cooled by breezes from the Southern Ocean.

notes.a: Not the book's reason: the larger Central Valley makes a range of qualities (p. 74).
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 74).
notes.c: Altitude is the book's explanation for Elgin and Adelaide Hills; Casablanca is coastal.
notes.d: Right idea, wrong ocean: Casablanca's breezes and fogs come from the Pacific (p. 54); the Southern Ocean cools Constantia (p. 74).

Q-L2-11-18.stem: How does a typical Elgin Sauvignon Blanc differ from one from Constantia?

options.a: Elgin shows more ripe tropical fruit and less acidity.
options.b: Elgin is usually blended with Semillon and oaked.
options.c: Elgin shows more green fruit (apple) and wet stones.
options.d: Elgin is warmer, as it lies inland, away from the sea.

notes.a: Reversed: ripe tropical fruit is the book's Constantia description.
notes.b: Not the book's description of Elgin; Semillon blends are typical of Margaret River.
notes.c: Correct: Elgin gives apple and sometimes wet stones; Constantia shows ripe tropical fruit and herbaceous aromas.
notes.d: Elgin is cooled by altitude and often cited as the coolest wine region in South Africa.

Q-L2-11-19.stem: For which of these Sauvignon Blanc regions does the book NOT give altitude as the cooling influence?

options.a: Constantia
options.b: Languedoc-Roussillon
options.c: Elgin
options.d: Adelaide Hills

notes.a: Correct: Constantia, south of Cape Town, is cooled by sea breezes from the Southern Ocean (p. 74).
notes.b: Its best Sauvignon Blanc comes from areas cooled by altitude (p. 73).
notes.c: Cooled by altitude; often cited as the coolest wine region in South Africa (p. 74).
notes.d: Cooled by altitude; Sauvignon Blanc is its most widely planted grape (p. 74).

Q-L2-11-20.stem: Which describes the quality of Sauvignon Blanc from Chile's larger Central Valley, in contrast to Casablanca Valley's reputation for very good quality?

options.a: It is cooler, thanks to more sea breezes and morning fog.
options.b: It ranges from inexpensive high-volume brands to very good.
options.c: It is typically matured in new oak and sold at a premium.
options.d: It is mostly an off-dry, simple style from warm sites.

notes.a: Reversed: it is coastal Casablanca that is cooled by sea breezes and fog.
notes.b: Correct: the larger Central Valley makes a range of quality levels (p. 74).
notes.c: Not given for Chile; the book's Central Valley point is a range of quality levels (p. 74).
notes.d: No: the book gives a range of quality, from inexpensive brands to very good (p. 74).

Q-L2-12-01.stem: Which grape-growing choices produce the light, simple, high-volume style of Pinot Grigio?

options.a: Controlled yields and a delayed harvest.
options.b: Allowing the grapes to freeze on the vine.
options.c: High yields and an early harvest to retain acidity.
options.d: Leaving grapes on the vine until botrytis develops.

notes.a: This gives the riper, fuller, more complex style (e.g. Alsace Pinot Gris).
notes.b: This is how icewine is made.
notes.c: Correct: the book says this gives a dry, light-bodied wine with medium to high acidity and simple pear and lemon.
notes.d: Botrytis is used for sweet wines, not this style.

Q-L2-12-02.stem: What is the relationship between Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris?

options.a: They are the Italian and French names for one grape.
options.b: Pinot Gris is the name used only for sweet wines.
options.c: They are two different grapes from the same grape family.
options.d: Pinot Grigio is a black grape; Pinot Gris is white.

notes.a: Correct: Pinot Grigio is the Italian name and Pinot Gris the French name for the same white variety.
notes.b: Alsace Pinot Gris ranges from dry to medium (p. 77); the name is simply the French one.
notes.c: No: the book says they are two names for the same white grape variety.
notes.d: Both names refer to the same white grape (p. 76).

Q-L2-12-03.stem: What style of Pinot Gris comes from controlled yields and a delayed harvest?

options.a: Full body, high acidity, grass and green apple
options.b: Light body, low acidity, rose and lychee
options.c: Full body, medium acidity, peach, mango and banana
options.d: Light body, medium to high acidity, simple pear and lemon

notes.a: Riper grapes have lower acidity, and grass and green apple suggest Sauvignon Blanc.
notes.b: Rose and lychee belong to Gewurztraminer, which is full-bodied (p. 79).
notes.c: Correct: powerful and full-bodied, medium acidity, pronounced lemon, peach, mango and banana (p. 76).
notes.d: This is the common style from high yields picked early (p. 76).

Q-L2-12-04.stem: According to the book, what mainly determines which of Pinot Grigio's two very different styles is produced?

options.a: Grape-growing and harvesting choices
options.b: The use of oak barrels or inert vessels
options.c: Whether malolactic conversion takes place
options.d: The length of ageing in bottle before release

notes.a: Correct: the two styles are determined principally by grape-growing and harvesting choices (p. 76).
notes.b: Both styles are typically fermented in inert vessels (p. 76).
notes.c: The book says the styles are decided mainly in the vineyard: yields and harvest timing.
notes.d: Bottle age can add ginger and honey to fuller styles, but the style is set in the vineyard.

Q-L2-12-05.stem: How do some producers of the riper, fuller-bodied Pinot Gris style keep an off-dry or medium level of sweetness?

options.a: They ferment the wine in new oak barrels.
options.b: They interrupt fermentation by removing the yeasts.
options.c: They leave the grapes to freeze on the vine.
options.d: They add grape spirit to stop the fermentation early.

notes.a: Oak does not add sweetness, and Pinot Gris is typically fermented in inert vessels.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 76); the lighter Italian style is almost always fermented to dryness.
notes.c: That is how icewine is made, not the book's method for Pinot Gris.
notes.d: That is fortification (15-20% abv), used for Port (p. 44), not for still Pinot Gris.

Q-L2-12-06.stem: How do light Pinot Grigio and concentrated, full-bodied Pinot Gris typically differ in their ageing?

options.a: The light style fades fast; the full style can gain ginger and honey.
options.b: Both styles develop petrol and toast notes after several years.
options.c: Both styles should be drunk young, as their fruit fades quickly in bottle.
options.d: The light style gains honey and nuts; the full style fades fast.

notes.a: Correct: simple flavours fade quickly; full-bodied examples can develop ginger and honey in bottle (p. 76).
notes.b: Petrol is the book's tertiary note for aged Riesling (p. 59), not Pinot Gris.
notes.c: Only the light style; concentrated, full-bodied examples can develop in bottle.
notes.d: Reversed: it is the light style that should be drunk young and fresh.

Q-L2-12-07.stem: Much high-volume Pinot Grigio comes from the Veneto. Under which labels is it typically sold?

options.a: Friuli-Venezia Giulia DOC or Veneto IGT
options.b: delle Venezie DOC or Veneto IGT
options.c: Soave DOC or Veneto IGT
options.d: Veneto DOC or delle Venezie IGT

notes.a: Friuli-Venezia Giulia is a separate region, known for a fuller style (p. 77).
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 77). Veneto IGT is the PGI; delle Venezie DOC is a PDO.
notes.c: Soave is a Veneto GI for Garganega, not Pinot Grigio.
notes.d: Levels swapped: the book gives delle Venezie DOC and Veneto IGT.

Q-L2-12-08.stem: Which of the following is NOT typical of most Italian Pinot Grigio?

options.a: No oak influence
options.b: A light body
options.c: A long finish
options.d: An inexpensive price

notes.a: Typical: the book describes them as unoaked.
notes.b: Typical: with few exceptions they are simple, unoaked and light in body.
notes.c: Correct: they typically have a short finish and are most commonly acceptable to good in quality (p. 77).
notes.d: Typical: high-volume production keeps them inexpensive.

Q-L2-12-09.stem: In which Italian region does the book say a more complex, fuller-bodied style of Pinot Grigio can be found?

options.a: Tuscany, on the central-west coast of Italy
options.b: Puglia, in the heel of the south-east
options.c: Piemonte, in the far north-west corner
options.d: Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in the north-east

notes.a: Not given for Pinot Grigio in the book; Tuscany is known for Sangiovese.
notes.b: Not given for Pinot Grigio in the book.
notes.c: Not given for Pinot Grigio in the book; Piemonte is known for Nebbiolo, Barbera and Cortese.
notes.d: Correct: Friuli-Venezia Giulia is in northern Italy's eastern corner (p. 77).

Q-L2-12-10.stem: Why is Pinot Grigio/Pinot Gris typically fermented in inert vessels?

options.a: To raise its acidity before bottling
options.b: To preserve its fruity flavours
options.c: To add body and toasty flavours
options.d: To let in oxygen slowly through the walls

notes.a: Inert vessels do not raise acidity; the aim is to keep the fruit.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book (p. 76).
notes.c: Toast and extra body would come from oak barrels, not inert vessels.
notes.d: That is a feature of oak barrels; inert vessels such as stainless steel do not do this.

Q-L2-12-17.stem: Outside Italy and France, what does a producer usually signal by labelling a wine 'Pinot Gris' rather than 'Pinot Grigio'?

options.a: A style with more body and complexity
options.b: A wine made from a different grape variety
options.c: A lighter-bodied style with higher acidity
options.d: A wine matured in new oak barrels

notes.a: Correct: 'Pinot Grigio' signals a higher-acid, lighter-bodied style (p. 78).
notes.b: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape (p. 76).
notes.c: Reversed: that is what 'Pinot Grigio' signals.
notes.d: The book says the names signal body and complexity, not oak use.

Q-L2-13-01.stem: A dry white is full-bodied and high in alcohol, with low acidity and pronounced aromas of rose and lychee. Which grape is it MOST LIKELY made from?

options.a: Sauvignon Blanc
options.b: Gewurztraminer
options.c: Pinot Grigio
options.d: Albariño

notes.a: Sauvignon Blanc has high acidity, a light to medium body and herbaceous aromas (p. 72).
notes.b: Correct: full body, low to medium acidity, rose, peach, apricot and lychee (p. 79).
notes.c: Typical Pinot Grigio is light-bodied with simple pear and lemon (p. 76).
notes.d: Albariño is medium-bodied with high acidity and citrus and stone fruit (p. 80).

Q-L2-13-02.stem: Why is a dry Gewurztraminer typically high in alcohol?

options.a: It is fortified with grape spirit after fermentation.
options.b: It is fermented with the skins in new oak barrels.
options.c: Its grapes build up high sugar levels as they ripen.
options.d: It is grown in very hot climates with high yields.

notes.a: Fortification is used for fortified wines such as Port, not Gewurztraminer.
notes.b: Gewurztraminer is typically unoaked; the alcohol comes from the grape's sugar.
notes.c: Correct: when that sugar is fermented to dryness, the result is a high-alcohol wine (p. 79).
notes.d: It grows best in cool to moderate climates (p. 79).

Q-L2-13-03.stem: Which of the following is NOT typical of Gewurztraminer?

options.a: Unoaked winemaking
options.b: Full body
options.c: High acidity
options.d: Lychee flavours

notes.a: Typical: it is usually unoaked to preserve its floral aromas.
notes.b: Typical: high sugar gives high alcohol and a full body.
notes.c: Correct: a typical Gewurztraminer has low to medium acidity (p. 79).
notes.d: Typical: tropical fruit (lychee) alongside rose, peach and apricot (p. 79).

Q-L2-13-08.stem: Why is Rías Baixas DO well suited to refreshing white wines such as Albariño?

options.a: Near the Atlantic, it is cooler, wetter and cloudier.
options.b: High altitude on the central plateau gives cool nights.
options.c: Mediterranean breezes cool its hot, dry summers.
options.d: Mountains shelter it from the rain-bearing Atlantic.

notes.a: Correct: a moderate climate, notably cooler, wetter and cloudier than many other Spanish regions (p. 80).
notes.b: Rías Baixas is in Spain's north-west corner, close to the Atlantic.
notes.c: It is on the Atlantic side, in Spain's north-west corner (p. 80).
notes.d: The reverse: its Atlantic position makes it wetter and cloudier.

Q-L2-13-09.stem: What is the typical style of an Albariño from Rías Baixas?

options.a: Dry, high acidity, medium body, citrus and stone fruit
options.b: Dry, medium acidity, full body, oaky vanilla and toast
options.c: Dry, high acidity, light body, grass and asparagus
options.d: Dry, low acidity, full body, rose and lychee

notes.a: Correct: lemon, grapefruit, peach and apricot; usually unoaked and drunk young (p. 80).
notes.b: Albariño is most commonly unoaked; a little lees contact, not oak, may add body.
notes.c: Herbaceous aromas suggest Sauvignon Blanc; Albariño is medium-bodied with citrus and stone fruit.
notes.d: This describes Gewurztraminer (p. 79).

Q-L2-14-02.stem: What levels of acidity and tannin does a typical single-varietal Merlot have?

options.a: Low acidity and low tannins
options.b: High acidity and low tannins
options.c: High acidity with high, firm tannins
options.d: Medium acidity and medium tannins

notes.a: Merlot is medium in both; it softens blends but is not low in either.
notes.b: Not Merlot's profile; the book gives medium acidity and medium tannins.
notes.c: That is Cabernet Sauvignon, which Merlot is often blended with to soften.
notes.d: Correct: the book says single-varietal Merlot is typically dry with medium acidity and medium tannins.

Q-L2-14-03.stem: Which of these flavours is NOT typical of a wine made from just-ripe Merlot grapes?

options.a: Strawberry
options.b: Cooked blackberry
options.c: Red plum
options.d: Green bell pepper

notes.a: Typical: the book lists fresh red fruit (strawberry, red plum) for just-ripe Merlot.
notes.b: Correct: cooked black fruit (blackberry, black plum) comes from RIPER Merlot grapes.
notes.c: Typical: fresh red fruit is the just-ripe Merlot profile.
notes.d: Typical: just-ripe Merlot shows herbaceous notes such as green bell pepper.

Q-L2-14-04.stem: How can a producer in a moderate climate make a riper, fuller-bodied style of Merlot?

options.a: By harvesting the grapes earlier
options.b: By encouraging full malolactic conversion
options.c: By fermenting in stainless steel tanks
options.d: By harvesting the grapes later

notes.a: Earlier picking gives just-ripe grapes: lighter body, fresh red fruit, green bell pepper.
notes.b: MLF softens acidity; it does not make the grapes riper.
notes.c: Vessel choice does not change grape ripeness; ripeness is decided in the vineyard.
notes.d: Correct: the riper style is easy in a warm climate but can be achieved by harvesting later in a moderate one.

Q-L2-14-05.stem: What does Merlot typically add when it is blended with Cabernet Sauvignon?

options.a: Higher acidity and firmer tannin, so it ages for longer
options.b: Black pepper and floral aromas, so it is more complex
options.c: Red fruit and lower tannin, so the wine is ready sooner
options.d: Vanilla and smoky flavours, so it needs no oak ageing

notes.a: Reversed: Merlot has medium acidity and tannin; it softens high-tannin Cabernet.
notes.b: Black pepper is the hallmark of Syrah, not Merlot.
notes.c: Correct: the book says Merlot adds red fruit and lowers tannin, so blends are ready to drink earlier.
notes.d: Vanilla and smoke come from oak, not from the grape itself.

Q-L2-14-06.stem: How does the use of oak typically differ between lighter and fuller-bodied styles of Merlot?

options.a: Lighter styles need little oak; fuller ones may benefit.
options.b: Fuller styles avoid oak, as it adds too much tannin to them.
options.c: Lighter styles need long oak ageing to soften their tannins.
options.d: Both styles are normally unoaked, as oak hides Merlot's fruit.

notes.a: Correct: fuller styles may gain softness and flavour complexity from oak; lighter ones have little need for it.
notes.b: The book says fuller-bodied styles may benefit from the softness oak maturation gives.
notes.c: Lighter Merlot has little need for extended barrel maturation; Merlot is medium in tannin.
notes.d: Both oaked and unoaked styles are made; fuller-bodied styles may benefit from oak.

Q-L2-14-07.stem: Which Australian GI is listed for Merlot in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Margaret River
options.b: Hunter Valley
options.c: Coonawarra
options.d: Barossa Valley

notes.a: Correct: the book notes Merlot blended with Cabernet Sauvignon in high-quality Margaret River wines.
notes.b: Listed for Shiraz and Semillon, not Merlot.
notes.c: Listed for Cabernet Sauvignon only, not Merlot.
notes.d: Listed for Shiraz, Grenache and Semillon, not Merlot.

Q-L2-14-13.stem: A soft, medium-bodied Merlot from a high-volume brand, made from fully ripe fruit and intended for immediate drinking, is MOST LIKELY from:

options.a: Pomerol
