options.b: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru
options.c: Stellenbosch
options.d: Central Valley

notes.a: Pomerol's most famous wines are full-bodied, oaked and age-worthy, not high-volume brands.
notes.b: The more prestigious Saint-Émilion appellation, for age-worthy wines.
notes.c: Stellenbosch is known for complex, age-worthy reds from Bordeaux varieties.
notes.d: Correct: warm, dry Central Valley gives high yields of fully ripe Merlot for soft, medium-bodied brands.

Q-L2-14-14.stem: In Chile, what allows producers to make fresher styles of Merlot than the typical soft Central Valley style?

options.a: Higher yields from flat valley-floor sites
options.b: Harvesting the grapes later in the season
options.c: Ageing the wine for longer in new oak
options.d: The moderating effect of altitude

notes.a: Valley floors are flatter and more fertile; high yields do not bring freshness.
notes.b: A later harvest gives riper, fuller wines, not fresher ones.
notes.c: Oak adds flavour and softens tannin; it does not make a wine fresher.
notes.d: Correct: the book says the moderating effects of altitude allow fresher styles.

Q-L2-14-15.stem: How does a typical Merlot labelled 'California' differ from one labelled Napa Valley?

options.a: It is fuller-bodied and more concentrated than Napa's.
options.b: It is fruity and medium-bodied; Napa's is more concentrated.
options.c: It comes from cooler sites, so it is more herbaceous.
options.d: It must be unoaked, while Napa's must be aged in new oak.

notes.a: Reversed: Napa Valley and Sonoma give the concentrated, full-bodied examples.
notes.b: Correct: the book contrasts fruity, medium-bodied 'California' wines with concentrated, full-bodied Napa and Sonoma.
notes.c: Not the book's contrast, which is about concentration and body.
notes.d: No such rules: top wines often use new barrels; high-volume ones may use chips or staves.

Q-L2-14-17.stem: What causes the climate of Stellenbosch to vary from moderate to warm?

options.a: Cloud cover and cooling breezes from the south
options.b: Plentiful rainfall during the ripening season
options.c: Vineyard altitude and sea breezes
options.d: Distance from the Andes and the Coastal Ranges

notes.a: That is the book's explanation for Coonawarra.
notes.b: Not given; the book credits altitude and sea breezes.
notes.c: Correct: the book says it varies with vineyard altitude and the influence of sea breezes.
notes.d: That describes Chile's valleys, not Stellenbosch.

Q-L2-14-19.stem: Where does most of New Zealand's Merlot come from, and what is the climate there?

options.a: Hawke's Bay, North Island: hot with very dry summers
options.b: Hawke's Bay, North Island: moderate, plentiful rain
options.c: Central Otago, South Island: sunny days, cool nights
options.d: Marlborough, South Island: cool but sunny

notes.a: Right region, wrong climate: the book says moderate with plentiful rainfall.
notes.b: Correct: per the book; there Merlot is more widely grown than Cabernet Sauvignon.
notes.c: A Pinot Noir GI; New Zealand Merlot comes mainly from Hawke's Bay.
notes.d: Marlborough is known for Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, not Merlot.

Q-L2-15-03.stem: Why is Cabernet Sauvignon deeply coloured and high in tannin?

options.a: Its grapes ripen early in the season.
options.b: It is usually aged in new oak barrels.
options.c: Its grapes have thick skins.
options.d: It is usually picked before full ripeness.

notes.a: The reverse: it needs a long, warm growing season to ripen fully.
notes.b: Oak adds flavours and softens tannin; colour and tannin come from the skins.
notes.c: Correct: the thick skins contain high levels of colour, flavour and tannin.
notes.d: Not the reason; colour and tannin come from its thick skins.

Q-L2-15-04.stem: Which of these is NOT typical of a single-varietal Cabernet Sauvignon?

options.a: Blackcurrant and black cherry
options.b: Medium acidity and tannin
options.c: Deep colour
options.d: Mint or green bell pepper

notes.a: Typical: the book's black-fruit descriptors for Cabernet.
notes.b: Correct: that is Merlot's profile. Cabernet is high in acidity and high in tannin.
notes.c: Typical: its thick skins give high levels of colour.
notes.d: Typical: the book says usually herbal (mint) or herbaceous (green bell pepper) notes.

Q-L2-15-06.stem: Which of these flavours does new oak NOT typically give to Cabernet Sauvignon?

options.a: Mint
options.b: Cloves
options.c: Smoke
options.d: Cedar

notes.a: Correct: mint is a primary, herbal note from the grape itself, not from oak.
notes.b: From new oak: the book lists smoke, vanilla, cloves and cedar.
notes.c: From new oak: the book lists smoke, vanilla, cloves and cedar.
notes.d: From new oak: the book lists smoke, vanilla, cloves and cedar.

Q-L2-15-14.stem: Which Napa Valley sub-region, in the far north of the valley, is warmer still and gives some of Napa's ripest, most full-bodied Cabernets?

options.a: Oakville
options.b: Calistoga
options.c: Sonoma
options.d: Rutherford

notes.a: Full-bodied, ripe Cabernet, but Calistoga is the warmer far-north sub-region.
notes.b: Correct: per the book, Calistoga in the far north is warmer still.
notes.c: Sonoma is a separate neighbouring region, not a Napa sub-region.
notes.d: Like Oakville: full-bodied and ripe, but the book names Calistoga as warmer still.

Q-L2-15-15.stem: Which statement about Californian Cabernet Sauvignon is correct?

options.a: Warmer inland Sonoma can make wines as powerful as Napa's.
options.b: Wines labelled California come mainly from Napa and Sonoma.
options.c: Oakville is the warmest Napa sub-region, in the far north.
options.d: A Napa wine labelled Cabernet Sauvignon must be 100% Cabernet.

notes.a: Correct: the book says the warmer inland areas of Sonoma can produce similarly powerful wines.
notes.b: They can be blended from across the state, much of it from the hot Central Valley.
notes.c: Calistoga is in the far north and is warmer still.
notes.d: The book says such wines may contain small quantities of other grapes.

Q-L2-15-16.stem: Cabernet Sauvignon from the Andes foothills of Chile's Maipo or Colchagua Valley often shows which distinctive notes alongside black fruit?

options.a: Mint and green bell pepper
options.b: Banana and candy
options.c: Strawberry and red plum
options.d: Black pepper and liquorice

notes.a: Correct: foothill wines often show herbal (mint) and herbaceous (green bell pepper) notes.
notes.b: From Beaujolais-style winemaking (Gamay).
notes.c: Fresh red fruit of just-ripe Merlot.
notes.d: These are Syrah/Shiraz descriptors.

Q-L2-15-17.stem: In South Africa, what is a 'Cape Blend'?

options.a: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot with Pinotage
options.b: Shiraz blended with Grenache and other grapes
options.c: Cabernet Sauvignon blended with Carmenère
options.d: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot with Malbec

notes.a: Correct: the book says Cabernet and Merlot are sometimes blended with the local speciality, Pinotage.
notes.b: That is a 'Rhône Blend'.
notes.c: Carmenère is Chile's local speciality, blended with Cabernet there.
notes.d: Malbec is Argentina's speciality; the Cape Blend partner is Pinotage.

Q-L2-15-18.stem: Which influences moderate the climate of South Australia's Coonawarra region?

options.a: Shelter from a nearby mountain range
options.b: Coastal breezes and plentiful winter rain
options.c: Altitude and breezes in mountain valleys
options.d: Cloud cover and cool southern breezes

notes.a: Not the book's explanation; it credits cloud cover and cooling southern breezes.
notes.b: That is the book's description of warm Margaret River.
notes.c: Altitude moderates Stellenbosch and Chile's foothills, not Coonawarra.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; its Cabernet shows mint, pronounced blackcurrant, and ages for many years.

Q-L2-15-19.stem: A Cabernet Sauvignon-Merlot blend with fresh red- and black-fruit flavours and green bell pepper, from a moderate climate, is MOST LIKELY from:

options.a: Margaret River
options.b: Pays d'Oc
options.c: Calistoga
options.d: Hawke's Bay

notes.a: A warm region: ripe black fruit and subtle oak.
notes.b: Warm Languedoc, where Cabernet ripens reliably; not this fresh, herbaceous style.
notes.c: Warmer still than the rest of Napa: some of its ripest, most full-bodied wines.
notes.d: Correct: in moderate Hawke's Bay Cabernet needs the warmest sites; blended with Merlot; fresh fruit, bell pepper.

Q-L2-16-02.stem: What is the difference between Syrah and Shiraz?

options.a: Shiraz is a clone that ripens only in hot regions.
options.b: They are two names for the same grape variety.
options.c: Syrah is a black grape; Shiraz is a white grape.
options.d: Shiraz is a crossing of Syrah and Grenache.

notes.a: They are the same variety; the name used hints at style, not a different vine.
notes.b: Correct: Syrah is the French name; Shiraz is the name mostly used in Australia.
notes.c: Both names refer to the same black grape.
notes.d: No: the book says they are two names for the same variety.

Q-L2-16-03.stem: Which description best fits the Syrah/Shiraz grape?

options.a: Thick-skinned and small; best suited to cool climates
options.b: Thin-skinned and large; best suited to cool, cloudy climates
options.c: Thin-skinned and large; best in hot, dry climates
options.d: Thick-skinned and small; needs a moderate to warm climate

notes.a: Right grape traits, but it needs a moderate to warm climate to ripen fully.
notes.b: The reverse: thick skins and small grapes, needing moderate to warm climates.
notes.c: Syrah has thick skins and small grapes.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; it gives medium to high levels of tannin and acidity.

Q-L2-16-05.stem: Which flavours are typical of warm-climate Shiraz, such as the riper Australian style?

options.a: Fresh black cherry and herbal notes
options.b: Cooked black fruit and liquorice
options.c: Fresh red fruit and green bell pepper
options.d: Mint and pronounced blackcurrant

notes.a: The moderate-climate (Northern Rhône) style.
notes.b: Correct: warm-climate Shiraz is full-bodied and high in alcohol, with cooked black fruit and liquorice.
notes.c: Just-ripe Merlot.
notes.d: Classic Cabernet Sauvignon descriptors (e.g. Coonawarra).

Q-L2-16-07.stem: Which of these is NOT a tertiary flavour that fine Syrah/Shiraz typically develops with bottle age?

options.a: Meat
options.b: Leather
options.c: Earth
options.d: Vanilla

notes.a: Tertiary: listed in the book.
notes.b: Tertiary: the book lists dried fruit, leather, meat and earth.
notes.c: Tertiary: listed in the book.
notes.d: Correct: vanilla is a secondary flavour from oak, not a tertiary one from bottle age.

Q-L2-16-15.stem: An inexpensive, high-volume Shiraz made from grapes grown in Australia's warm inland regions is MOST LIKELY labelled:

options.a: South Eastern Australia
options.b: Margaret River, Western Australia
options.c: Hunter Valley, New South Wales
options.d: Barossa Valley, South Australia

notes.a: Correct: much warm inland Shiraz goes into high-volume brands with this label.
notes.b: Spec GI for Cabernet, Merlot and some whites, but not Shiraz.
notes.c: A specific region giving a medium-bodied Shiraz that develops with age.
notes.d: Barossa makes concentrated wines from some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines.

Q-L2-16-16.stem: Why are Barossa Valley Shiraz wines often so concentrated?

options.a: Irrigation gives very high yields.
options.b: Cloud cover slows ripening there.
options.c: Its grapes are dried before fermenting.
options.d: Its very old vines give low yields.

notes.a: No: the book credits Barossa's concentration to very old vines giving LOW yields.
notes.b: That is the Hunter Valley, and it gives medium-bodied wines.
notes.c: That is appassimento (Amarone), not Barossa practice.
notes.d: Correct: Barossa has some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines, giving low yields of very concentrated fruit.

Q-L2-16-17.stem: The Hunter Valley has very hot summers, yet its Shiraz is typically medium-bodied with fresh black fruit. Why?

options.a: Its vineyards are at high altitude, far from the sea.
options.b: Its grapes are picked very late in the season.
options.c: Its old vines are kept to very low yields.
options.d: High cloud cover and sea breezes slow ripening.

notes.a: Not the book's explanation; it credits cloud cover and sea breezes.
notes.b: Late picking would give riper, fuller wines.
notes.c: Old, low-yielding vines explain Barossa's concentration, not freshness.
notes.d: Correct: per the book, despite its relatively northerly latitude and hot summers.

Q-L2-16-18.stem: Which statement about Shiraz in Australia is correct?

options.a: It is legally required to be blended with Grenache.
options.b: It is rarely made as a single-varietal wine.
options.c: It is Australia's most widely planted grape variety.
options.d: It is mostly grown in cool coastal regions of the south.

notes.a: Most Australian Shiraz is single-varietal; blends are a choice.
notes.b: The reverse: it is most often single-varietal, also blended with Cabernet or Grenache.
notes.c: Correct: and Australia has by far the largest plantings outside France.
notes.d: Much is concentrated in warm inland regions for high-volume brands.

Q-L2-16-19.stem: Which of these Australian GIs is NOT listed for Shiraz in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: South Eastern Australia
options.b: Coonawarra
options.c: Barossa Valley
options.d: Hunter Valley

notes.a: Listed for Shiraz.
notes.b: Correct: Coonawarra is listed for Cabernet Sauvignon, not Shiraz.
notes.c: Listed for Shiraz (and for Grenache and Semillon).
notes.d: Listed for Shiraz (and for Semillon).

Q-L2-17-02.stem: Which combination of acidity and tannin is typical of wines made from Gamay?

options.a: High acidity with high tannins
options.b: Low acidity with low to medium tannins
options.c: Medium acidity with medium levels of tannin
options.d: High acidity with low to medium tannins

notes.a: Gamay is only low to medium in tannin; Beaujolais techniques keep tannin extraction low.
notes.b: Acidity is high. Low acidity with high sugar is what the book gives for ripe Grenache.
notes.c: That is the profile the book gives for Tempranillo.
notes.d: Correct: the book gives high acidity, low to medium tannins and red fruit (raspberry, red cherry, red plum).

Q-L2-18-02.stem: When Grenache grapes are fully ripe, what levels of sugar and acidity do they typically have?

options.a: Low sugar and high acidity
options.b: Medium sugar and medium acidity
options.c: High sugar and high acidity
options.d: High sugar and low acidity

notes.a: That fits unripe or early-picked grapes; Grenache needs a warm climate and ripens to high sugar.
notes.b: Grenache ripens in warm climates to high sugar with low acidity.
notes.c: Acidity is low; that is why partners such as Syrah or Tempranillo add acidity.
notes.d: Correct: the book says ripe Grenache typically has high sugar and low acidity.

Q-L2-18-04.stem: Grenache is often made into rosé by short maceration. How is the style of these wines BEST described?

options.a: Deep in colour and tannic, aged in new oak
options.b: Dry to medium, built to develop in the bottle
options.c: Sweet and full-bodied, from partly dried grapes
options.d: Dry to medium, to be drunk chilled while young

notes.a: Short maceration drains the juice off the skins after a few hours, so little tannin is extracted.
notes.b: They are intended to be drunk chilled while young and fruity.
notes.c: Partly dried grapes are used for Recioto della Valpolicella, not Grenache rosé.
notes.d: Correct: dry to medium in sweetness, typically drunk chilled while young and fruity.

Q-L2-18-05.stem: Why do some producers of top-quality Grenache prefer to mature it in old oak rather than new oak?

options.a: Old oak raises the acidity of a low-acid grape
options.b: New oak is not permitted in Southern Rhône AOCs
options.c: New oak can mask Grenache's delicate red fruit
options.d: Old oak adds more tannin to a thin-skinned grape

notes.a: Oak does not add acidity; the book's reason is the delicate red fruit.
notes.b: No such rule is given; it is a stylistic choice by some producers.
notes.c: Correct: the book cites Grenache's delicate red-fruit flavours.
notes.d: Used barrels add less flavour than new oak (p. 47); the reason given is the delicate fruit.

Q-L2-18-09.stem: Why does Priorat DOCa produce Spain's most powerful and full-bodied Garnacha-based wines?

options.a: Its moderate climate allows a long, slow ripening season.
options.b: Its grapes are partially dried before fermentation.
options.c: Very old vines in a warm, dry area give tiny yields.
options.d: High-altitude vineyards give warm days and cool nights.

notes.a: The book calls Rioja moderate; Priorat is warm and dry.
notes.b: Drying grapes is the Amarone and Recioto method, not Priorat's.
notes.c: Correct: tiny yields of concentrated grapes; usually blended with other black grapes.
notes.d: That is the book's explanation for Ribera del Duero Tempranillo.

Q-L2-18-10.stem: Which of these GIs is NOT listed for Grenache/Garnacha in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Navarra
options.b: McLaren Vale
options.c: Barossa Valley
options.d: Ribera del Duero

notes.a: Listed: Garnacha reds, and also known for dry rosé.
notes.b: Listed: a warm South Australian region with many very old Grenache vines.
notes.c: Listed: old vines give concentrated red fruit, spice and long ageing potential.
notes.d: Correct: listed for Tempranillo only.

Q-L2-19-01.stem: Which of these Spanish GIs is listed for Tempranillo but NOT for Garnacha in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Rioja
options.b: Navarra
options.c: Priorat
options.d: Catalunya

notes.a: Listed for both Tempranillo and Garnacha.
notes.b: Listed for Garnacha only.
notes.c: Listed for Garnacha only (though it lies within Catalunya).
notes.d: Correct: listed for Tempranillo only.

Q-L2-19-02.stem: Which description BEST fits a typical wine made from Tempranillo?

options.a: Full body, high tannin, green bell pepper and blackberry
options.b: Light body, high acidity, low tannin and red fruit only
options.c: Medium to full body, medium acidity, red and black fruit
options.d: Full body, low acidity, strawberry and white pepper spice

notes.a: Closer to Carmenère, especially when not fully ripe.
notes.b: Closer to Gamay (Beaujolais).
notes.c: Correct: also medium tannins; strawberry, red cherry, blackberry, black plum.
notes.d: Closer to Grenache (ripe: high sugar, low acidity).

Q-L2-19-03.stem: Which broad Spanish DO produces high volumes of Tempranillo and Tempranillo-based blends, in styles from simple and fruity to powerful and oak-aged?

options.a: Priorat
options.b: Catalunya
options.c: Ribera del Duero
options.d: Navarra

notes.a: Within Catalunya, but known for powerful Garnacha-based wines from tiny yields.
notes.b: Correct: a broad DO; the spec lists it for Tempranillo only.
notes.c: High-altitude DO known for very full-bodied Tempranillo, not high volumes.
notes.d: Known for Garnacha reds and dry rosé; listed for Garnacha only.

Q-L2-19-04.stem: Why can Ribera del Duero produce very full-bodied Tempranillo that still has fresh black-fruit flavours?

options.a: Sea breezes from the nearby coast cool its vineyards.
options.b: Its high altitude gives warm days, cool nights.
options.c: Morning fogs slow ripening through the season.
options.d: Very old vines on stony soils give tiny yields.

notes.a: Ribera del Duero lies further inland; the book credits altitude, not the sea.
notes.b: Correct: as the book says; warm days ripen the grapes, cool nights help keep the fruit fresh.
notes.c: Fog is not mentioned for Ribera del Duero; the book credits altitude.
notes.d: That is closer to the book's explanation for Priorat.

Q-L2-19-05.stem: In Rioja, for which style of wine is Tempranillo sometimes blended with Garnacha?

options.a: Wines intended for long-term ageing
options.b: Wines intended for early drinking
options.c: Wines labelled as Gran Reserva only
options.d: The region's dry white wines

notes.a: For these, other local grapes are added to provide tannin and acidity.
notes.b: Correct: per the book; other local grapes add tannin and acidity for long-ageing wines.
notes.c: Gran Reserva is the longest-aged style; the book links Garnacha to early drinking.
notes.d: Garnacha is a black grape; the book is describing Rioja's red blends.

Q-L2-19-06.stem: Which list puts the Spanish ageing terms in order, from the shortest to the longest ageing?

options.a: Joven, Crianza, Gran Reserva, Reserva
options.b: Crianza, Joven, Reserva, Gran Reserva
options.c: Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva
options.d: Joven, Reserva, Crianza, Gran Reserva

notes.a: Gran Reserva has the highest minimum ageing requirements.
notes.b: Joven has no minimum ageing, so it comes first.
notes.c: Correct: the book says the order, and the style each term indicates, matter most.
notes.d: Crianza is aged for the shortest period of the three oak-aged terms.

Q-L2-19-08.stem: A Spanish red shows primary red and black fruit with vanilla, smoke and coconut from oak, but no tertiary notes. Which label term is it MOST LIKELY to carry?

options.a: Gran Reserva
options.b: Crianza
options.c: Reserva
options.d: Joven

notes.a: The longest ageing gives the most pronounced secondary AND tertiary aromas.
notes.b: Correct: aged in oak before release, gaining vanilla, smoke and coconut alongside primary fruit.
notes.c: Extended oak and bottle ageing adds tertiary notes such as dried fruit and mushroom.
notes.d: Joven wines show primary fruit flavours and have no ageing requirement.

Q-L2-19-07.stem: What does the term Joven indicate on a Spanish wine label, and what is the equivalent term in Rioja?

options.a: Young and fruity, no minimum ageing; Genérico in Rioja
options.b: Young and fruity, no minimum ageing; Crianza in Rioja
options.c: Aged in oak barrels before release; Genérico in Rioja
options.d: Aged in oak barrels before release; Crianza in Rioja

notes.a: Correct: typically released the year after the vintage, with primary fruit flavours.
notes.b: Crianza is the oak-aged term, used throughout Spain.
notes.c: Oak ageing before release defines Crianza; Joven has no minimum ageing.
notes.d: Both halves wrong: oak ageing defines Crianza, a national term; Rioja's Joven is Genérico.

Q-L2-19-09.stem: Why might a Spanish producer decide not to make a Gran Reserva in a particular vintage?

options.a: The wine must first spend a year sold as a Reserva.
options.b: The Gran Reserva term may only be used in Rioja DOCa.
options.c: Its grapes lacked the quality for long ageing.
options.d: The law caps how many Gran Reserva vintages are made.

notes.a: No such rule is given; the book's reason is the quality of the grapes.
notes.b: The ageing terms are national Spanish terms, not specific to Rioja.
notes.c: Correct: an inferior wine aged for long tastes stale and lacking in fruit (p. 100).
notes.d: No such cap is given; the book describes the producer's choice in weaker years.

Q-L2-20-01.stem: Which GI is listed for Carmenère in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Central Valley
options.b: Western Cape
options.c: Casablanca Valley
options.d: Mendoza

notes.a: Correct: its only spec GI; it ripens best in the warmest, sunniest Central Valley sites (p. 101).
notes.b: Pinotage's spec GI; Pinotage is grown throughout the Western Cape (p. 102).
notes.c: Coastal, cooled by sea breezes and fog; listed for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc.
notes.d: Malbec's spec GI, in Argentina; most Malbec plantings are in high-altitude Mendoza (p. 102).

Q-L2-20-02.stem: In the Level 2 specification, which three grape varieties have Western Cape listed as a GI?

options.a: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinotage
options.b: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon
options.c: Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinotage
options.d: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinotage

notes.a: Pinot Noir's South African GI is Walker Bay.
notes.b: Cabernet Sauvignon's South African GI is Stellenbosch.
notes.c: Sauvignon Blanc's South African GIs are Elgin and Constantia.
notes.d: Correct: spec p. 11 (Chardonnay) and p. 13 (Chenin Blanc, Pinotage).

Q-L2-20-03.stem: Carmenère needs a long, sunny growing season. Where in Chile does it ripen MOST successfully?

options.a: The warmest, sunniest sites of the Central Valley
options.b: Short-season sites, since it ripens early and easily
options.c: Coastal sites cooled by Pacific breezes and fog
options.d: The coolest and highest sites in the Andes foothills

notes.a: Correct: even in Chile it struggles to ripen in all but these sites.
notes.b: The reverse: it needs a long, sunny growing season (p. 101).
notes.c: Cooling slows ripening (e.g. Casablanca Valley, p. 70); Carmenère needs warmth.
notes.d: Not given; the book says it needs the warmest, sunniest sites.

Q-L2-20-04.stem: A deeply coloured Chilean Carmenère shows pungent green bell pepper and tomato leaf aromas. What is the MOST LIKELY explanation?

options.a: The wine was aged for many years in the bottle.
options.b: The grapes were picked before fully ripe.
options.c: The grapes were left on the vine until very ripe.
options.d: The wine was matured for a long time in new oak.

notes.a: Bottle age brings tertiary notes such as leather and earth.
notes.b: Correct: unripe Carmenère gives pungent herbaceous notes; ripe gives fresh blackberry.
notes.c: Ripe Carmenère gives fresh black fruit (blackberry), not green notes.
notes.d: Oak softens its tannins and adds coffee and chocolate, not green notes.

Q-L2-20-05.stem: What does the term 'Cape Blend' usually refer to on a South African red wine?

options.a: Chenin Blanc blended with Chardonnay for volume brands
options.b: A single-varietal Pinotage from old Western Cape vines
options.c: Pinotage blended with grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon
options.d: A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, without Pinotage

notes.a: That describes some inexpensive Western Cape whites (p. 63), not Cape Blends.
notes.b: A single-varietal wine is not a blend; Pinotage is also made this way.
notes.c: Correct: Pinotage blends with e.g. Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are commonly called Cape Blends.
notes.d: The book uses Cape Blend for Pinotage blends; without Pinotage it is not one.

Q-L2-20-06.stem: A deeply coloured, full-bodied red has high tannins, blackberry and black plum fruit, and clove and vanilla from new oak. Which wine is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Beaujolais Villages
options.b: Côtes du Rhône
options.c: Mendoza Malbec
options.d: Rioja Genérico

notes.a: Gamay: low to medium tannin and red fruit; rarely oaked.
notes.b: Simple and medium-bodied, with red fruit and white pepper.
notes.c: Correct: the book's description of Malbec, most of which is planted in high-altitude Mendoza.
notes.d: Young and fruity with primary fruit, not new-oak spice.

Q-L2-20-07.stem: Which statement about Malbec in Argentina is correct?

options.a: It gives pale, light-bodied wines with low tannin.
options.b: It was developed specially for Argentina's climate.
options.c: It is only made as part of Bordeaux-style blends.
options.d: Most plantings are in high-altitude Mendoza.

notes.a: Malbec gives deeply coloured, full-bodied wines with high tannins.
notes.b: That is true of Pinotage in South Africa; Malbec is native to south-west France.
notes.c: Often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and/or Merlot, but also frequently single-varietal.
notes.d: Correct: grown widely in Argentina, but the majority of plantings are in Mendoza.

Q-L2-20-08.stem: How does the origin of Pinotage differ from that of Carmenère and Malbec?

options.a: It is native to south-west France, like Malbec.
options.b: It is native to Burgundy, alongside Pinot Noir.
options.c: It was developed specially for South Africa.
options.d: It is native to Bordeaux but now rare there.

notes.a: Carmenère and Malbec are French in origin; Pinotage is not.
notes.b: Closely related to Pinot Noir, but developed for South Africa.
notes.c: Correct: for South Africa's warm, dry climate; it is closely related to Pinot Noir.
notes.d: That describes Carmenère.

Q-L2-20-09.stem: Which of these is NOT typical of Pinotage?

options.a: Low acidity and high tannins
options.b: Coffee, chocolate and smoke when made with oak
options.c: Styles from medium-bodied to powerful, full-bodied
options.d: Red fruit such as strawberry and red cherry

notes.a: Correct to choose: Pinotage typically has medium tannins and HIGH acidity.
notes.b: Typical: oak contact can give pronounced coffee, chocolate and smoke.
notes.c: Typical: from fruity and medium-bodied to powerful and full-bodied.
notes.d: Typical: similar red fruit to its relative Pinot Noir.

Q-L2-20-10.stem: In what form is Carmenère MOST commonly found?

options.a: Made into a light rosé by short maceration
options.b: As an unoaked, light-bodied single varietal
options.c: Blended with Pinotage as a Cape Blend
options.d: Blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot

notes.a: Not described; Carmenère gives deeply coloured, full-bodied reds.
notes.b: It is full-bodied and high in tannin, and often matured in oak.
notes.c: Cape Blends are South African Pinotage blends.
notes.d: Correct: it can be single-varietal but is more commonly part of a blend.

Q-L2-21-01.stem: Which white grape variety is used to make Gavi DOCG?

options.a: Fiano
options.b: Verdicchio
options.c: Garganega
options.d: Cortese

notes.a: Fiano is a southern Italian grape; its spec GI is Fiano di Avellino, in Campania.
notes.b: Verdicchio is grown mainly in the Marche; its famous wine is Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi.
notes.c: Garganega is the most important grape of Soave, in the Veneto.
notes.d: Correct: the book says Cortese is best known as the variety used in Gavi DOCG, in Piemonte.

Q-L2-21-02.stem: Which of these pairings of an Italian white-wine GI and its region is NOT correct?

options.a: Gavi - Veneto
options.b: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi - Marche
options.c: Soave - Veneto
options.d: Fiano di Avellino - Campania

notes.a: Correct: this pairing is wrong. Gavi DOCG is in Piemonte, north-west Italy.
notes.b: This pairing IS correct: Verdicchio is grown particularly in the Marche, on the east coast.
notes.c: This pairing IS correct: Garganega is widely planted in the Veneto, north-east Italy.
notes.d: This pairing IS correct: Fiano di Avellino DOCG is from mountainous Campania.

Q-L2-21-03.stem: What style of wine is Recioto di Soave DOCG?

options.a: A sweet white made from grapes dried by appassimento.
options.b: A sweet red made from partially dried Corvina grapes.
options.c: A dry white from the hilly historic centre of Soave.
options.d: A sweet white made from grapes affected by noble rot.

notes.a: Correct: the book says the grapes are harvested and then dried using appassimento.
notes.b: That is Recioto della Valpolicella. Recioto di Soave is a white wine.
notes.c: That describes Soave DOC Classico, not Recioto di Soave.
notes.d: Recioto uses grapes dried after harvest, not botrytis (the Sauternes and Tokaji route).

Q-L2-21-04.stem: How can the best Soave DOC Classico wines differ from most Soave DOC?

options.a: They can gain honey and almond flavours in bottle.
options.b: They are sweet, from grapes dried after harvest.
options.c: They gain vanilla and smoke from new-oak maturation.
options.d: They are made from Cortese rather than Garganega.

notes.a: Correct: the book says most Soave DOC is drunk young, but the best Classico gains honey and almonds.
notes.b: That is Recioto di Soave DOCG, made by appassimento.
notes.c: Soave is typically fermented in inert vessels and is not matured in oak.
notes.d: Garganega is the most important variety in both Soave DOC and Soave DOC Classico.

Q-L2-21-05.stem: A white wine has medium acidity, a medium to full body and flavours of peach, melon and mango. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Gavi
options.b: Soave
options.c: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi
options.d: Fiano di Avellino

notes.a: Cortese is light-bodied with high acidity: blossom, apple, pear and lemon.
notes.b: Garganega has high acidity: apple, pear, lemon and peach, but no tropical fruit.
notes.c: Verdicchio has high acidity and medium body: apple, pear, lemon and fennel.
notes.d: Correct: the book gives Fiano medium acidity, medium to full body, peach, melon and mango.

Q-L2-21-06.stem: How is most Gavi typically made, and when is it best drunk?

options.a: Matured in new oak, then aged for several years before release.
options.b: Made from dried grapes, giving a sweet wine that ages for decades.
options.c: Aged on its lees in bottle, giving a sparkling wine with biscuit notes.
options.d: Fermented in inert vessels, unoaked, ready to drink on release.

notes.a: Gavi is not matured in oak, and most is not intended to age.
notes.b: That is the appassimento route, used for Recioto di Soave, not Gavi.
notes.c: That is the traditional method for sparkling wine; Gavi is a still, dry white.
notes.d: Correct: the book says Gavi is not matured in oak, and most is ready on release, not for ageing.

Q-L2-21-07.stem: A dry white has high acidity, a medium body and flavours of apple, pear and lemon with a herbal note of fennel. Which grape variety is it MOST LIKELY made from?

options.a: Verdicchio
options.b: Fiano
options.c: Cortese
options.d: Garganega

notes.a: Correct: the book gives Verdicchio high acid, medium body, apple, pear, lemon and fennel.
notes.b: Fiano has medium acidity and stone and tropical fruit (peach, melon, mango).
notes.c: Also high in acid, but light-bodied, with blossom rather than a herbal note.
notes.d: Close: also dry, high acid and medium body, but the book gives it peach, not fennel.

Q-L2-21-08.stem: How do most wines labelled Verdicchio differ from outstanding examples?

options.a: Most are simple and fruity; the best can gain honey and nuts.
options.b: Most are sweet whites made from grapes dried indoors after harvest.
options.c: Most are full-bodied and oaked, with flavours of mango and smoke.
options.d: Most are low in acidity and need many years in bottle to soften.

notes.a: Correct: most are not intended for ageing, but outstanding examples develop honey and nuts.
notes.b: That describes Recioto di Soave. The book describes Verdicchio as dry.
notes.c: Closer to some Fiano: medium to full body, tropical fruit, sometimes oak (smoke).
notes.d: Verdicchio has high acidity, and most is not intended for ageing.

Q-L2-22-01.stem: Which statement best describes Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG?

options.a: Light-bodied, simple and fruity, made to drink young.
options.b: Sweet, full-bodied red made from partially dried grapes.
options.c: Dry to off-dry, full-bodied and high in alcohol, from dried grapes.
options.d: Full-bodied red made from grapes concentrated by noble rot.

notes.a: That is basic Valpolicella DOC.
notes.b: That is Recioto della Valpolicella.
notes.c: Correct: appassimento gives about 15% abv, high tannin, red cherry plus prune, raisin, fig.
notes.d: Amarone uses dried grapes (appassimento), not botrytis.

Q-L2-22-02.stem: Which grape variety or varieties may be used to make Barolo DOCG?

options.a: Mainly Corvina, with Nebbiolo
options.b: Nebbiolo only
options.c: Nebbiolo with some Barbera
options.d: Mainly Barbera, with Nebbiolo

notes.a: Corvina is the main grape of Valpolicella, in the Veneto.
notes.b: Correct: the book says Nebbiolo is the only variety permitted in Barolo DOCG.
notes.c: Barbera is grown in Piemonte, but Nebbiolo is the only variety permitted in Barolo.
notes.d: Barbera's best wines are seen as Barbera d'Asti DOCG; Barolo is Nebbiolo only.

Q-L2-22-03.stem: Why is Nebbiolo often matured for extended periods in oak?

options.a: To raise its naturally low acidity.
options.b: To deepen its colour before bottling.
options.c: To add banana and candy aromas.
options.d: To soften its high levels of tannin.

notes.a: Nebbiolo has high acidity; oak maturation does not raise acidity.
notes.b: Not the book's reason: the long oak maturation is to soften the high tannins.
notes.c: Those aromas come from Beaujolais-style techniques, not from oak.
notes.d: Correct: as stated in the book; some use old oak, others new oak to add oak aromas.

Q-L2-22-04.stem: Which description of the Barolo DOCG region is correct?

options.a: A horseshoe-shaped valley of steep, south-facing slopes.
options.b: A broad, flat river plain with fertile soils and high yields.
options.c: A high plateau with north-facing, cool vineyards.
options.d: A coastal strip of low hills cooled by sea breezes.

notes.a: Correct: as described in the book.
notes.b: Not Barolo: the book describes a valley of steep, south-facing vineyards.
notes.c: The book says Barolo's vineyards face south, not north.
notes.d: Not the book's description: Barolo is a horseshoe-shaped valley with steep slopes.

Q-L2-22-05.stem: Where does Barbaresco DOCG lie in relation to Barolo, and what style of wine does it make?

options.a: A larger region south-west of Barolo, making lighter Nebbiolo.
options.b: A hilly zone in the Veneto, making dry Corvina from dried grapes.
options.c: A smaller region north-east of Barolo, making fruity Barbera.
options.d: A smaller region north-east of Barolo, making powerful Nebbiolo.

notes.a: It is smaller, lies north-east of Barolo, and its wines are similarly powerful.
notes.b: That is closer to Amarone della Valpolicella.
notes.c: Location right, grape wrong: Barbaresco is a Nebbiolo GI.
notes.d: Correct: the book says it makes similarly powerful and long-lived wines from Nebbiolo.

Q-L2-22-06.stem: Which of these GIs is listed for the Barbera grape in the Level 2 specification?

options.a: Barbaresco
options.b: Barbera d'Asti
options.c: Valpolicella Classico
options.d: Asti

notes.a: Barbaresco is a Nebbiolo GI, north-east of Barolo.
notes.b: Correct: the book says many see Barbera d'Asti DOCG as Barbera's highest-quality wines.
notes.c: A Corvina GI from the hillier heartland of Valpolicella, in the Veneto.
notes.d: Asti DOCG is a sweet, light, sparkling Piemonte wine made from Moscato (L2 book p. 115).

Q-L2-22-07.stem: Why is Barbera generally enjoyable to drink at a younger stage than Nebbiolo?

options.a: It is made from partly dried grapes.
options.b: It has lower levels of tannin.
options.c: It has lower levels of acidity.
options.d: It spends longer maturing in oak.

notes.a: Drying (appassimento) is a Veneto technique for Amarone and Recioto, not Barbera.
notes.b: Correct: the book gives Barbera's lower tannin levels as the reason.
notes.c: Barbera has high acidity, like Nebbiolo; the difference is tannin.
notes.d: Many Barbera wines are unoaked; it is Nebbiolo that often has long oak maturation.

Q-L2-22-08.stem: Corvina is the most important grape of Valpolicella. What tannin and acidity does the L2 book give its wines?

options.a: Medium to high tannins, high acidity
options.b: Low to medium tannins, high acidity
options.c: Low to medium tannins, low acidity
options.d: High tannins, medium acidity

notes.a: Too much tannin: the book gives Corvina low to medium tannins.
notes.b: Correct: with red-fruit flavours of red cherry and red plum.
notes.c: Tannin right, acidity wrong: Corvina is high in acidity.
notes.d: That is Montepulciano, which also has deep colour and black fruit.

Q-L2-22-09.stem: What does the term 'Classico' indicate on a label such as Valpolicella DOC Classico?

options.a: A wine made only from the Corvina grape
options.b: Grapes dried indoors before fermentation
options.c: Grapes grown in the historic centre of the region
options.d: Ageing for at least a set number of months

notes.a: Classico is about where the grapes are grown, not the grape variety.
notes.b: That is appassimento, used for Amarone and Recioto.
notes.c: Correct: often the hilliest part, typically giving more concentrated wines.
notes.d: That is Riserva.

Q-L2-22-10.stem: Which of these wines is NOT made using the appassimento method?

options.a: Recioto di Soave
options.b: Amarone della Valpolicella
options.c: Valpolicella DOC Classico
options.d: Recioto della Valpolicella

notes.a: A sweet white made from grapes dried by appassimento.
notes.b: Made from partially dried grapes: dry to off-dry, full-bodied, about 15% abv.
notes.c: Correct: made from fresh grapes; Classico refers to the hillier heartland, not drying.
notes.d: A sweet red made from partially dried grapes.

Q-L2-22-11.stem: A full-bodied red has high tannin and acidity, red cherry, dried herbs and rose, with mushroom and leather from age. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Valpolicella
options.b: Barolo
options.c: Barbera d'Asti
options.d: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo

notes.a: Basic Valpolicella is light-bodied, fruity and simple, made to drink young.
notes.b: Correct: Nebbiolo's red fruit, dried herbs and rose; full body, high tannin and acid; aged mushroom, leather.
notes.c: Barbera has low to medium tannins, not high, and sometimes black pepper.
notes.d: Montepulciano gives black fruit (black plum, black cherry); mostly simple and fruity.

Q-L2-22-12.stem: Why is Recioto della Valpolicella sweet?

options.a: Sweet juice is added to the wine before bottling.
options.b: Grape spirit is added to stop the fermentation early.
options.c: Dried grapes hold more sugar than the yeast can ferment.
options.d: Its grapes are concentrated by noble rot on the vine.

notes.a: Not the book's method for Recioto; its sweetness comes from dried grapes.
notes.b: That is fortification, as used for Port; Recioto is not fortified.
notes.c: Correct: per the book, the sugars are so concentrated that the yeast cannot ferment them to dryness.
notes.d: Recioto uses grapes dried indoors (appassimento), not botrytis.

Q-L2-23-01.stem: Which description best fits wines made from Sangiovese?

options.a: Deep colour, high tannin, medium acidity, black plum and black cherry
options.b: Dry, high tannin, high acidity, red cherry and dried herbs
options.c: High acidity, low to medium tannin, red cherry and black pepper
options.d: Low to medium tannin, high acidity, light body and simple red fruit

notes.a: That is Montepulciano.
notes.b: Correct: the book adds red plum; often blended with small amounts of other black grapes.
notes.c: That is Barbera.
notes.d: Closer to basic Valpolicella (Corvina).

Q-L2-23-02.stem: How do the growing conditions of Chianti Classico DOCG differ from those of the wider Chianti DOCG?

options.a: It lies lower, on flat and fertile land near the coast.
options.b: It sits at higher altitude, with a long ripening season.
options.c: It is warmer and lower, so the grapes ripen faster.
options.d: It lies east of the Apennines, in the Abruzzo region.

notes.a: No: Classico sits at HIGHER altitude than the wider Chianti area.
notes.b: Correct: as stated in the book.
notes.c: The reverse: higher altitude and a long ripening season.
notes.d: That is Montepulciano country; Chianti is in central Tuscany, west of the Apennines.

Q-L2-23-03.stem: Which statement best describes wines labelled Chianti DOCG?

options.a: Varied quality; many are simple, inexpensive and not for ageing.
options.b: Sweet reds made from grapes that are dried after harvest.
options.c: Full-bodied wines that must mature in oak for an extended period.
options.d: Made from Montepulciano and sold mostly in high volumes.

notes.a: Correct: Chianti DOCG covers a wide area in the Apennine foothills, with varied quality.
notes.b: That is Recioto della Valpolicella, from the Veneto.
notes.c: The L2 book gives this oak requirement for Brunello di Montalcino; many Chianti DOCG wines are simple, not for ageing.
notes.d: Chianti is Sangiovese-dominant; high-volume Montepulciano is Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.

Q-L2-23-04.stem: Which flavours does oak maturation typically add to Chianti Classico DOCG?

options.a: Banana and candy
options.b: Meat and leather
options.c: Cloves and cedar
options.d: Bread and biscuit

notes.a: These come from Beaujolais-style techniques (L2 book p. 94), not oak.
notes.b: These develop later in the bottle in the best wines, not from oak.
notes.c: Correct: oak also softens Sangiovese's high tannins (L2 book p. 108).
notes.d: These come from lees contact or autolysis, not oak.

Q-L2-23-06.stem: Why may a Chianti Classico DOCG Riserva already show some tertiary characters when it is released?

options.a: Its grapes are partially dried before fermentation.
options.b: It is made only from very old Sangiovese vines.
options.c: Its grapes come from the historic centre.
options.d: It is subject to stricter ageing requirements.

notes.a: That is appassimento, used in the Veneto for Amarone and Recioto.
notes.b: Riserva relates to ageing before release, not to vine age.
notes.c: That is what Classico means; it does not explain tertiary character.
notes.d: Correct: per the book, so it may show some tertiary characters on release.

Q-L2-23-07.stem: In Brunello di Montalcino DOCG, what is 'Brunello'?

options.a: A term for oak-aged Riserva wine
options.b: The local name for Nebbiolo
options.c: The local name for Sangiovese
options.d: The local name for Montepulciano

notes.a: Riserva is the ageing term; Brunello is a grape name.
notes.b: Nebbiolo is the Piemonte grape of Barolo and Barbaresco.
notes.c: Correct: as stated in the book.
notes.d: Montepulciano is the grape of Abruzzo, east of the Apennines.

Q-L2-23-08.stem: A powerful, full-bodied red from a warm, sunny part of southern Tuscany has very high tannin and acidity and long ageing potential. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
options.b: Chianti Classico
options.c: Brunello di Montalcino
options.d: Chianti

notes.a: Abruzzo is in east-central Italy, not Tuscany; mostly simple and fruity.
notes.b: Typically medium-bodied, from higher-altitude vineyards in central Tuscany.
notes.c: Correct: it must also mature in oak for an extended period before release.
notes.d: Many are simple, inexpensive and not intended for ageing.

Q-L2-23-09.stem: A deeply coloured red has medium acidity, high tannins and black plum and black cherry flavours. Which GI is it MOST LIKELY from?

options.a: Valpolicella Classico
options.b: Chianti Classico
options.c: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo
options.d: Barbera d'Asti

notes.a: Corvina has high acidity, low to medium tannins and red fruit.
notes.b: Sangiovese has high acidity and red fruit (red cherry, red plum).
notes.c: Correct: Montepulciano gives deep colour, medium acidity, high tannins and black fruit.
notes.d: Barbera has high acidity, low to medium tannins and red fruit.

Q-L2-23-10.stem: Which of these statements about Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC is NOT correct?

options.a: Some is matured briefly in oak.
options.b: It is made mainly from Sangiovese.
options.c: It comes from east-central Italy.
options.d: Much of it is simple and fruity.

notes.a: True: the more concentrated wines may be matured for a short time in oak.
notes.b: Correct: this is the false statement. It is made from the Montepulciano grape.
notes.c: True: from the Abruzzo region, east of the Apennines.
notes.d: True: Abruzzo makes high volumes of inexpensive wine, typically for early drinking.

Q-L2-23-05.stem: What does 'Riserva' indicate on an Italian DOC or DOCG wine label?

options.a: Grapes harvested from a single named vineyard.
options.b: Grapes grown in the historic centre of the region.
options.c: Grapes dried indoors to concentrate their sugars.
options.d: Ageing for a set minimum time before release.

notes.a: Not the book's definition; Riserva is about minimum ageing before release.
notes.b: That is Classico.
notes.c: That is appassimento.
notes.d: Correct: the book defines it as aged for at least a set number of months before release.

Q-L2-23-11.stem: Barbera d'Asti DOCG is named after what?

options.a: Its region only
options.b: Its grape and its producer
options.c: Its grape variety only
options.d: Its grape variety and its region

notes.a: That is how Barolo, Barbaresco and Valpolicella are named.
notes.b: Not the book's convention: the name is grape plus region.
notes.c: Asti is a place; the name combines grape and region.
notes.d: Correct: it means 'Barbera from Asti' (L2 book p. 109).

Q-L2-24-01.stem: In the traditional method, which stage actually removes the yeast sediment from the bottle?

options.a: Riddling
options.b: Disgorgement
options.c: Dosage
options.d: Autolysis

notes.a: Riddling only moves the sediment into the neck; it does not remove it.
notes.b: Correct: the frozen plug of lees is forced out by the pressure when the crown cap is removed.
notes.c: Dosage tops up the bottle and sets the sweetness after disgorgement.
notes.d: Autolysis is the breakdown of dead yeast that adds biscuit and bread flavours.

Q-L2-24-02.stem: How do most premium-quality sparkling wine producers create the bubbles in their wines?

options.a: By ageing the wine on its lees in an open tank for many months.
options.b: By adding a sparkling liqueur d'expédition after disgorgement.
options.c: By trapping CO2 from a second fermentation in a sealed vessel.
options.d: By pumping carbon dioxide gas through the finished still wine.

notes.a: An open vessel lets the CO2 escape; the second fermentation must take place in a sealed vessel.
notes.b: The liqueur d'expédition sets the final sweetness; it does not create the bubbles.
notes.c: Correct: sugar and yeast are added to the dry base wine in a sealed bottle or tank; this also adds about 1.5% abv.
notes.d: Possible, but the book says most premium producers harness the CO2 made by fermentation instead.

Q-L2-24-04.stem: In a traditional-method sparkling wine, what mainly determines how intense its autolytic (biscuit, bread) flavours are?

options.a: How much Chardonnay is used in the base wine blend
options.b: Whether riddling is done by hand or by gyropalette
options.c: How long the wine spends in contact with its lees
options.d: How much sugar is added in the liqueur d'expédition

notes.a: The grape mix shapes fruit character; autolytic intensity depends on time on the lees.
notes.b: Riddling only moves the lees into the neck of the bottle; it adds no flavour.
notes.c: Correct: the book says the number of months or years on the lees determines the intensity.
notes.d: Dosage sets the final sweetness, not the intensity of autolytic flavours.

Q-L2-24-06.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the traditional-method stages that follow the second fermentation in bottle?

options.a: Dosage, autolysis, riddling, disgorgement
options.b: Autolysis, disgorgement, riddling, dosage
options.c: Riddling, autolysis, dosage, disgorgement
options.d: Autolysis, riddling, disgorgement, dosage

notes.a: Dosage is added after disgorgement, just before the bottle is resealed.
notes.b: The lees must be riddled into the neck before they can be disgorged.
notes.c: Autolysis happens while the wine rests on its lees, before riddling; dosage comes last.
notes.d: Correct: the lees break down, are moved into the neck, are ejected, then the bottle is topped up.

Q-L2-24-07.stem: In the traditional method, what does the dosage stage determine?

options.a: The final alcohol level of the wine
options.b: The pressure of the bubbles in the wine
options.c: The intensity of the autolytic flavours
options.d: The final sweetness of the wine

notes.a: The second fermentation raises the abv (by about 1.5%); dosage is about sweetness.
notes.b: The pressure comes from CO2 trapped during the second fermentation.
notes.c: This is set by the time on the lees, before riddling and disgorgement.
notes.d: Correct: the liqueur d'expédition (wine plus, usually, sugar) sets the final sweetness.

Q-L2-24-08.stem: Wines labelled 'Brut' have a very small amount of sugar added at dosage. Why do they still taste dry?

options.a: Their high acidity and lively bubbles mask it.
options.b: The yeast ferment the added sugar in the bottle.
options.c: Their high alcohol balances out the sugar.
options.d: Their autolytic flavours hide the sweetness.

notes.a: Correct: as stated in the book.
notes.b: No: dosage comes after disgorgement, once the lees (yeast) have been removed.
notes.c: Sparkling base wines are low in alcohol; the book credits acidity and bubbles.
notes.d: The book credits the acidity and bubbles, not autolysis.

Q-L2-24-09.stem: What level of sweetness does the term 'Demi-Sec' indicate on a sparkling wine label?

options.a: Medium sweetness
options.b: No sweetness at all
options.c: Full, luscious sweetness
options.d: Very slight sweetness, tasting dry

notes.a: Correct: the liqueur d'expédition contains more sugar for these wines.
notes.b: Demi-Sec has more sugar added at dosage than Brut, so it is not bone dry.
notes.c: Too sweet: the book says Demi-Sec indicates medium sweetness.
notes.d: That describes Brut: a very small amount of sugar, but it tastes dry.

Q-L2-24-10.stem: What does the term 'Méthode traditionnelle' on a sparkling wine label tell you?

options.a: The second fermentation took place in the bottle.
options.b: The second fermentation took place in a sealed tank.
options.c: The wine was aged for at least three years on its lees.
options.d: The wine was made in the Champagne region of France.

notes.a: Correct: all wines labelled Traditional Method or Méthode traditionnelle are made this way.
notes.b: That is the tank method (e.g. Prosecco).
notes.c: No lees time is implied; even Champagne's legal minimum is 12 months.
notes.d: The method is used worldwide, e.g. for Cava and Cap Classique.

Q-L2-24-13.stem: Why are most Champagnes made as non-vintage wines?

options.a: Blending several vintages adds autolytic biscuit and toast notes.
options.b: Blending several vintages gives a consistent style each year.
options.c: Blending several vintages raises the alcohol of the base wine.
options.d: Blending several vintages lets them spend less time on lees.

notes.a: Autolytic notes come from time on the lees, not from blending vintages.
notes.b: Correct: the book says most Champagnes blend base wines from several vintages to achieve consistency.
notes.c: Base wines are meant to be low in alcohol; the blend is for consistency.
notes.d: Lees time is separate; even the cheapest Champagnes spend the 12-month legal minimum.

Q-L2-24-03.stem: Prosecco DOC rosé is made mainly from the same white grape as white Prosecco. Which grape is added in a small proportion to give the pink colour?

options.a: Garnacha
options.b: Meunier
options.c: Corvina
options.d: Pinot Noir

notes.a: Not a Prosecco grape in the book; Garnacha is linked to Spain and the Rhône.
notes.b: A black Champagne grape, but the book names Pinot Noir for Prosecco rosé.
notes.c: The main Valpolicella grape of north-east Italy, but not used for Prosecco rosé.
notes.d: Correct: the book says rosé Prosecco is mainly Glera with a small proportion of Pinot Noir.

Q-L2-24-05.stem: A sparkling wine is light-bodied and off-dry, with pear, melon and blossom aromas and no autolytic notes. Which wine is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Cava
options.b: Asti DOCG
options.c: Prosecco DOC
options.d: Champagne AOC

notes.a: Traditional method, so it has (subtle) autolytic character; light apple and lemon.
notes.b: Asti is sweet, not off-dry, with grape, peach and pear flavours from Moscato.
notes.c: Correct: Glera gives pear, melon and blossom; the tank method leaves no autolytic character; dry or off-dry.
notes.d: Traditional method, so it shows autolytic notes (biscuit, toast); usually Brut.

Q-L2-24-17.stem: Why may grapes for Cava in Catalunya need to be harvested early?

options.a: Early picking builds the sugar needed for the second fermentation.
options.b: The warm climate means they must be picked to keep high acidity.
options.c: Early picking adds the autolytic notes typical of Cava.
options.d: The cool climate brings a risk of autumn frosts and rot.

notes.a: Sugar for the second fermentation is added with the yeast; early picking keeps acid.
notes.b: Correct: per the book; the base wine typically has light apple and lemon flavours.
notes.c: Autolytic notes come from lees ageing, and Cava's are very subtle.
notes.d: The book describes Catalunya's climate as warm, not cool.

Q-L2-24-18.stem: Which of these sparkling wines is LEAST likely to show any autolytic (bread, biscuit) character?

options.a: Cava
options.b: Cap Classique
options.c: Prosecco DOC
options.d: Non-vintage Champagne

notes.a: Traditional method; shorter lees ageing than Champagne gives subtle, but present, autolytic notes.
notes.b: South African traditional method, so the wine ages on its lees in bottle.
notes.c: Correct: typically tank method; the lees are filtered out, so it tastes of the base wine.
notes.d: Traditional method, with at least 12 months on the lees.

Q-L2-24-22.stem: Which of these is NOT a feature of the tank method for dry sparkling wines?

options.a: Second fermentation in a sealed tank, not a bottle
options.b: Lower cost and less labour than bottle fermentation
options.c: Autolytic flavours from long contact with the lees
options.d: Removal of the lees by filtration before bottling

notes.a: This IS a feature: base wine, yeast and sugar go into a sealed tank.
notes.b: This IS a feature: the book says it is significantly less expensive and labour intensive.
notes.c: Correct: tank-method wines have no autolytic character and taste mainly of the base wine.
notes.d: This IS a feature: the lees are filtered out and the wine is bottled under pressure.

Q-L2-24-23.stem: In the Asti method, how is the fermentation stopped so the wine stays sweet and low in alcohol?

options.a: Sugar is added to the tank after the yeasts have finished.
options.b: The yeasts are filtered out before all the sugar has fermented.
options.c: The tank is opened so that the CO2 escapes and the yeasts die.
options.d: Grape spirit is added to kill the yeasts part-way through.

notes.a: The sweetness is grape sugar left unfermented, not sugar added afterwards.
notes.b: Correct: per the book; the tank is sealed part-way through so the CO2 is kept.
notes.c: CO2 escapes at the START; the tank is then sealed to keep the bubbles.
notes.d: That is fortification, as for Port; it would also raise the alcohol.

Q-L2-24-24.stem: A sparkling wine is sweet, light-bodied and low in alcohol, with pronounced blossom, grape and peach aromas. Which wine is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Asti DOCG
options.b: Cava
options.c: Cap Classique
options.d: Prosecco DOC

notes.a: Correct: Moscato from Piemonte, made by the Asti method; usually fully sparkling.
notes.b: Traditional method: light apple and lemon with subtle autolytic notes; not grapey or sweet.
notes.c: Traditional method, so it has autolytic notes; not grapey and sweet.
notes.d: Glera gives pear, melon and blossom, but Prosecco is typically dry or off-dry.

Q-L2-24-25.stem: Which grape variety is used to make the base wine for Prosecco DOC?

options.a: Chardonnay
options.b: Garganega
options.c: Glera
options.d: Moscato

notes.a: A Champagne grape; Prosecco is made from Glera.
notes.b: The grape of Soave, a still white from the Veneto.
notes.c: Correct: a white variety giving light- to medium-bodied wines with pear, melon and blossom (p. 115).
notes.d: Moscato (Muscat) is the grape of Asti DOCG, also from Italy.

Q-L2-24-26.stem: Which grape variety is Asti DOCG made from, and what aromas does it give?

options.a: Moscato, giving blossom, grape and peach
options.b: Cortese, giving apple, lemon and pear
options.c: Barbera, giving red cherry and red plum
options.d: Glera, giving pear, melon and blossom

notes.a: Correct: Asti DOCG is sweet, fruity and light-bodied, from Piemonte (p. 115).
notes.b: Cortese makes still, dry Gavi DOCG, also in Piemonte.
notes.c: Barbera makes the still red Barbera d'Asti DOCG; don't confuse the two.
notes.d: Glera is the grape of Prosecco DOC.

Q-L2-25-02.stem: Why does flor not develop on Oloroso Sherry?

options.a: It is aged in stainless steel tanks rather than in the oak-cask solera.
options.b: It is fortified to only about 15% abv, which is too weak for flor to grow.
options.c: It is made from sun-dried Pedro Ximénez grapes rather than Palomino.
options.d: It is fortified to about 17% abv, too strong for flor to survive.

notes.a: All these Sherries age in the solera of old-oak casks.
notes.b: 15% is the Fino level, where flor DOES grow.
notes.c: Oloroso is a dry style from the Palomino base wine.
notes.d: Correct: without flor's protection it ages oxidatively.

Q-L2-25-03.stem: What is the key difference in when Sherry and Port are fortified?

options.a: Each is fortified during fermentation, Sherry earlier than Port.
options.b: Sherry during fermentation; Port after fermentation is complete.
options.c: Each is fortified after fermentation, Port longer after than Sherry.
options.d: Sherry after fermentation is complete; Port during fermentation.

notes.a: Sherry is fortified only after fermentation is complete.
notes.b: Reversed. That is why all Port is sweet while most Sherry is dry.
notes.c: Port is fortified to interrupt fermentation, which leaves sugar in the wine.
notes.d: Correct: Sherry is fortified once fermentation is complete; grape spirit interrupts Port's fermentation.

Q-L2-25-04.stem: What does the grape spirit added during Port fermentation do?

options.a: It speeds up fermentation, so all the sugar is used.
options.b: It sweetens the wine, as it is made from sun-dried grapes.
options.c: It adds oxidative flavours to create the tawny styles.
options.d: It kills the yeast, leaving a sweet wine high in alcohol.

notes.a: The reverse: it stops fermentation, leaving sugar unfermented.
notes.b: Grape spirit adds alcohol, not sugar; PX wine is used to sweeten some Sherries.
notes.c: Tawny character comes from long barrel ageing, not from the spirit.
notes.d: Correct: the fermentation is interrupted, so sugar remains (p. 118).

Q-L2-25-05.stem: From which grape variety is the base wine for almost all Sherry made?

options.a: Moscato
options.b: Palomino
options.c: Pedro Ximénez
options.d: Albariño

notes.a: In the L2 book this is a grape for sweet sparkling wines such as Asti, not Sherry.
notes.b: Correct: a local white grape that gives a simple, dry base wine.
notes.c: Used for the sweet PX style, from sun-dried grapes; not the base for most Sherry.
notes.d: A Spanish white grape from Rías Baixas, used for still, unfortified wines.

Q-L2-25-06.stem: What is the main purpose of the solera system in Sherry production?

options.a: To ferment the base wine slowly at a cool temperature.
options.b: To add new-oak flavours such as vanilla to the maturing wine.
options.c: To keep each vintage separate so it can be sold with its year.
options.d: To blend wines of different ages for a consistent, complex style.

notes.a: The wine is fortified after fermentation, before it enters the solera.
notes.b: The solera uses OLD-oak casks; its purpose is blending, not oak flavour.
notes.c: The reverse: continual blending of different ages gives consistency.
notes.d: Correct: old-oak casks of wines of different ages are continually blended as they age.

Q-L2-25-07.stem: In biological ageing, how does the layer of flor affect a Fino Sherry?

options.a: It shields the wine from oxygen and adds bread-dough notes.
options.b: It adds sweetness and dried fruit such as fig and raisin.
options.c: It exposes the wine to oxygen and adds walnut and caramel.
options.d: It raises the alcohol and gives a deep brown colour.

notes.a: Correct: flor forms on the surface, protecting from oxygen, and gives Fino's bread-dough character.
notes.b: These describe PX; Fino is a dry style.
notes.c: These are oxidative notes, as in Oloroso, where there is no flor.
notes.d: Fino is pale lemon; a brown colour comes from oxidative ageing.

Q-L2-25-08.stem: A dry Sherry is pale lemon, with aromas of apple, almonds and pronounced bread dough. Which style is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Pale Cream
options.b: Fino
options.c: Oloroso
options.d: Amontillado

notes.a: A sweetened Fino; the stem says the wine is dry.
notes.b: Correct: biological ageing under flor gives bread dough; protection from oxygen keeps it pale.
notes.c: Brown, with raisin, prune, walnut and caramel; no flor character.
notes.d: Has bread dough too, but is notably deeper in colour, with walnut and caramel.

Q-L2-25-09.stem: When should a Fino Sherry be drunk after bottling, and how should it be served?

options.a: Drunk as early as possible, at room temperature
options.b: Cellared for several years, and decanted first
options.c: Cellared for several years, and served chilled
options.d: Drunk as early as possible, and served chilled

notes.a: Right on timing, but the book says Fino is best served chilled.
notes.b: Decanting off a deposit applies to Vintage Port, not Fino.
notes.c: Fino loses its freshness rapidly after bottling; it does not improve.
notes.d: Correct: Fino rapidly loses its freshness after bottling and is best served chilled.

options.a: Made from sun-dried grapes, then fortified and aged oxidatively.
options.b: Aged under flor, then refortified so it ages oxidatively.
options.c: Aged under flor throughout, then sweetened before bottling.
options.d: Fortified to about 17% at the start, so flor never grows on it.

notes.a: That is PX (Pedro Ximénez).
notes.b: Correct: refortifying to about 17% abv kills the flor; it gains walnut and caramel on top of bread dough.
notes.c: That is Pale Cream (a sweetened Fino).
notes.d: That is Oloroso.

Q-L2-25-11.stem: A dry Sherry is brown, with aromas of raisin, prune, walnut and caramel and no bread-dough character. Which style is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Fino
options.b: Oloroso
options.c: PX
options.d: Amontillado

notes.a: Pale lemon, with apple, almond and bread dough from flor.
notes.b: Correct: fortified to about 17% so no flor grows; oxidative ageing gives these notes.
notes.c: Brown, with dried fruit, but sweet; the stem says the wine is dry.
notes.d: Would also show bread-dough notes from its time under flor.

Q-L2-25-12.stem: What is a Pale Cream Sherry?

options.a: A dry, pale Amontillado
options.b: A naturally sweet PX
options.c: A sweetened Fino
options.d: A sweetened Oloroso

notes.a: Amontillado is dry and deeper than Fino; Pale Cream is sweet.
notes.b: PX is labelled PX (Pedro Ximénez): sun-dried grapes, deep brown.
notes.c: Correct: per the book.
notes.d: Sweetened Oloroso is usually labelled Medium or Cream.

Q-L2-25-13.stem: The terms 'Medium' and 'Cream' on a Sherry label are often used for which wines?

options.a: Sweetened Fino Sherries
options.b: Naturally sweet PX wines
options.c: Unsweetened Oloroso or Amontillado
options.d: Sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso

notes.a: A sweetened Fino is labelled Pale Cream.
notes.b: These are labelled PX; PX is often the sweetening component IN Cream Sherry.
notes.c: Dry Sherries that are sweetened must carry a different term, such as Medium or Cream.
notes.d: Correct: per the book.

Q-L2-25-14.stem: How is PX (Pedro Ximénez) Sherry made sweet?

options.a: Its black grapes are dried indoors before a slow fermentation.
options.b: Its white grapes are sun-dried to concentrate their sugar.
options.c: Its grapes are left on the vine until affected by noble rot.
options.d: Its dry base wine is sweetened with sugar before bottling.

notes.a: PX grapes are white, not black, and they are dried in the sun.
notes.b: Correct: the wine is then fortified and aged oxidatively in the solera.
notes.c: Noble rot is used for wines such as Sauternes and Tokaj, not PX.
notes.d: Its sweetness comes from sun-dried grapes, not from added sugar.

Q-L2-25-15.stem: A Sherry is deep brown and sweet, with pronounced fig, prune, raisin, liquorice and molasses. Which style is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: Pedro Ximénez
options.b: Oloroso
options.c: Pale Cream
options.d: Amontillado

notes.a: Correct: PX, from sun-dried white Pedro Ximénez grapes, fortified and aged oxidatively.
notes.b: Brown, with raisin and prune, but a dry style.
notes.c: A sweetened Fino, so it is pale, not deep brown.
notes.d: A dry style, with bread dough plus walnut and caramel.

Q-L2-25-16.stem: What labelling rule applies when a dry Sherry is sweetened before sale?

options.a: It must carry a different or supplementary term.
options.b: It must be labelled PX, as PX is the usual sweetener.
options.c: It must state the level of sugar in grams per litre.
options.d: It may keep its dry style name with no other term.

notes.a: Correct: e.g. Pale Cream for a sweetened Fino; Medium or Cream for sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso.
notes.b: PX is a specific sweet style made from sun-dried Pedro Ximénez grapes.
notes.c: Not the book's rule; it requires a different or supplementary term.
notes.d: No: the book says a different or supplementary term must be used.

Q-L2-25-17.stem: Which of these Sherry labelling terms does NOT indicate a sweet style?

options.a: Cream
options.b: Amontillado
options.c: PX
options.d: Pale Cream

notes.a: Sweet: often a sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso.
notes.b: Correct: a dry style (flor, then oxidative ageing).
notes.c: Sweet: from sun-dried Pedro Ximénez grapes.
notes.d: Sweet: a sweetened Fino.

Q-L2-25-01.stem: What distinguishes a Reserve Ruby Port from a standard Ruby Port?

options.a: It is made entirely from the wine of one single, stated vintage.
options.b: It is only released in years that producers declare as exceptional.
options.c: Better-quality wines with more intensity, sometimes matured longer.
options.d: It is aged oxidatively in small barrels for many years before bottling.

notes.a: That describes LBV (and Vintage Port).
notes.b: That describes Vintage Port.
notes.c: Correct: as described in the book.
notes.d: That describes the best tawny-style Ports.

Q-L2-25-18.stem: What is the first step in Port making after the harvest, and how is it traditionally done?

options.a: Slow extraction of colour and tannin, by long maceration
options.b: Rapid extraction of colour and tannin, by foot treading
options.c: Gentle whole-bunch pressing, to avoid extracting tannin
options.d: Drying the grapes in the sun, to concentrate the sugar

notes.a: The book stresses RAPID extraction from the skins.
notes.b: Correct: machines now also exist for this purpose.
notes.c: Port needs colour and tannin from the skins of black grapes.
notes.d: Sun-drying is used for PX Sherry, not Port.

Q-L2-25-19.stem: Which description best fits an inexpensive Ruby Port?

options.a: Sweet and highly tannic, with very concentrated black fruit.
options.b: Sweet and pale, with walnut, coffee and caramel notes.
options.c: Dry and pale, with bread dough and almond flavours.
options.d: Sweet and simple, with lower tannin and some red fruit.

notes.a: That fits Vintage Port.
notes.b: Walnut, coffee and caramel come from long oxidative ageing (aged tawny styles).
notes.c: That describes Fino Sherry; all Port is sweet.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; other ruby styles have more tannin and intensity.

Q-L2-25-20.stem: Why are some Reserve Ruby Ports matured for longer than standard Ruby Ports?

options.a: To let the wines of a single vintage be declared.
options.b: To develop a tawny colour and walnut and caramel notes.
options.c: To build a thick deposit so the wine must be decanted.
options.d: To soften the wine and integrate the added alcohol.

notes.a: Declaring a single vintage relates to Vintage Port, not Reserve Ruby.
notes.b: That comes from long oxidative ageing in small barrels (tawny styles).
notes.c: That is Vintage Port, after long maturation in bottle.
notes.d: Correct: per the book; Reserve Ruby also uses better-quality, more intense wines.

Q-L2-25-21.stem: How does a Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port differ from a Reserve Ruby Port?

options.a: It is a blend of several older vintages.
options.b: It is pale and simple, with low tannin.
options.c: It contains wines from a single vintage.
options.d: It is aged oxidatively in small barrels.

notes.a: That fits Reserve Ruby and most Ports; LBV is from one vintage.
notes.b: That describes inexpensive Tawny Port; LBV is a deeply coloured ruby style.
notes.c: Correct: otherwise the book says LBV is similar in style to a Reserve Ruby.
notes.d: That is how the best tawny styles get their colour.

Q-L2-25-22.stem: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of Vintage Port?

options.a: Low in tannin and ready to drink on release
options.b: Throws a thick deposit, so needs decanting
options.c: Made only in years that producers declare
options.d: Turns from ruby to garnet as it ages

notes.a: Correct: Vintage Port is high in tannin and can mature in bottle for at least 20 years.
notes.b: True: a thick deposit forms as it matures in bottle.
notes.c: True: producers only 'declare' a Vintage Port in the best years.
notes.d: True: it also develops dried fruit, leather and forest floor.

Q-L2-25-23.stem: A sweet Port is brown, with complex dried fruit, walnut, coffee and caramel notes. Which style is it MOST LIKELY to be?

options.a: 20 Year Old Tawny Port
options.b: Reserve Ruby Port
options.c: Late Bottled Vintage Port
options.d: Inexpensive Tawny Port

notes.a: Correct: long oxidative ageing in small barrels gives the brown colour and these notes.
notes.b: A ruby style: deep colour and more intense cooked black fruit.
notes.c: A ruby style: deep colour and cooked black fruit.
notes.d: Simple, fruity, low in tannin and pale; not complex oxidative notes.

Q-L2-25-24.stem: How does an inexpensive wine labelled simply 'Tawny Port' differ from a tawny with an indication of age?

options.a: It comes from a single vintage, stated on the label.
options.b: It is simple and fruity, pale, with low tannin.
options.c: It is high in tannin and needs years in bottle.
options.d: It is more complex, with stronger walnut and coffee.

notes.a: The single-vintage Ports in the book are LBV and Vintage.
notes.b: Correct: per the book; age-indicated tawnies are complex, from long oxidative ageing.
notes.c: That describes Vintage Port.
notes.d: Reversed: complexity comes from the long ageing of age-indicated tawnies.
