fr-burgundy.lead: Burgundy runs from cool Chablis in the north to the Mâconnais in the south, making Pinot Noir reds and Chardonnay whites.

p: Burgundy runs from **Chablis** in the cool north, through the moderate **Côte d'Or**, to the **Mâconnais** in the south. Pinot Noir makes its reds and Chardonnay is its main white grape. The climate is cool in the north and moderate further south, and Pinot Noir does best in the moderate areas.
The Côte d'Or comes in two halves: the **Côte de Nuits** to the north, with Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges, and the **Côte de Beaune** to the south, with Beaune and Pommard.
Regional **Bourgogne** red is light to medium-bodied, with high acidity, low tannin and fresh red fruit: drink it young. Village wines add intensity, complexity and length.
White Bourgogne is simple, with apple, lemon and high acidity. In the moderate Côte d'Or, Chardonnay gains body and riper peach and melon, with complexity from oak and lees.
Slopes facing **south or south-east** catch extra sunlight, and that is where the premier and grand cru vineyards are, giving concentrated fruit.
From broadest to rarest, there are four levels:
list: **Bourgogne AOC**: regional, covering all of Burgundy
**Grand cru**: each one an appellation of its own, the rarest and most age-worthy wines

p: Village vineyards tend to sit on flat land or at the foot of slopes. Premier and grand crus are often mid-slope: less prone to frost, on shallower, better-drained soils.

fr-inao-146.lead: Chablis is Chardonnay from the cool north of Burgundy: dry, high in acidity and almost never oaky.

p: Chablis lies in the cool north of Burgundy and makes **Chardonnay only**. The label rarely names the grape: EU rules can fix it, so 'Chablis' already means Chardonnay.
Because the climate is cool, Chablis is **dry**, with **high acidity** and a **light to medium body**, and tastes of apple, lemon and wet stones.
Oak is almost never noticeable: producers use inert vessels to keep the wine's delicacy, and that unoaked style helped make Chablis popular.
**Chablis AOC** is a village appellation. The best vineyards sit on hillsides facing south or south-west and are classed **Premier Cru** and **Grand Cru**; their wines are riper and more flavourful.
Spring frost, as late as May, is the main hazard. Growers fight it with sprinklers and heaters.

fr-bordeaux.lead: Bordeaux makes blends, mainly of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, either side of the Gironde Estuary.

p: Bordeaux sits around the **Gironde Estuary**, where the Garonne and Dordogne meet, and its wines are typically **blends**, mainly of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon.
The climate is moderate, with high rainfall from the Atlantic, so the weather varies a lot from year to year; in poor years, more Merlot goes into the blend.

Gravel soils on the Left Bank drain quickly after rain and hold heat into the evening, which lets Cabernet Sauvignon ripen, even in a maritime climate. On the Right Bank, **Saint-Émilion** and **Pomerol** are the most famous Merlot-dominated wines: full-bodied, with pronounced black fruit and oak, ageing to dried fruit and tobacco.

left.head: Left Bank
left.body: West and south of the Gironde and Garonne: Haut-Médoc and Graves. Cabernet Sauvignon typically dominates.

right.head: Right Bank
right.body: North and east of the Gironde and Dordogne: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Merlot is most important.

p: **Bordeaux AOC** and **Bordeaux Supérieur AOC** can use grapes from anywhere in the region and are typically Merlot-dominated; Supérieur has slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol.
**Grand Cru Classé** ranks the best châteaux in some sub-regions, among Bordeaux's most expensive wines. **Cru Bourgeois** is for Médoc wines not classified as Grand Cru Classé.
Why blend? Grapes flower and ripen at different times, so one frost or shower won't ruin everything.

topic-6-t47.title: Pinot Noir: the grape
topic-6-t47.lead: A thin-skinned black grape that needs a cool to moderate climate, making pale reds with high acidity and red fruit.

p: Pinot Noir is a black grape with **thin skins**, and it is hard to grow. It needs a **cool to moderate climate**: where it is too warm, the grape loses its fresh fruit and the wine tastes unattractively cooked, and planting in regions that are too warm has produced some overly alcoholic wines.
It is also **prone to rot and disease**, so in poor vintages very little good wine may be made.

Pinot Noir is usually **pale to medium** in colour, with **high acidity** and **low to medium tannins**. Its fruit is red (strawberry, raspberry and red cherry), tasting fresh or cooked depending on how ripe the grapes were.
It is usually a single-varietal wine, with sparkling wines such as Champagne the exception, and it is renowned for expressing small differences between vineyards.
Pinot Noir is often matured in oak, but small new barrels can overwhelm it, so producers often use **older or larger barrels**. The best wines have subtle oak: smoke, cloves and vanilla.
Most Pinot Noir is drunk young and fruity. Very good and outstanding wines can develop **forest floor and mushroom** over several years.

topic-6-t49.title: Pinot Noir outside France
topic-6-t49.lead: Outside France, Pinot Noir is grown where fogs, sea breezes or a northerly latitude keep the climate cool enough.

p: Most of California is too warm for Pinot Noir, so it is grown only in coastal regions. **Los Carneros** is cooled by morning fogs from San Pablo Bay, **western Sonoma** by Pacific breezes, and **Santa Barbara County** by sea breezes from the west and south. Expect ripe strawberry and red cherry, often with notable oak; the finest develop forest floor and mushroom.
In **Oregon**, a northerly latitude and Pacific exposure make the climate mostly moderate, which is ideal. The wines have complex, fresh red fruit and subtle oak, and age to earth and mushroom.
Chile's **Casablanca Valley** is cooled by sea breezes and morning fogs. Its Pinot Noir has red fruit, sometimes herbal, and is good value.
In South Africa, Pinot Noir comes from the coolest coastal regions. In **Walker Bay**, strong southerly sea breezes encourage vibrant red fruit, and the wines are very good to outstanding.

Australia is warm overall, with some moderate and cool areas. The **Yarra Valley** and **Mornington Peninsula**, in Victoria, are cooled by breezes from the Southern Ocean. Styles run from light and fragrant to riper wines with cooked red fruit, with medium tannins.
Pinot Noir is New Zealand's premier black grape. It grows in cool **Martinborough** and **Marlborough**, and in **Central Otago**, which makes the ripest, most powerful examples.

In Central Otago a ring of mountains blocks sea breezes and rain, giving intensely sunny days and cool nights. The wines have pronounced strawberry and red cherry, medium to full body and medium tannins; they are often oak-matured and may need a few years of bottle age.
