4.name: PDO and PGI terms by country

L2-card-79.head: CH 20: CARMENÈRE, MALBEC, PINOTAGE
L2-card-79.body:
- Each a "regional speciality" tied to one country: Carmenère - Chile; Malbec - Argentina; Pinotage - South Africa.
- Carmenère: native to Bordeaux, now rare there; needs a long sunny season; struggles except in the warmest, sunniest Central Valley sites. Unripe: pungent green bell pepper, tomato leaf. Ripe: fresh blackberry. Deep colour, medium to high acid, high tannin, full body; oak softens tannins (coffee, chocolate). Ages to leather, earth. Widely grown in Chile. More commonly blended (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot) than single-varietal.

L2-card-14.head: GERMANY: LANDWEIN, QUALITÄTSWEIN, PRÄDIKATSWEIN
L2-card-14.body:
- Landwein: PGI; typically light-bodied, dry to off-dry.
- Qualitätswein: PDO; must come from one of 13 winegrowing areas (e.g. Rheingau, Mosel); higher ripeness than Landwein; typically more intense flavour and fuller body.
- Germany's cool climate means growers often struggle to ripen grapes, so much label terminology reflects ripeness (sugar) at harvest (p. 60).

L2-card-49.head: CH 6: PINOT NOIR - OUTSIDE FRANCE
L2-card-49.body:
- California: mostly too warm; coastal regions only. Los Carneros cooled by morning fogs from San Pablo Bay; western Sonoma by Pacific breezes; Santa Barbara County by sea breezes from west and south. Ripe red fruit (strawberry, red cherry), often notable oak; finest develop forest floor, mushroom.
- Oregon: northerly latitude + Pacific exposure = mostly moderate, ideal; complex fresh red fruit, subtle oak; ages to earth, mushroom.
- Chile: Casablanca Valley, cooled by sea breezes and morning fogs; red fruit, sometimes herbal; good value.

L2-card-04b.head: NOSE DETAIL
L2-card-04b.body: - Character and clarity of aromas account for much of the difference between basic and very fine wines (p. 9). Simple wine = few primary aromas, often in one cluster; complex = many, across clusters. Most wines are fruity; also check for floral, herbaceous etc. (p. 10).

L2-card-55b.head: CH 9: SÉMILLON/SEMILLON
L2-card-55b.body:
- Barossa Valley: range from Hunter-like styles to full-bodied, oak-matured.
- Spelling: Sémillon in France, Semillon in English-speaking countries. Australia: significant plantings; often blended (e.g. with Sauvignon Blanc); used for botrytised sweet and various dry styles (p. 64-65).

L2-card-37.head: SPEC GIs: REGIONALLY IMPORTANT BLACK GRAPES
L2-card-37.body:
- Gamay: Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages, Beaujolais Cru (Fleurie).
- Grenache/Garnacha: Southern Rhône Côtes du Rhône, Côtes du Rhône Villages, Châteauneuf-du-Pape; Languedoc-Roussillon and Provence Minervois, Côtes de Provence; Spain Rioja, Navarra, Priorat; Australia Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale.
- Tempranillo: Spain Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Catalunya. Terms: Joven/Genérico, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva.
- Nebbiolo: Barolo, Barbaresco. Barbera: Barbera d'Asti.
- Sangiovese: Chianti, Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino. Term: Riserva.
- Corvina: Valpolicella, Amarone della Valpolicella, Recioto della Valpolicella. Term: Classico.
- Montepulciano: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.
- Zinfandel/Primitivo: USA California; Italy Puglia.
- Pinotage: South Africa Western Cape. Term: Cape Blend.
- Carmenère: Chile Central Valley. Malbec: Argentina Mendoza.

L2-card-24.head: FOOD AND WINE TABLE: FOOD IS... WINE SEEMS...
L2-card-24.body:
- Sweet: more drying and bitter, more acidic; less sweet and fruity. Rule: choose a wine sweeter than the dish.
- Umami: more drying and bitter, more acidic; less sweet and fruity. Examples: cooked or dried mushrooms, air-dried meats, aged cheeses, miso.
- Salty: less drying and bitter, less acidic; more fruity, more body. Salt softens tannin.
- Acidic: less drying and bitter, less acidic; more sweet and fruity. (But if wine acidity is low, acidic food makes it seem less fruity.)
- Highly flavoured: wine overwhelmed by the food flavours. Match flavour intensities.
- Fatty/oily: wine seems less acidic. Acidic wine "cuts through" fat (very subjective).
- Hot (chilli heat): alcohol in the wine seems more noticeable, and alcohol increases the burning sensation of chilli.
Individual sensitivities and preferences vary; take them into account.
- Umami is hard to isolate: it tends to come with other tastes, such as salt, that balance its negative effects (p. 17).

L2-card-75.head: CH 17: GAMAY AND BEAUJOLAIS
L2-card-75.body:
- Black grape; wines almost exclusively from one region, Beaujolais (moderate climate, directly south of Burgundy).
- High acidity, low to medium tannins, red fruit (raspberry, red cherry, red plum). Usually inert vessels; rarely shows oak.
- Winemakers use techniques that maximise colour and minimise tannin; these can create banana and candy aromas.
- Beaujolais wines: light to medium body, low to medium tannin, red fruit. Sometimes served lightly chilled. Most for immediate drinking; lose fresh fruit quickly.
- Hierarchy: Beaujolais AOC (flat, fertile south; high yields; lightest, simplest) -> Beaujolais Villages AOC (northern villages; slopes give more sun exposure, warm well-drained soils; more intensity and body) -> 10 crus with own appellations, all within the Beaujolais Villages area, e.g. Fleurie AOC (most concentrated and structured; medium to pronounced red fruit, medium to long finish; some can develop in bottle).

L2-card-51.head: CH 7: ZINFANDEL/PRIMITIVO
L2-card-51.body:
- Black grape, needs a warm climate. Ripens from red fruit (strawberry, raspberry) to black fruit (black plum, blackberry, blueberry). Uneven ripening: some berries raisin before others ripen -> high sugar, dried fruit (prune, raisin).
- White Zinfandel (California): medium-sweet rosé; typically short maceration; low alcohol (8-10%) by removing yeast before fermentation finishes; pink, simple strawberry, raspberry.
- Red Zinfandel (California): full red fermentation on skins; often oak to soften tannins and add complexity. Pronounced red and black fruit, dried fruit, oak (vanilla, coffee); dry, medium to high acidity and tannin, HIGH alcohol, full body. Very old vines -> concentrated; tertiary earth, meat.
- Labels: rosé Zinfandel low abv; red Zinfandel high abv (e.g. 15.5%).
- Italy: Primitivo in warm Puglia; soft, fruity, dry reds for high-volume brands; top examples from controlled yields can be excellent value.

L2-card-10.head: BOTTLE AGEING CHANGES
L2-card-10.body:
- Most wines do not improve in bottle: fruit fades, replaced with vegetal notes.
- Wines that age well OFTEN have high acidity, high sugar (sweet wines) and high tannin (reds). Above all, they NEED enough flavour concentration to evolve positively.
- Whites: colour lemon -> gold -> amber, and DEEPER in intensity. Tertiary: dried apricot, honey, nut, spice.
- Reds: colour ruby -> garnet -> tawny -> brown, and typically PALER in intensity. Tannins softer and smoother. Tertiary: fig, prune, meat, wet leaves. Deposits can form; decant if heavy.

L2-card-94.head: CH 25: PORT
L2-card-94.body:
- Ruby: sweet, simple, fruity, lower tannin, some red fruit. Reserve Ruby: better wines, more intensity, sometimes longer maturation to soften and integrate the spirit. LBV: like Reserve Ruby but from a single vintage.
- Vintage Port: best wines of a single exceptional vintage; high tannin, very concentrated; matures in bottle 20+ years: ruby to garnet, dried fruit, leather, forest floor; thick deposit, must be decanted. Only "declared" in the best years.
- Tawny styles: best get colour from long oxidative ageing in small barrels; increasingly brown; dried fruit, walnut, coffee, caramel; age indications 10, 20, 30, 40 years. Inexpensive "Tawny Port": simple, fruity, low tannin, pale.

L2-card-28.head: OPENING AND DECANTING
L2-card-28.body:
- Still wine (method applies only to cork or synthetic cork): remove top of capsule, clean the neck; centre the corkscrew, draw cork gently; wipe inside and outside of neck.
- Sparkling: high pressure; chilling reduces it, but the cork can still fly out and injure someone. Remove foil, loosen wire cage, keep hand on cork from then on; bottle at an angle; hold the cork in one hand and the base of the bottle in the other, and TURN THE BOTTLE; release pressure with a quiet "phut".
- Decanting (wines with heavy deposit; the deposit is natural, formed during bottle ageing of some reds): keep bottle horizontal (decanting basket), gently remove capsule top, clean shoulder and neck, remove cork gently, pour in front of a light, stop when deposit reaches the neck.

L2-card-59.head: CH 10: CHARDONNAY - FRANCE
L2-card-59.body:
- Côte d'Or: moderate; more body, riper (peach, melon). Chardonnay focus is the Côte de Beaune: Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. Oak fermentation/maturation and lees ageing add complexity and body. Premier and grand crus develop hazelnut, mushroom for decades; considered the pinnacle of Chardonnay.
- Mâconnais: fruity, mostly unoaked, simple (lemon, peach, melon) = Mâcon AOC. Pouilly-Fuissé: steep east and south-east slopes; concentrated stone and tropical fruit; often oak.
- Languedoc-Roussillon: warm; mostly Pays d'Oc IGP; peach, pineapple, banana; chips/staves in cheaper wines.
- Languedoc-Roussillon: Mediterranean coast of southern France, from the Spanish border to the Rhône; AOCs plus Pays d'Oc IGP; best may be barrel-fermented/matured (p. 69).

L2-card-50.head: CH 6: PINOT NOIR - OUTSIDE FRANCE
L2-card-50.body:
- South Africa: coolest coastal regions; Walker Bay, strong southerly sea breezes encourage vibrant red fruit; very good to outstanding.
- Australia (overall warm; some moderate and cool areas): Yarra Valley and Mornington Peninsula (Victoria), cooled by Southern Ocean breezes; light and fragrant to riper, cooked red fruit, medium tannins.
- New Zealand: premier black grape. Martinborough, Marlborough (cool). Central Otago: ripest, most powerful; ring of mountains blocks sea breezes and rain; intensely sunny days, cool nights; pronounced strawberry, red cherry, medium to full body, medium tannins.
- Central Otago Pinot is often oak-matured and may need a few years of bottle age (p. 55).

L2-card-12.head: PDO AND PGI LABELLING TERMS BY COUNTRY
L2-card-12.body:
- France: PDO = Appellation d'origine protégée (AOP) or Appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC). PGI = Indication géographique protégée (IGP).
- Italy: PDO = Denominazione di Origine Controllata (DOC), Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita (DOCG). PGI = Indicazione Geografica Tipica (IGT).
- Spain: PDO = Denominación de Origen (DO), Denominación de Origen Calificada (DOCa). PGI = Vino de la Tierra.
- Germany: PDO = Qualitätswein, Prädikatswein. PGI = Landwein.
Examples of PGIs named in the book: Pays d'Oc IGP (Languedoc-Roussillon), Veneto IGT, Vino de la Tierra, Landwein.

L2-card-26.head: SERVICE TEMPERATURES
L2-card-26.body:
- Sweet wines (e.g. Sauternes): well chilled, 6-8°C (43-46°F)
- Sparkling wines (e.g. Champagne): well chilled, 6-10°C (43-50°F)
- Light-, medium-bodied white and rosé (e.g. Pinot Grigio): chilled, 7-10°C (45-50°F)
- Full-bodied white (e.g. oaked Chardonnay): lightly chilled, 10-13°C (50-55°F)
- Light-bodied red (e.g. Beaujolais): room temperature or lightly chilled, 13-18°C (55-64°F)
- Medium-, full-bodied red (e.g. Shiraz): room temperature, 15-18°C (59-64°F)
- Ice bucket: fill with ice AND cold water. Never heat wine (e.g. by a radiator); let it warm naturally in the room.
- Room temperatures vary (air conditioning, central heating), so use the ranges. A guest's preferred temperature overrides the guidance. An insulated container can keep wine chilled (p. 19-21).

L2-card-52.head: CH 8: RIESLING - THE GRAPE
L2-card-52.body:
- Cold-hardy white grape; prefers cool to moderate climates. Naturally high acidity and susceptible to botrytis -> outstanding wines at all sweetness levels.
- Aromatic: pronounced fruity and floral aromas, high acidity.
- Just-ripe: green fruit (apple, pear), citrus (lemon, lime), floral (blossom). Extra-ripe: stone fruit (peach, apricot), tropical (mango, pineapple), sometimes dried apricot.
- Builds sugar and flavour slowly while retaining acid -> suited to late harvest where autumns are dry and sunny.
- Off-dry/medium: interrupt fermentation by removing yeast (lower alcohol, residual sugar) or add unfermented grape juice (Süssreserve). Sweetest: extra-ripe grapes, fermentation stops naturally.
- Fermented in inert vessels (stainless steel) to preserve floral aromas. Finest age for years or decades; high acid keeps them fresh while developing honey and petrol.

L2-card-63.head: CH 11: SAUVIGNON BLANC - REGIONS
L2-card-63.body:
- Loire: Sancerre AOC and Pouilly-Fumé AOC face each other across the Loire; cool; Sauvignon the only white permitted. Dry, high acid, apple, grass, asparagus, sometimes wet stones. Touraine AOC: wider sub-region west of Sancerre; fruity, inexpensive.
- Bordeaux: Bordeaux AOC (grass, green apple; varietal or with Sémillon). Graves and Pessac-Léognan: more concentrated, complex blends with Sémillon (adds body, ageing); best oak-matured, develop honey and nuts.
- Languedoc-Roussillon: mostly too warm; best where cooled by altitude; tropical (passion fruit) and grass; Pays d'Oc IGP.

L2-card-13b.head: OTHER GRAPE-GROWING LABEL TERMS
L2-card-13b.body:
- Botrytis (noble rot): fungus makes tiny holes in ripe grapes, water evaporates, concentrating sugars, acids, flavours. Must grow on ripe grapes, with damp misty mornings then warm, dry afternoons; otherwise it can easily destroy the grapes (p. 30).
- Vintage: most wines are best young, so it shows whether a wine is past its best; for age-worthy wines, whether it is at its best. In some regions weather varies considerably year to year, which matters when buying very expensive wines from prestigious regions (p. 38).

L2-card-29.head: COMMON FAULTS
L2-card-29.body:
- Cork taint: TCA (trichloroanisole), mainly from contaminated cork; "corked"; damp cardboard aromas; fruit muted, less fresh.
- Failure of closure (oxidation): browner than expected; honey, caramel, coffee; lacks freshness and fruit. (Not a fault in oxidative styles or very old wines.)
- Heat damage: too hot, direct sunlight or bright artificial light; loses freshness and fruit character quickly.

L2-card-77b.head: CH 18: GRENACHE/GARNACHA
L2-card-77b.body:
- Australia: Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale; very old vines give concentrated red fruit, spice, long ageing; Shiraz blends can resemble Châteauneuf-du-Pape in style and quality.
- Best Châteauneuf-du-Pape develops dried fruit, earth and meat with bottle age (p. 97).

L2-card-80.head: CH 20: CARMENÈRE, MALBEC, PINOTAGE
L2-card-80.body:
- Malbec: Argentina's most important black grape; native to south-west France; most plantings in high-altitude Mendoza. Deep colour, full body, high tannin, blackberry, black plum; new oak softness and clove, vanilla; ages to dried fruit, meat. Varietal or blended with Cabernet/Merlot.
- Pinotage: developed for South Africa's warm, dry climate; closely related to Pinot Noir; red fruit (strawberry, raspberry, red cherry). Medium tannin, high acidity. Fruity medium-bodied to full-bodied (red plum, blackberry). With oak: pronounced coffee, chocolate, smoke. Grown throughout Western Cape. Blends with Cabernet and Merlot = Cape Blends.

L2-card-53.head: CH 8: RIESLING - REGIONS
L2-card-53.body:
- Germany: Riesling is the most important grape, widely planted; predominantly cool; some vineyards above 50°N.
- Mosel: one of the most northerly; lighter body; commonly medium sweetness balancing very high acidity. Best on steep south- or south-west-facing slopes by the river: aspect, stony soils, reflected sunlight.
- Rheingau: steep south-facing slopes on the north bank of the Rhine; drier and more body than Mosel.
- Pfalz: near France, mountains to the west, dry and sunny; like an extension of Alsace; typically dry and medium-bodied.
- Alsace AOC: east of the Vosges Mountains (block rain-bearing westerly winds) -> one of France's driest, sunniest regions. Best vineyards in foothills facing east/south-east (morning sun). Dry, pronounced, ripe citrus and stone fruit, medium body, high acid. Best = grands crus. Sweeter = Vendanges tardives.

L2-card-41.head: CH 4: WEATHER HAZARDS AND GROWING
L2-card-41.body:
- Cool vintage: acid too high, sugar too low, signature aromas may not develop.
- Hot vintage: uncharacteristic dried-fruit aromas, sunburn; water-stressed vines shut down and grapes stop ripening; extreme cases vines die.
- Drought: below-average rain, worse with heat; irrigation helps if water available.
- High rain: fungal disease; heavy rain near harvest swells grapes and dilutes flavour.
- Hail: can destroy an entire crop. Frost: particular risk in spring, kills new growth, reduces that year's crop.
- Training (mostly on trellises) and pruning (typically in winter while dormant) keep a healthy, viable crop.

L2-card-84.head: CH 23: SANGIOVESE AND MONTEPULCIANO
L2-card-84.body:
- Central Italy's two key black grapes; warm climate; Apennines divide Tuscany (Sangiovese) from Abruzzo (Montepulciano).
- Sangiovese: dry, high tannin, high acid; red cherry, red plum, dried herbs. Dominant in Chianti (central Tuscany), often with small amounts of other black grapes.
- Chianti DOCG: wide area in the Apennine foothills; varied quality; many simple, inexpensive, not for ageing.
- Chianti Classico DOCG: higher altitude, long ripening season; medium body, pronounced red fruit, dried herbs; often oak (cloves, cedar); best develop meat, leather.
- Chianti Classico DOCG Riserva: stricter ageing requirements; may show some tertiary character on release.

L2-card-78.head: CH 19: TEMPRANILLO
L2-card-78.body:
- Spain's most prized black grape. Medium to full body, medium acid, medium tannin; red fruit (strawberry, red cherry) and black fruit (blackberry, black plum).
- Simple to complex age-worthy; other grapes sometimes added for acid and tannin in long-ageing wines.
- Traditional: small new-oak barrels (vanilla, smoke, cedar; softens tannin); best often bottle-aged before release. Very good/outstanding develop mushroom, leather, dried fruit.
- Catalunya DO: broad region, high volumes of Tempranillo and blends; simple to powerful oak-aged.
- Rioja DOCa (north-east Spain, moderate): usually a blend, Tempranillo dominant in the best; Garnacha for early-drinking wines; other local grapes for tannin and acid in long-ageing wines.
- Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva are national Spanish ageing terms, not just Rioja.
- Ribera del Duero DO: high-altitude, further inland; warm days and cool nights -> very full-bodied with fresh black fruit.

L2-card-13.head: OTHER GRAPE-GROWING LABEL TERMS
L2-card-13.body:
- Old Vine / Vieilles vignes: older vines give fewer grapes, more concentrated and complex. NOT legally defined.
- Vintage: year the grapes were harvested. Southern hemisphere wine is about half a year older than a northern hemisphere wine of the same vintage.
- Late Harvest (Vendanges tardives in France): picked much later; riper flavours, higher sugar, fuller body. Can be dry, off-dry, medium or sweet.
- Botrytis/Noble Rot: very concentrated sugar and acid; nearly always sweet wines.
- Icewine/Eiswein: healthy grapes left on the vine into winter, frozen, pressed before they thaw; ice and skins separated from a little concentrated liquid; sweet, concentrated, pure varietal character (p. 30).
- Organic: grapes grown without most chemicals (some sprays still permitted).
- In the EU the grape variety does not necessarily appear on PDO labels (e.g. Chablis = Chardonnay). Outside the EU wines are commonly varietally labelled.

L2-card-01.head: PREPARING FOR TASTING
L2-card-01.body:
- Environment: good lighting, free of strong odours, space for glasses and notes, spittoons.
- You: clean palate (no toothpaste or strongly flavoured food); no perfume/aftershave.
- Glass: odourless, colourless, transparent, no residues. ISO glass. Two key features:
  1. Rounded bowl - aids swirling to release aromas.
  2. Inward-sloping walls - capture aromas at the top of the glass.
- Sample: 5 cL. Enough to assess appearance, nose and palate; small enough to swirl in the base of the bowl without spilling.

L2-card-11.head: GEOGRAPHICAL INDICATIONS
L2-card-11.body:
- A GI is a legally defined vineyard area: can be a whole region or country, or as small as one vineyard. Not every wine comes from a GI, but some statement of origin (e.g. country) is legally required.
- GIs outside the EU: indicate where the grapes were grown; minimal restrictions on grapes or winemaking, so styles vary; consumers look to grape variety to predict style.
- GIs inside the EU: also come with regulations on which grapes may be grown and how wines are made, so a relatively reliable guide to style.
- PDO (Protected Designation of Origin): typically small areas, tightly defined rules; many of Europe's most famous wines.
- PGI (Protected Geographical Indication): typically much wider areas, less strict rules, more flexibility on grapes and techniques; ranges from high-volume inexpensive acceptable wines to low-volume outstanding wines.

L2-card-34.head: SPEC GIs: SYRAH/SHIRAZ AND PINOT NOIR
L2-card-34.body:
SYRAH/SHIRAZ
- PGI: France Pays d'Oc. PDOs: Northern Rhône Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Côte Rôtie; Languedoc-Roussillon Minervois.
- Other: Australia South Eastern Australia, Barossa Valley, Hunter Valley.
PINOT NOIR
- PDOs: France Bourgogne/Burgundy, Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Beaune, Pommard. (No PGI listed.)
- Other: USA Sonoma, Los Carneros, Santa Barbara County, Oregon; Chile Casablanca Valley; South Africa Walker Bay; Australia Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula; New Zealand Martinborough, Marlborough, Central Otago.

L2-card-21b.head: FRANCE: BORDEAUX LABELLING TERMS
L2-card-21b.body:
- Gironde Estuary = where the Garonne and Dordogne meet (p. 82).
  - Classified wines: some classifications are old, but widely seen as a strong quality signal; among Bordeaux's most expensive; can mature for many years or decades. Cru Bourgeois: mostly lower prices, but some very good to outstanding and long-lived (p. 87).

L2-card-74.head: CH 16: SYRAH/SHIRAZ
L2-card-74.body:
- Northern Rhône: only black grape permitted in AOC wines; narrow valley, steep slopes, moderate climate, aspect aids ripening; hand-worked, expensive. Côte Rôtie: far north, northern limit for ripening Syrah; exceptionally steep, stony slopes -> complex, peppery, long-lived; some (not all) co-ferment a little Viognier (floral). Hermitage: one steep south-facing hill. Crozes-Hermitage: larger, flatter, surrounds Hermitage; less intense, cheaper (higher yields, mechanisation).
- Languedoc-Roussillon: ripens reliably; blends (e.g. Minervois AOC) or Pays d'Oc IGP.

L2-card-33.head: SPEC GIs: MERLOT AND CABERNET SAUVIGNON
L2-card-33.body:
MERLOT
- PGI: France Pays d'Oc. PDOs: France Bordeaux, Saint-Émilion, Pomerol.
- Other: USA California, Napa Valley, Sonoma; Chile Central Valley; South Africa Stellenbosch; Australia Margaret River; New Zealand Hawke's Bay.
CABERNET SAUVIGNON
- PGI: France Pays d'Oc. PDOs: France Bordeaux, Haut-Médoc, Pauillac, Margaux, Graves, Pessac-Léognan.
- Other: USA California, Napa Valley (Oakville, Rutherford, Calistoga), Sonoma; Chile Central Valley, Maipo Valley, Colchagua Valley; South Africa Stellenbosch; Australia Coonawarra, Margaret River; New Zealand Hawke's Bay.

L2-card-09.head: WSET LEVEL 2 WINE-LEXICON: SECONDARY AND TERTIARY AROMAS
L2-card-09.body:
SECONDARY AROMAS AND FLAVOURS (post-fermentation winemaking)
- Yeast (lees, autolysis, flor): biscuit, pastry, bread, toasted bread, bread dough, cheese, yogurt
- Malolactic conversion: butter, cheese, cream
- Oak: vanilla, cloves, coconut, cedar, charred wood, smoke, chocolate, coffee
TERTIARY AROMAS AND FLAVOURS (maturation)
- Red wine: dried fruit, leather, earth, mushroom, meat, tobacco, wet leaves, forest floor, caramel
- White wine: dried fruit, orange marmalade, petrol (gasoline), cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, almond, hazelnut, honey, caramel
- Deliberately oxidised wines: almond, hazelnut, walnut, chocolate, coffee, caramel

L2-card-72.head: CH 15: CABERNET SAUVIGNON - REGIONS
L2-card-72.body:
- Chile: most planted variety. Maipo and Colchagua Valleys within Central Valley, Andes to Coastal Ranges. Foothill wines: mint and green bell pepper with black fruit.
- South Africa Stellenbosch: mountainous, moderate to warm by altitude; fresh herbal to full-bodied cooked fruit. Cape Blend with Pinotage.
- Australia: Margaret River (warm, coastal breezes, winter rain; sometimes blended with Merlot; ripe black fruit, subtle oak); Coonawarra (cloud cover and cool southern breezes; mint, pronounced blackcurrant, smoke, cedar; ages long).
- NZ Hawke's Bay: needs the warmest sites; blended with Merlot; red and black fruit, green bell pepper.
- Chile: single-varietal or blended with Merlot and Carmenère; flatter, more fertile valley-floor sites too (p. 88).
- Food can sometimes help soften Cabernet's high tannin and acidity. Gentler, low-extraction winemaking gives wines to enjoy younger; Chile is having success with this style (p. 89).

L2-card-39.head: CH 4: THE GRAPE AND RIPENING
L2-card-39.body:
- Parts of the grape: skin = colour, tannins, flavours (colour and tannin much higher in black grapes); pulp = water, sugar, acids, flavours (pale in almost all grapes); seeds and stems = tannins, bitter if handled roughly.
- Stages: flowering (vines are self-pollinating) -> fruit set (flower becomes a small, hard, green grape) -> véraison (green colour lost; whites turn golden, blacks red then purple) -> ripening.
- During ripening: grapes swell with water, soften; acidity falls; sugar rises; herbaceous flavours decrease.
- White grapes: green fruit -> stone fruit -> tropical fruit as ripeness increases. Black grapes: fresh fruit -> cooked fruit.
- Black grape tannins become riper; unripe tannins taste bitter.
- Extra-ripe: left on the vine past normal harvest (needs dry, warm weather); exaggerated ripe aromas, more sugar; later grapes raisin, concentrating acid and sugar with dried-fruit aromas; used for sweet wines.

L2-card-65.head: CH 12: PINOT GRIGIO/PINOT GRIS
L2-card-65.body:
- Same white grape: Pinot Grigio (Italian name), Pinot Gris (French). Cool or moderate climates. Two styles decided mainly in the vineyard.
- Most common: high yields, picked early to keep acid -> dry, light body, medium to high acid, simple pear and lemon. Usually inert vessels, fermented dry. Drink young.
- Riper: controlled yields, delayed harvest -> more sugar, less acid, more complex: powerful, full body, medium acid, pronounced lemon, peach, mango, banana. Sometimes off-dry/medium (yeast removed). Can develop ginger and honey.

L2-card-39b.head: CH 4: THE GRAPE AND RIPENING
L2-card-39b.body:
- Vines can live 60+ years. Most wine is made from one European species. Year: spring shoots, leaves, flowers; grapes by end of summer; leaves drop in autumn; dormant in winter (p. 26).
- Photosynthesis: sunlight lets the vine combine CO2 (taken in by leaves) and water (from roots) into sugars, which power growth and ripening. Without enough heat the vine cannot grow, so it is dormant in winter (p. 27).
- Each flower cluster becomes a bunch; by mid-summer grapes are big enough for ripening to begin (véraison) (p. 28).

L2-card-48.head: CH 6: PINOT NOIR - BURGUNDY
L2-card-48.body:
- Climate cool in the north to moderate further south; Pinot best in the moderate areas. Best sites on south- and south-east-facing slopes (extra sunlight).
- Côte d'Or: northern half Côte de Nuits, southern half Côte de Beaune.
- Bourgogne AOC: light to medium body, low tannin, high acid, fresh red fruit; drink young; can still be high priced.
- Village wines: better sited; more intensity, complexity, length. Côte de Nuits: Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges. Côte de Beaune: Beaune, Pommard.
- Premier and grand cru: slopes facing south or south-east; concentrated fruit, subtle oak, pronounced tertiary (forest floor, mushroom). Grands crus are the best individual vineyards: most concentrated, complex, longest-lived, exceptionally high prices.

L2-card-86.head: CH 24: SPARKLING - PRINCIPLES AND TRADITIONAL METHOD
L2-card-86.body:
- Bubbles = dissolved CO2. Can be pumped in, but most premium producers use CO2 from a second fermentation in a sealed vessel (bottle or tank).
- Base wine: typically dry, high acid, low alcohol; usually a blend (vintages, varieties, vineyards).
- Second fermentation: add sugar and yeast; adds about 1.5% abv.

L2-card-47.head: CH 6: PINOT NOIR - THE GRAPE
L2-card-47.body:
- Black, THIN-skinned; hard to grow; needs cool to moderate climate. Too warm -> loses fresh fruit, tastes unattractively cooked. Prone to rot and disease; poor vintages can yield very little good wine.
- Wine: usually pale to medium colour; high acidity; low to medium tannins; red fruit (strawberry, raspberry, red cherry), fresh to cooked depending on ripeness.
- Usually single-varietal (exception: sparkling such as Champagne). Often oak-matured but small new oak can overwhelm it; older and/or larger barrels often used. Best have subtle oak (smoke, cloves, vanilla).
- Most drunk young and fruity; very good/outstanding can develop forest floor, mushroom over several years.
- Renowned for expressing small vineyard differences. Planting in too-warm regions has produced some overly alcoholic wines lacking identifiable Pinot fruit (p. 55).

L2-card-69.head: CH 14: MERLOT
L2-card-69.body:
- Bordeaux: moderate climate, high rainfall (Atlantic). Most widely planted variety. Left Bank (west/south of Gironde/Garonne: Médoc, Graves, Sauternes); Right Bank (north/east of Gironde and Dordogne: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol). Bordeaux AOC and Bordeaux Supérieur AOC typically Merlot-dominated. Most famous Merlot-dominated: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol; full body, pronounced black fruit, oak; age to dried fruit, tobacco.
- Bordeaux wines are typically blends, mainly Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon; proportions depend on intended style, but soil types and each year's weather also matter (p. 82).

L2-card-73.head: CH 16: SYRAH/SHIRAZ
L2-card-73.body:
- Same black grape: Syrah (France), Shiraz (Australia). Thick-skinned, small grapes; needs moderate to warm climate; medium to high tannin and acidity.
- Moderate climate (Northern Rhône style, "Syrah"): medium body, fresh black cherry, blackberry, herbal notes, black pepper. Warm climate (Australian style, "Shiraz"): full body, high alcohol, cooked black fruit, liquorice. Outside France and Australia the name used hints at style.
- Adds colour, black fruit, tannin to blends, often with Grenache ("Rhône Blends"). Oak common (softens tannin; smoke, spice). Best age a decade or more: dried fruit, leather, meat, earth.

L2-card-67b.head: CH 13: GEWURZTRAMINER, VIOGNIER, ALBARIÑO
L2-card-67b.body: - Gewurztraminer and Viognier make some of the world's fullest-bodied, most floral whites (p. 79). Viognier is now widely planted; used single-varietal or as a blending partner to add floral notes and body (p. 80).

L2-card-71.head: CH 15: CABERNET SAUVIGNON - REGIONS
L2-card-71.body:
- Bordeaux Left Bank: gravel soils drain quickly after rain and hold heat into the evening, helping Cabernet ripen in a maritime climate. Haut-Médoc (incl. Margaux, Pauillac), Graves (incl. Pessac-Léognan). Weather varies a lot; in poor years more Merlot goes into the blend.
- Languedoc-Roussillon: warm, reliable; Pays d'Oc IGP.
- California: Napa Valley (warm, sunny, long season): Oakville and Rutherford (full body, ripe black fruit, high ripe tannins); Calistoga in the far north is warmer still, ripest. Warmer inland Sonoma similar. "California" = blends from across the state, much from hot Central Valley; oak via chips/staves.
- Napa/Sonoma wines labelled Cabernet Sauvignon may contain small quantities of other grapes (p. 87).

L2-card-54.head: CH 9: CHENIN BLANC
L2-card-54.body:
- Very versatile; grows in cool, moderate and warm climates. Flavours by ripeness: green fruit (apple), citrus (lemon) -> stone fruit (peach), tropical (pineapple, mango).
- Naturally high acidity; suits late harvest; susceptible to botrytis -> dry to sweet styles; oaked and unoaked. Best age for many years.
- Vouvray AOC (Loire): only Chenin permitted; dry, off-dry, medium, sweet and sparkling. Dry: fresh apple. Off-dry/medium labelled Demi-Sec. Sweeter: extra-ripe or botrytis grapes, stone/tropical fruit. Typically unoaked. Best age to honey, dried fruit.
- South Africa: most planted white grape; prized for keeping high acidity in a warm climate. High-volume "Western Cape" from warmer inland areas, often blended (e.g. with Chardonnay); dry, medium body, peach, pineapple, sometimes vanilla from chips/staves. Old vines -> very good/outstanding, tropical fruit, smoke, vanilla from oak.

L2-card-88.head: CH 24: SPARKLING - PRINCIPLES AND TRADITIONAL METHOD
L2-card-88.body:
- Brut: very small amount of sugar but tastes dry (high acid, lively bubbles). Demi-Sec: medium sweetness.
- Champagne AOC: northern France; cool climate gives low-alcohol, high-acid base. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier. Most non-vintage (blends of vintages for consistency). Legal minimum 12 months on lees for the cheapest (apple, light autolytic). Very good: apple, lemon, toasted bread, biscuit. Vintage Champagne: exceptional years; long on lees plus bottle age; nuts and honey; small quantities, very high prices.
- 'Dosage' also means the amount of sugar added. Most traditional-method wines are labelled Brut. Better Champagnes: riper grapes, longer on lees (p. 113).

L2-card-70.head: CH 15: CABERNET SAUVIGNON - THE GRAPE
L2-card-70.body:
- Black grape from south-west France; pronounced black fruit and herbaceous aromas, high tannins, high acidity.
- Moderate and warm climates; in moderate climates struggles to ripen except in the warmest sites. THICK skins: high colour, flavour, tannin. Needs a long, warm season.
- Single-varietal: deep colour, dry, high acid, high tannin, medium to full body; pronounced blackcurrant, black cherry; usually mint or green bell pepper. Warm climates: fruit can turn cooked.
- Often blended (e.g. with Merlot) to soften tannin and acid - especially in cool vintages in moderate regions.
- Newly fermented can taste very tannic; oak matured months or years: oxygen softens tannin; new oak adds smoke, vanilla, cloves, cedar.
- Tannin and acid act as preservatives; best age many years: dried fruit, earth, forest floor.

L2-card-07.head: QUALITY: FOUR CRITERIA
L2-card-07.body:
- Balance: e.g. sugar balanced by acidity; alcohol less burning if enough fruit intensity; high acid seems thin without enough fruit. Out of balance = rarely more than acceptable.
- Length/finish: short finish = lower quality; how it finishes also matters (alcohol burn is negative).
- Intensity: weak, dilute = seldom good; beyond a point more intensity is not necessarily better. Also called "concentration".
- Complexity: desirable in many wines, but not all premium wines are complex; purity and definition can make a wine great (e.g. ice wines), and oak/tertiary could detract.
Scoring:
- Outstanding = positive on all four.
- Very good = positive on three, short on one.
- Good = positive on two, short on two.
- Acceptable = positive on one, short on three.
- Poor = problems on all four.
- Complexity can come from primary aromas alone, or from primary combined with secondary/tertiary. Example: very good = balanced, a range of flavours, medium intensity, but a short finish (p. 14).

L2-card-05.head: PALATE: SWEETNESS, ACIDITY, TANNIN
L2-card-05.body:
- Sweetness: dry = none detectable; off-dry = tiny detectable amount; medium = distinct sugar but generally not sweet enough for most desserts; sweet = sugar is the prominent feature (e.g. Sauternes, Port).
- Acidity: tingling, makes mouth water; more acid = more and longer watering. Sugar and acid mask each other (sweet wine acidity seems less obvious than e.g. Chablis), but mouth-watering is always the reliable guide. Alcohol burn can feel like acidity - check mouth-watering.
- Tannin: mostly from grape skins during fermentation; binds to saliva, drying, rough; can taste bitter.
- All wines have acid: even low-acid wines have noticeable acidity; high-acid wines are still less acidic than vinegar (p. 11).

L2-card-74b.head: CH 16: SYRAH/SHIRAZ
L2-card-74b.body:
- Australia: most planted grape. South Eastern Australia (warm inland, high volume). Barossa Valley (warm): some of the world's oldest Shiraz vines, low yields, full body, high ripe tannins, cooked black fruit, black pepper, often vanilla/coconut oak. Hunter Valley: very hot summers (relatively northerly latitude) but cloud cover and sea breezes slow ripening; medium body, fresh black fruit; ages to earth, meat.
- Australia has by far the largest Shiraz plantings outside France. Most often single-varietal; also commonly blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache; some sparkling red Shiraz (p. 92-93).

L2-card-76.head: CH 18: GRENACHE/GARNACHA
L2-card-76.body:
- Black grape, probably evolved in Spain (Garnacha); "Grenache" in France and most of the world. Needs a warm climate. Ripe grapes: high sugar, low acidity. Thin-skinned: low to medium tannin; red fruit (strawberry, red plum, red cherry), sometimes white pepper, liquorice. Finest from controlled yields.
- Much used for short-maceration rosé (dry to medium; drink chilled and young).
- Often blended with Syrah (France) or Tempranillo (Spain), which add colour, acid, tannin. Simple versions unoaked; best often barrel-matured, some prefer old oak over new, to protect Grenache's delicate red fruit. Ages to earth, meat, dried fruit.

L2-card-40.head: CH 4: CLIMATE INFLUENCES
L2-card-40.body:
- Latitude: most important factor; nearer the equator = hotter. Most vineyards 30°-50° N or S.
- Altitude: higher = cooler.
- Seas: moderating; cold currents cool the Cape (South Africa); warm currents warm northern Europe.
- Rivers: warm up and cool down slower than land; warmth in cooler regions, frost protection, longer warm period; reflect sunlight.
- Air: cool sea/mountain air moderates; cold mountain air descends at night to cool warm vineyards.
- Cloud blocks sunlight, slowing ripening (important in some warmer Australian regions). Fog cools at ground level (coastal California and Chile). Mist near autumn rivers is essential for botrytis.
- Mountains: barrier against cloud, rain, cold winds -> sunny summers, dry autumns, extended season.
- Slope and aspect: slopes facing the equator get more heat and light -> riper grapes.
- Soil: water and nutrients; stony surfaces absorb heat and warm the vineyard.

L2-card-16.head: GERMANY: PRÄDIKAT CATEGORIES 4-6 AND RULES
L2-card-16.body:
Six Prädikat categories continued (ascending order of required sugar):
  4. Eiswein (ice wine) - grapes frozen on the vine; NO botrytis; vibrant fresh peach, apricot, mango, pineapple. Weather needed does not occur every year; tiny yields; high prices.
  5. Beerenauslese / BA (selected berry harvest) - botrytis-concentrated bunches or berries; apricot, mango, dried fruit, honey. Always sweet.
  6. Trockenbeerenauslese / TBA (selected dried berry harvest) - individually selected berries 'dried' by botrytis; rare, concentrated; flavours similar to BA but more intense (p. 61).
  Exception to the ascending order: Eiswein and Beerenauslese require the SAME minimum sugar level.
- Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese can be dry; a dry Auslese is higher in alcohol than a dry Spätlese, which is higher than a dry Kabinett.
- BA, TBA, Eiswein: sugars concentrated on the vine; naturally low alcohol and sweet; age for decades.

L2-card-04.head: NOSE DETAIL
L2-card-04.body:
- Swirl, then a short sniff. A quick sniff before swirling can catch delicate aromas.
- Condition: likely faulty if it smells of damp cardboard; honey, caramel or coffee (when not the expected style); or lacks freshness and expected fruit.
- Aroma intensity: immediately apparent = pronounced; faint even after swirling = light; otherwise medium.
- Primary = from the grapes or created during fermentation.
- Secondary = post-fermentation winemaking: oak (vanilla, smoke), malolactic conversion (cream, butter), autolysis in sparkling wines (toasted bread, biscuit).
- Tertiary = ageing. Oxidative (e.g. long period in oak) -> coffee, caramel. Protected from oxygen (e.g. long period in bottle) -> petrol (gasoline), honey, mushroom. In both, fruit becomes less fresh and can take on dried-fruit character.
- Not every wine has primary, secondary and tertiary aromas.

L2-card-69b.head: CH 14: MERLOT
L2-card-69b.body: - Languedoc-Roussillon: single-varietal Merlot at all quality levels, or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Syrah; Pays d'Oc IGP. California: styles from fruity, medium-bodied 'California' to concentrated, full-bodied Napa Valley and Sonoma; blends common but single-varietal Merlot important; pronounced oak (vanilla, coconut, smoke); best often in new barrels, high-volume producers use chips or staves. Chile Central Valley: warm, dry; high yields of fully ripe fruit every year; soft, medium-bodied, high-volume; altitude allows fresher styles. South Africa Stellenbosch: known for complex, age-worthy Bordeaux-variety reds; moderate to warm depending on altitude and sea breezes. Australia: blended with Cabernet, e.g. Margaret River. NZ: most Merlot comes from Hawke's Bay (North Island); moderate, plentiful rainfall; more widely grown there than Cabernet; single-varietal or blended with Cabernet; light to full-bodied.

L2-card-56.head: CH 9: FURMINT AND TOKAJI ASZÚ
L2-card-56.body:
- White grape, mainly Hungary; naturally high acidity, very susceptible to botrytis -> ideal for sweet wines. Most planted grape in Tokaj (north-east Hungary).
- Tokaj also makes dry and medium wines but is most famous for Tokaji Aszú: sweet, from botrytis-affected grapes; Furmint principal, often blended with other local grapes for aroma complexity.
- Always sweet. Puttonyos indicate sweetness: most labelled 5 or 6 Puttonyos; 6 is sweeter than 5.
- Amber colour (significant time ageing in oak). Pronounced nose with primary, secondary and tertiary aromas: fresh and dried apricot, citrus, oak (vanilla, smoke), tertiary (dried fruit, caramel, nuts). Sweet, full body, balanced by high acidity; long, intense finish.
- Among the world's best and most complex sweet wines; usually very good or outstanding; develop for many years in bottle.

L2-card-25.head: STORAGE
L2-card-25.body:
1. Long-term: cool, constant temperature (extremes and big swings damage wine).
2. Away from strong sunshine and bright artificial light (light and heat lose fruit character).
3. Cork-sealed bottles on their side so the cork stays moist (dry cork lets air in -> oxidation). Screwcaps can stand up.

L2-card-55.head: CH 9: SÉMILLON/SEMILLON
L2-card-55.body:
- White grape, mainly moderate and warm climates. Young: simple apple, lemon, grass. Medium to high acid, light to full body depending on ripeness. Can age to dried fruit, nuts, honey.
- Bordeaux: blended with Sauvignon Blanc for dry and sweet wines; Sémillon adds body and ageing potential; very good/outstanding blends often oak-matured, develop for many years.
- Sauternes AOC: sweet white from botrytis-concentrated grapes; Sémillon most important because particularly susceptible to botrytis. Sweet, medium to high alcohol, full body, high acidity; pronounced apricot plus oak (smoke, vanilla). Very good/outstanding; ages for many years to dried fruit, honey, caramel.
- Hunter Valley (Australia): dry, single-varietal, light body, low alcohol. Warm climate, so harvested EARLY (low sugar, high acid); inert vessels, bottled young; neutral at first, then several years -> pronounced honey and nuts.

L2-card-06b.head: PALATE: ALCOHOL, BODY, FLAVOUR, FINISH
L2-card-06b.body:
- Alcohol: high = heavier in the mouth plus a hot, burning sensation (pain receptors), especially after spitting or swallowing; low = can seem watery unless e.g. sugar adds body (p. 12).
- Flavour characteristics: generally the same as the aromas on the nose; note any extra ones that appear as the wine warms in the mouth (p. 12).

L2-card-82.head: CH 22: NEBBIOLO, BARBERA, CORVINA
L2-card-82.body:
- Northern Italy: Alps foothills and river plains; mountains protect from the north; generally moderate.
- Nebbiolo: high acid, high tannin; red cherry, red plum, dried herbs, sometimes rose, violet. Long oak (old or new) to soften tannin; improves with age: mushroom, tobacco, leather. Barolo DOCG (Piemonte, north-west Italy; perhaps Piemonte's most famous wine; only Nebbiolo; horseshoe-shaped valley, steep south-facing slopes; full body, pronounced, high tannin and acid, long-lived). Barbaresco DOCG (smaller, north-east of Barolo; similarly powerful).
- Barbera: high acid, low to medium tannin; red cherry, red plum, sometimes black pepper; many unoaked and fruity, some oak-matured for complexity. Piemonte; Barbera d'Asti DOCG (seen by many as Barbera's highest quality). Drinkable younger than Nebbiolo; shorter ageing potential.

L2-card-45.head: CH 5: WINEMAKING OPTIONS
L2-card-45.body:
- Adjustments: add sugar in cool climates/vintages (more alcohol); add acid in warm climates; neutralise acid in cool climates.
- Fermentation temperature: reds 20-32°C (helps extract colour and tannin); whites 12-22°C (cooler end gives notable fruity aromas); short-maceration rosé at white temperatures.
- Inert vessels (stainless steel, concrete): add no flavour; can be airtight, preventing oxygen changing flavours.
- Why add sugar: low-sugar grapes give low-alcohol wines lacking body. Why add acid: low-acid wines would be unbalanced (p. 45).

L2-card-90.head: CH 24: SPARKLING - CAVA, NEW WORLD, TANK METHOD
L2-card-90.body:
- Tank method (dry): base wine, sugar, yeast in sealed tank; lees removed by filtration; bottled under pressure. No autolytic character; tastes of the base wine; good for aromatic grapes; cheaper, less labour.
- Asti method (sweet): starts from juice not base wine; CO2 escapes at first, then tank sealed; stopped by filtering out yeast -> low alcohol, sweet, sparkling.
- Prosecco DOC: north-east Italy; typically tank method; Glera (pear, melon, blossom); light to medium body; dry or off-dry; white and rosé (rosé mainly Glera with a little Pinot Noir).
- Asti DOCG: Piemonte; Moscato; sweet, fruity, light body; blossom, grape, peach, pear; usually fully sparkling.
- Champagne and Cava don't have to state PDO status on the label.
- Trend: fully or lightly sparkling Moscato made worldwide; typically sweet, low alcohol, Asti method (p. 115).

L2-card-36.head: SPEC GIs: SAUVIGNON BLANC AND PINOT GRIGIO/GRIS
L2-card-36.body:
SAUVIGNON BLANC
- PGI: France Pays d'Oc. PDOs: Loire Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Touraine; Bordeaux Bordeaux, Graves, Pessac-Léognan.
- Other: USA Napa Valley; Chile Central Valley, Casablanca Valley; South Africa Elgin, Constantia; Australia Adelaide Hills, Margaret River; New Zealand Marlborough.
PINOT GRIS/PINOT GRIGIO
- PGI: Italy Veneto. PDOs: France Alsace; Italy Delle Venezie, Friuli-Venezia Giulia.
REGIONAL LABEL TERMS FOR PRINCIPAL GRAPES (p. 11)
- Burgundy: Premier Cru, Grand Cru. Bordeaux: Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur, Cru Bourgeois, Grand Cru Classé. Alsace: Grand Cru.
- Germany: Prädikatswein, Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, BA, TBA, Eiswein; Trocken, Halbtrocken.

L2-card-22.head: SPARKLING AND FORTIFIED LABEL TERMS
L2-card-22.body:
- Traditional Method / Méthode traditionnelle: second fermentation in the bottle (book p. 112).
- Brut: very small amount of sugar added, tastes dry. Demi-Sec: medium sweetness (book p. 113).
- Non-vintage: blend of several vintages (most Champagne). Vintage Champagne: exceptional years only (book p. 113).
- Champagne and Cava do not have to mention PDO status on the label (book p. 115).
- Cap Classique: South African traditional-method sparkling wine (book p. 114).
- Sherry: Pale Cream = sweetened Fino; Medium and Cream = often sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso; PX (Pedro Ximénez) = sweet, from sun-dried PX grapes (book p. 118).
- Port: Ruby, Reserve Ruby, LBV (single vintage, similar to Reserve Ruby), Vintage Port (declared in the best years); Tawny with age indications 10, 20, 30 or 40 years; inexpensive "Tawny Port" is simple, fruity, pale (book p. 118-119).

L2-card-68.head: CH 14: MERLOT
L2-card-68.body:
- Black grape; moderate and warm climates. Single-varietal typically dry, medium acidity, medium tannins.
- Just-ripe: light to medium body, fresh red fruit (strawberry, red plum), herbaceous (green bell pepper). Riper: medium to full body, cooked black fruit (blackberry, black plum) - easy in warm climates or by later harvest in moderate ones.
- Often blended with higher-tannin grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon: Merlot adds red fruit and lowers tannin, making wines ready sooner. Lighter styles need little oak; fuller-bodied styles may gain softness and flavour complexity from oak. Best age to dried fruit and tobacco.

L2-card-23.head: FOOD AND WINE
L2-card-23.body:
Two food components make wine taste "harder" (more drying and bitter, more acidic, less sweet, less fruity): SWEETNESS and UMAMI.
Two make wine taste "softer" (less drying and bitter, less acidic, sweeter, more fruity): SALT and ACID.
Food generally affects wine more than the reverse, and more likely negatively.
- Taste adapts to what you just ate (e.g. orange juice after toothpaste). Chocolate and thick creamy dishes coat the mouth and impair taste (p. 16).

L2-card-19.head: FRANCE: BURGUNDY AND BEAUJOLAIS HIERARCHIES
L2-card-19.body:
Burgundy (Chapter 6, book p. 53), lowest to highest:
  Regional (Bourgogne AOC, the broadest: covers all of Burgundy) -> Village (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin AOC) -> Premier Cru (village name + Premier Cru; may name the vineyard) -> Grand Cru (own appellation; vineyard name + Grand Cru AOC; rarest, most age-worthy).
Beaujolais (Chapter 17, book p. 95):
  Beaujolais AOC (mostly flat, fertile south; high yields; lightest) -> Beaujolais Villages AOC (villages in the north; slopes, warm well-drained soils) -> 10 crus with own appellations (e.g. Fleurie AOC).

L2-card-58.head: CH 10: CHARDONNAY - FRANCE
L2-card-58.body:
- Burgundy: cool Chablis in the north, moderate Côte d'Or, Mâconnais in the south.
- Bourgogne AOC: simple apple, lemon, high acid.
- Chablis AOC (village appellation): cool; dry, light to medium body, high acid, apple, lemon, wet stones. Premier/Grand Cru on south/south-west-facing hillsides: riper, more flavourful. Frost a key concern. With very few exceptions no detectable oak; inert vessels preserve delicacy.
- Chardonnay is Burgundy's main white grape. Bourgogne AOC: grapes from anywhere in Burgundy (p. 68).

L2-card-27.head: GLASSES AND SERVING
L2-card-27.body:
- Best glasses narrow at the rim (concentrates aromas). Red glasses slightly larger than white; sparkling in flutes or tulips.
- Glasses completely clean, polished before use.
- Before serving check: appearance (haze could mean fault), no bits floating, aroma for faults (e.g. wet cardboard, vinegar).
- Keeping opened wine: fridge with cork in; vacuum systems (pump air out); inert gas systems (nitrogen, argon).
- An opened wine slowly becomes stale (loses fresh character) as it reacts with air. Inert gases do not react with the wine; they keep air away from it (p. 20).

L2-card-85.head: CH 23: SANGIOVESE AND MONTEPULCIANO
L2-card-85.body:
- Brunello di Montalcino DOCG: warm, sunny southern Tuscany; powerful, full body, very high tannin and acid; must mature in oak for an extended period before release; very long-lived. Brunello = local name for Sangiovese.
- Montepulciano: deep colour, medium acid, high tannin, black plum, black cherry. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC (east-central Italy); high volumes, mostly simple and fruity; more concentrated ones get short oak.
- Wider context (not from the L2 book): Montepulciano the grape is unrelated to the Tuscan town of Montepulciano, whose wines are Sangiovese-based.

L2-card-42.head: CH 4: WEATHER HAZARDS AND GROWING
L2-card-42.body:
- Irrigation: allowed in most dry regions; water is increasingly scarce and expensive.
- Fungicides, insecticides, herbicides; organic = most chemicals not used, some sprays still allowed.
- Yield: too high -> diluted flavours, lower sugar; too low -> not commercially viable. Max yields set by law in some regions.
- Harvest: earlier = less sugar, more acid, less-ripe flavours; later = more sugar, less acid, riper. Hand or machine: neither is fundamentally better; machines can't work steep slopes.
- Nets and fences keep out birds and animals; fungal diseases and insects are very hard to control and cut quality and quantity; many growers minimise chemicals. Yield = fruit produced per unit of area. Hand or machine harvest normally depends on the style of wine (p. 34-35).

L2-card-44.head: CH 5: WINEMAKING STAGES
L2-card-44.body:
- White: crushing -> pressing -> alcoholic fermentation -> storage or maturation -> packaging. Black grapes pressed very gently can make white wine.
- Sweet: concentrated grape sugars (yeast can't eat it all; e.g. Tokaji Aszú); removing the yeast with fine filters (e.g. White Zinfandel); killing the yeast by fortification to 15-20% abv (e.g. Port); adding sweetness to a dry wine (grape juice, concentrated grape juice, or blending with sweet wine).
- Residual sugar = sugar left after fermentation. Adding sweetness gives precise control; used for red, white and rosé. Fortified wines carry no risk of re-fermenting (p. 44).

L2-card-77.head: CH 18: GRENACHE/GARNACHA
L2-card-77.body:
- Southern Rhône: valley flattens, warm southerly climate; blends with local grapes incl. Syrah. Côtes du Rhône (simple, medium body, red fruit, white pepper) -> Côtes du Rhône Villages -> Châteauneuf-du-Pape (full body, high alcohol; large round stones absorb heat by day and radiate it at night).
- Languedoc-Roussillon: Grenache important for south-of-France reds and rosés; Minervois AOC is one of the most important red AOCs (Grenache with Syrah etc.). Provence (east of Languedoc-Roussillon; Grenache often key in its rosé blends): dry, pale rosé, mostly Côtes de Provence AOC.
- Spain: Rioja DOCa and Navarra DO (body, red fruit; Navarra rosé too); Priorat DOCa in Catalunya (warm, dry; very old vines, tiny yields; most powerful; typically blended with other black grapes; can mature for long periods; dried fruit, caramel with age).

L2-card-54b.head: CH 9: CHENIN BLANC
L2-card-54b.body: - South Africa: some blend Chenin with aromatic varieties such as Viognier for a refreshing, floral style (p. 64).

L2-card-35.head: SPEC GIs: CHARDONNAY AND RIESLING
L2-card-35.body:
CHARDONNAY
- PGI: France Pays d'Oc. PDOs: France Bourgogne/Burgundy, Chablis, Puligny-Montrachet, Meursault, Mâcon, Pouilly-Fuissé.
- Other: USA California, Sonoma, Los Carneros, Napa Valley, Santa Barbara County, Oregon; Chile Central Valley, Casablanca Valley; South Africa Western Cape, Walker Bay; Australia South Eastern Australia, Yarra Valley, Adelaide Hills, Margaret River; New Zealand Marlborough, Hawke's Bay.
RIESLING
- PDOs: France Alsace; Germany Mosel, Rheingau, Pfalz. (No PGI listed.)
- Other: Australia Clare Valley, Eden Valley.

L2-card-21.head: FRANCE: BORDEAUX LABELLING TERMS
L2-card-21.body:
Bordeaux (Chapters 14-15, book p. 82, 87):
  - Regional: Bordeaux AOC; Bordeaux Supérieur AOC (slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing, minimum alcohol). Both typically Merlot-dominated; grapes can come from anywhere in the Bordeaux region.
  - Left Bank: Haut-Médoc AOC, north of Bordeaux city (includes Margaux AOC, Pauillac AOC); Graves AOC, south of the city (includes Pessac-Léognan AOC). Cabernet Sauvignon typically dominant.
  - Right Bank: Pomerol AOC; Saint-Émilion AOC (includes the more prestigious Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC); these two are the most important Right Bank AOCs. Merlot most important.
  - Château: wine made from grapes grown on the producer's own land (not necessarily a grand building).
  - Grand Cru Classé / Cru Classé: wines from classifications ranking the best châteaux in some sub-regions.
  - Cru Bourgeois: Médoc wines NOT classified as Grand Cru Classé can apply to use this term.

L2-card-89.head: CH 24: SPARKLING - CAVA, NEW WORLD, TANK METHOD
L2-card-89.body:
- Cava: Spanish term for traditional-method sparkling from certain regions; vast majority from Catalunya. Mainly local Spanish grapes; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also permitted (add fruit flavour and acidity). Warm climate -> grapes may be picked early to keep acid; base wine light apple and lemon. Shorter on lees than Champagne -> very subtle autolytic character. Big brands dominate; some smaller producers age long on lees.
- South Africa, USA, Australia, NZ: best from coolest regions; often Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; slightly riper fruit than Champagne (extra sunlight and warmth); best are intense, complex, long finish. Cap Classique = South African traditional method (Champagne grapes or e.g. Chenin Blanc).

L2-card-08.head: WSET LEVEL 2 WINE-LEXICON: PRIMARY AROMAS
L2-card-08.body:
PRIMARY AROMAS AND FLAVOURS (the grape and alcoholic fermentation)
- Floral: blossom, rose, violet
- Green fruit: apple, pear, gooseberry, grape
- Citrus fruit: grapefruit, lemon, lime, orange
- Stone fruit: peach, apricot, nectarine
- Tropical fruit: banana, lychee, mango, melon, passion fruit, pineapple
- Red fruit: redcurrant, cranberry, raspberry, strawberry, red cherry, red plum
- Black fruit: blackcurrant, blackberry, blueberry, black cherry, black plum
- Herbaceous: green bell pepper (capsicum), grass, tomato leaf, asparagus
- Herbal: eucalyptus, mint, fennel, dill, dried herbs
- Spice: black/white pepper, liquorice
- Fruit ripeness: unripe fruit, ripe fruit, dried fruit, cooked fruit
- Other: wet stones, candy

L2-card-81.head: CH 21: CORTESE, GARGANEGA, VERDICCHIO, FIANO
L2-card-81.body:
- Cortese: dry, light body, high acid; blossom, apple, pear, lemon. Gavi DOCG (Piemonte, north-west Italy); inert vessels, no oak; most ready on release, not for ageing.
- Garganega: dry, medium body, high acid; apple, pear, lemon, peach. Veneto (north-east); Soave DOC and Soave DOC Classico; inert vessels, no oak. Most Soave drunk young; best Classico gains honey, almonds. Recioto di Soave DOCG = sweet white from grapes dried by appassimento.
- Verdicchio: dry, high acid, medium body; apple, pear, lemon, fennel. Mostly simple, fruity; outstanding can develop honey, nuts. Central Italy, especially Marche (east coast); Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC.
- Fiano: medium acid, medium to full body; peach, melon, mango. Mostly inert vessels; some lees (bread, biscuit) or oak (smoke). Usually drunk young; best develop honey. Southern Italy; Fiano di Avellino DOCG in mountainous Campania.

L2-card-22b.head: SPARKLING AND FORTIFIED LABEL TERMS
L2-card-22b.body: - Many sparkling wines are non-vintage; vintage sparkling usually costs more than the same producer's non-vintage (p. 115).

L2-card-64.head: CH 11: SAUVIGNON BLANC - REGIONS
L2-card-64.body:
- New Zealand Marlborough: cool; more pronounced than Loire; blending sites/ripeness gives grapefruit, peach, passion fruit plus pronounced green bell pepper and asparagus. Some experiment with Loire-like styles, oak or lees.
- Australia: Margaret River (often blended with Semillon; concentrated grass); Adelaide Hills (most planted variety there; altitude; citrus to tropical; some blended with Semillon for fuller, more age-worthy wines). Some Margaret River has oak contact.
- Chile: Casablanca Valley (sea breezes, fog); Central Valley (range of quality).
- South Africa: coastal only. Constantia (south of Cape Town; Southern Ocean breezes; tropical and herbaceous). Elgin (altitude; often cited as coolest; apple, wet stones).
- USA California: mostly too warm; cooler parts of Napa Valley; may be harvested early; sometimes oak (smoke).

L2-card-62.head: CH 11: SAUVIGNON BLANC - THE GRAPE
L2-card-62.body:
- Aromatic white grape; grows best in cool and moderate climates. Usually dry, light to medium body, high acidity.
- Pronounced herbaceous aromas: grass, green bell pepper (capsicum), asparagus.
- By ripeness: green fruit (apple, gooseberry), citrus (grapefruit), wet stones -> stone fruit (peach), tropical (passion fruit). Blending sites of different ripeness adds complexity.
- Usually single-varietal; sometimes blended with Semillon.
- Mostly inert vessels; new oak can overwhelm the herbaceous character. Oak use shown by terms such as "barrel aged".
- Best drunk young; even outstanding examples can lose fresh aromas within a couple of years and develop unattractive vegetal notes.

L2-card-18.head: ITALY
L2-card-18.body:
- Some wines named after region (Barolo DOCG, Barbaresco DOCG, Valpolicella DOC); some after grape + region (Barbera d'Asti DOCG = "Barbera from Asti").
- Classico: grapes from the historic centre of a region; often hilliest part; typically more concentrated.
- Riserva: DOC or DOCG wine aged for at least a set number of months before release.

L2-card-66.head: CH 12: PINOT GRIGIO/PINOT GRIS
L2-card-66.body:
- Italy: mostly simple, unoaked, light; Veneto, labelled delle Venezie DOC or Veneto IGT; inexpensive, high volume, short finish, acceptable to good. Fuller style in Friuli-Venezia Giulia.
- Alsace AOC: later-picked extra-ripe grapes; medium acid; dry to medium; medium to full body, pronounced peach and mango; honey and ginger with age; best from grand cru vineyards.
- Elsewhere: "Pinot Grigio" signals higher-acid, lighter; "Pinot Gris" more body and complexity.
- Riper Pinot Gris styles give exceptional complexity and pair well with strongly flavoured food (p. 78).

L2-card-40b.head: CH 4: CLIMATE INFLUENCES
L2-card-40b.body: - Climate = long-term average temperature, sunlight, rainfall; weather = day-to-day. Climate change: rising temperatures, more variability, more extreme events (p. 31, 33).

L2-card-15.head: GERMANY: PRÄDIKAT CATEGORIES 1-3
L2-card-15.body:
- Prädikatswein: higher minimum sugar than Qualitätswein; grapes from a single winegrowing area. Six Prädikat categories in ascending order of required sugar at harvest:
  1. Kabinett - lightest, most delicate; green apple, lime, blossom.
  2. Spätlese (late harvest) - more concentrated, fuller; riper citrus, some peach.
  3. Auslese (selected harvest) - selected extra-ripe bunches; apricot, mango, dried fruit; can be trocken but most have some sweetness.

L2-card-02.head: WSET LEVEL 2 SYSTEMATIC APPROACH TO TASTING WINE
L2-card-02.body:
APPEARANCE
- Clarity: clear - hazy (faulty?)
- Intensity: pale - medium - deep
- Colour, white: lemon-green - lemon - gold - amber - brown
- Colour, rosé: pink - pink-orange - orange
- Colour, red: purple - ruby - garnet - tawny - brown
NOSE
- Condition: clean - unclean (faulty?)
- Intensity: light - medium - pronounced
- Aroma characteristics: e.g. primary, secondary, tertiary
PALATE
- Sweetness: dry - off-dry - medium - sweet
- Acidity: low - medium - high
- Tannin: low - medium - high
- Alcohol: low - medium - high
- Body: light - medium - full
- Flavour intensity: light - medium - pronounced
- Flavour characteristics: e.g. primary, secondary, tertiary
- Finish: short - medium - long
CONCLUSIONS
- Quality level: faulty - poor - acceptable - good - very good - outstanding

L2 rosé colours: pink - pink-orange - orange (p. 14). (L3 stretch only: the 2016 L3 book says "salmon"; in the L2 exam always say "pink-orange".)

L2-card-43b.head: CH 5: WINEMAKING STAGES
L2-card-43b.body: - Storage: under a year for most wines, little flavour change. Maturation: extended storage; flavours move from primary towards tertiary, tannins integrate; normally in oak, which may add secondary flavours. Glass bottles most popular; also bag-in-box, plastic, cartons (p. 40).

L2-card-57.head: CH 10: CHARDONNAY - THE GRAPE
L2-card-57.body:
- White grape; outstanding wines in cool, moderate AND warm climates. Climate strongly affects fruit, alcohol, body, acidity.
- Cool: high acid, light to medium body; green fruit (apple, pear), citrus (lemon), wet stones.
- Moderate: medium to high acid, medium to full body; lemon, stone fruit (peach), sometimes melon.
- Warm: full body, medium acid; stone fruit (peach), tropical (pineapple, banana).
- Acidification common in warm-climate Chardonnay, to balance alcohol and body.
- Optional secondary flavours: MLF (butter, cream; softens harsh acid); lees (body, bread, biscuit); oak fermentation/maturation (body, smoke, vanilla, coconut); chips/staves cheaper. Only wines with enough intensity benefit. Unoaked styles labelled "unoaked" or "unwooded".
- Very good/outstanding age for years: hazelnut, mushroom.
- More likely to show oak than Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc; suffered from heavily oaked 1980s-90s styles; Chablis popular (unoaked, labelled by region) (p. 71).

L2-card-53b.head: CH 8: RIESLING - REGIONS
L2-card-53b.body:
- Australia: Eden Valley and Clare Valley (South Australia); moderate thanks to altitude (unlike warm Barossa nearby); dry, pronounced lime, lemon, sometimes petrol.
- Alsace: dry autumns extend ripening (p. 62).
- Riesling today: because of its German roots it is often wrongly linked with low-quality sweetened Liebfraumilch; premium wines drive its sales worldwide (p. 62).

L2-card-43.head: CH 5: WINEMAKING STAGES
L2-card-43.body:
- Alcoholic fermentation: yeast eat sugar -> alcohol + CO2 (escapes) + heat. Usually stops when sugar is used up -> dry. Most dry wines 11.5-16% abv.
- Red: crushing -> alcoholic fermentation (with skins) -> draining -> pressing -> storage or maturation -> packaging. Heat helps extraction but the cap of skins floats; mix it by punching down (plunger) or pumping over (liquid sprayed over the cap).
- Rosé: short maceration (red-wine start, drained after a few hours, then white-wine temperatures) or blending red and white (not permitted in many parts of Europe). Rosés rarely stored or matured in oak.
- Alcoholic fermentation is the one thing common to all wines; final alcohol depends on how much sugar is in the grapes. Crushing splits skins to release some juice; pressing squeezes out as much liquid as possible, before or after fermentation (p. 40).

L2-card-60.head: CH 10: CHARDONNAY - OUTSIDE FRANCE
L2-card-60.body:
- California Central Valley: very warm, dry, irrigated, high yields; labelled California; peach, pineapple, medium acid and body; oak from chips/staves.
- Coastal California: Los Carneros (San Pablo Bay fog), Sonoma (Pacific breezes); Napa gets warmer going north: full body, pronounced tropical fruit, new oak vanilla and spice. Santa Barbara County: breezes funnelled inland by lateral valleys.
- Oregon: generally moderate; high acidity, lemon to melon; small production.
- California Central Valley is cut off from sea influence by mountains; coastal influences slow ripening and keep acidity. Santa Barbara ranges from Côte de Beaune-like to tropical-fruit styles (p. 69).

L2-card-93.head: CH 25: PORT
L2-card-93.body:
- Sweet fortified wine from grapes grown in the Upper Douro, Portugal; blend of local black grapes; most Ports blend several vintages.
- Process: rapid extraction of colour and tannin (traditionally foot treading, now also machines) -> fermentation interrupted by adding grape spirit (kills yeast) -> sweet, high alcohol -> matured, then blended and bottled.
- Ruby styles: deep colour, fruity; aged in large vessels (old-oak casks or steel) then bottled ready to drink; cooked black cherry, blackberry.

L2-card-61.head: CH 10: CHARDONNAY - OUTSIDE FRANCE
L2-card-61.body:
- Australia: South Eastern Australia (high volume, warm irrigated inland, sometimes blended with Semillon). Adelaide Hills (altitude) and Yarra Valley (ocean currents): ripe peach, sometimes pineapple, banana, medium-high acid, balanced oak. Margaret River (warm, sea breezes; smaller volume, consistently high quality): medium-full body, peach, pineapple.
- New Zealand: Marlborough (cool, sunny, sea breezes, plentiful rain; ripe lemon, peach, melon, high acid, subtle oak); Hawke's Bay (North Island east coast; moderate; Chardonnay its most planted white; full body, high acid, pronounced stone fruit).
- Chile: Casablanca Valley (sea breezes, fog; lemon, peach); Central Valley (all quality levels; altitude moderates the best).
- South Africa: hot inland Western Cape (high-volume brands, sometimes blended with Chenin); Walker Bay (cool, sea breezes; high acid, peach, pineapple, oak).

L2-card-38.head: SPEC GIs: REGIONALLY IMPORTANT WHITE GRAPES, SPARKLING, FORTIFIED
L2-card-38.body:
- Chenin Blanc: France Vouvray; South Africa Western Cape.
- Sémillon/Semillon: France Sauternes; Australia Hunter Valley, Barossa Valley.
- Viognier: Northern Rhône Condrieu. Gewurztraminer: Alsace, Alsace Grand Cru.
- Verdicchio: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi. Cortese: Gavi. Garganega: Soave, Recioto di Soave (term: Classico). Fiano: Fiano di Avellino.
- Albariño: Rías Baixas. Furmint: Hungary Tokaj (term: Aszú).
- Sparkling grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier, Moscato (Muscat), Glera. Regions: Champagne, Asti, Prosecco, Cava; South Africa, USA, Australia, New Zealand.
- Sparkling terms: Brut, Demi-Sec, Vintage/Non-Vintage, Traditional Method, Cap Classique.
- Sherry terms: Fino, Amontillado, Oloroso, Pale Cream, Medium, Cream, PX. Port terms: Ruby, Reserve Ruby, LBV, Vintage, Tawny.

L2-card-16b.head: GERMANY: PRÄDIKAT CATEGORIES 4-6 AND RULES
L2-card-16b.body: - Sweetness terms: Trocken = dry; Halbtrocken = some sweetness.

L2-card-46.head: CH 5: WINEMAKING OPTIONS
L2-card-46.body:
- Oak: adds flavour directly (toasting -> sweet spice, charred wood; new oak -> vanilla, coconut, charred wood, spice; little flavour left after two or three uses) and lets oxygen in (caramel, dried fruit, nuts; softens red tannins). Changes faster in small barrels (more wine-to-wood contact); large vessels rarely used to give oak flavour.
- Oak alternatives: staves or chips in inert vessels, much cheaper.
- Malolactic conversion: bacteria, after fermentation; lowers acidity, can give buttery flavours. Nearly always in reds (buttery flavours not really noticeable); a choice in whites (often blocked for aromatic grapes like Riesling).
- Lees: dead yeast; stirring adds body and flavours (biscuit, bread).
- Blending: consistency (brands), complexity. Clarification: e.g. filtration; some skip it, so wine may be less than perfectly clear.

L2-card-67.head: CH 13: GEWURZTRAMINER, VIOGNIER, ALBARIÑO
L2-card-67.body:
- Gewurztraminer: aromatic; cool to moderate climates; dry to sweet. High sugar -> high alcohol when dry; full body, LOW to medium acidity; pronounced rose, peach, apricot, lychee. Typically unoaked. Best develop honey, dried fruit. Most famous in Alsace AOC (grand crus alongside Riesling and Pinot Gris).
- Viognier: aromatic; mainly moderate climates. Dry, low to medium acid, high alcohol, medium to full body; pronounced blossom, peach, apricot. Mostly inert vessels, but unusually for an aromatic grape some are oaked. Condrieu AOC (Northern Rhône) is dedicated to single-varietal Viognier; light vanilla from oak common.
- Albariño: Rías Baixas DO, north-west Spain; Atlantic influence -> moderate, notably cooler, wetter, cloudier than many of Spain's other wine regions. Dry, high acid, medium body; lemon, grapefruit, peach, apricot. Usually unoaked, drunk young; sometimes a little lees contact to add body and complexity.

L2-card-20.head: FRANCE: RHÔNE AND ALSACE HIERARCHIES
L2-card-20.body:
Rhône (Chapter 18, book p. 98):
  Côtes du Rhône AOC (covers the whole valley, but almost all from the south) -> Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC -> crus (North: Crozes-Hermitage, Hermitage, Côte Rôtie, Condrieu; South: Châteauneuf-du-Pape).
  One hierarchy across North and South Rhône, similar to Beaujolais (p. 98).
Alsace (Chapter 12, book p. 78):
  Alsace AOC (usually labelled by grape; from 2021 vintage sweetness must be shown on a standardised scale) -> Alsace Grand Cru AOCs (specific vineyards, mostly on the steep foothills of the Vosges, facing east/south-east; more sunlight, so typically riper in flavour and fuller in body; typical grand cru grapes Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewurztraminer). Vendanges tardives (VT) = late harvest, typically medium to sweet, from Pinot Gris, Riesling or Gewurztraminer; both Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru can be VT.

L2-card-83.head: CH 22: NEBBIOLO, BARBERA, CORVINA
L2-card-83.body:
- Corvina: low to medium tannin, high acid, red cherry, red plum. Valpolicella (Veneto): Valpolicella DOC (light, fruity, simple; rarely new oak; drink young); Valpolicella DOC Classico (hillier heartland; more body, complexity).
- Appassimento: pick and dry grapes indoors to concentrate sugar, acid, tannin, flavour. Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG: dry to off-dry, full body, high alcohol (~15%), high tannin, red cherry plus prune, raisin, fig; can age. Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG: sweet red; yeast can't ferment all the sugar.
- Corvina: most important Valpolicella grape; typically dominates the blend, other local grapes permitted (p. 106).

L2-card-17.head: SPAIN: AGEING TERMS
L2-card-17.body:
In order of ageing: Joven -> Crianza -> Reserva -> Gran Reserva.
- Joven: young, fruity, no minimum ageing, typically released the year after vintage; primary fruit. Called Genérico in Rioja.
- Crianza: aged in oak before release; gains secondary oak flavours (vanilla, smoke, coconut).
- Reserva: extended ageing in oak and bottle; softer tannins, some cooked/dried fruit; primary, secondary and tertiary (dried fruit, mushrooms).
- Gran Reserva: highest minimum ageing; most pronounced secondary and tertiary aromas.
- These are national Spanish terms, not specific to Rioja DOCa. Some regions are stricter; many producers exceed minimums.
- Only wines with enough flavour intensity, acidity and (reds) tannin suit long ageing.
- Long-ageing an inferior wine makes it taste stale and lacking in fruit; a producer may choose not to make a Gran Reserva in some years (p. 100).

L2-card-06.head: PALATE: ALCOHOL, BODY, FLAVOUR, FINISH
L2-card-06.body:
- Alcohol bands, still wines: low = below 11% abv; medium = 11-13.9% abv; high = 14% abv and above.
- Alcohol bands, fortified wines: low = 15-16.4% abv; medium = 16.5-18.4% abv; high = 18.5% abv and above.
- Body: overall impression of how the wine feels (touch, not taste). Created by sugar, acidity, tannin and alcohol together. Alcohol is the main factor for most wines. Sugar adds body; high acidity makes it feel lighter; high ripe tannin feels fuller; low unripe tannin seems harsher, thinner, lighter.
- Flavour intensity: usually matches aroma intensity, but warming in the mouth can make spice more prominent; floral can be less prominent.
- Finish: count only the persistence of DESIRABLE sensations. If pleasant flavours vanish and a structural component (e.g. acid) lingers = short. Flavours last as long as or beyond structural components = long.

L2-card-87.head: CH 24: SPARKLING - PRINCIPLES AND TRADITIONAL METHOD
L2-card-87.body: - Traditional method (e.g. Champagne, Cava): bottle sealed with crown cap -> second fermentation in bottle -> lees (must be removed or the wine is hazy) -> yeast autolysis (biscuit, bread; longer on lees = more intense) -> riddling (bottle moved slowly from horizontal to inverted; traditionally by hand, now mostly automated by gyropalette, a machine moving hundreds of bottles at once) -> disgorgement (neck frozen, ice plug of lees ejected) -> dosage (liqueur d'expédition: wine plus usually sugar; sets final sweetness) -> resealed with thick cork and wire cage.

L2-card-91.head: CH 25: SHERRY
L2-card-91.body:
- Fortified wine from around Jerez de la Frontera, southern Spain. Almost all start as a simple dry base wine from Palomino (white). Fortified after fermentation, then aged in the solera: old-oak casks of different ages, continually blended -> consistent, complex style.
- Fino: biological ageing under flor (thick layer of yeast that protects from oxygen). Fortified to about 15%. Pale lemon; apple, almond, pronounced bread dough from flor. Loses freshness fast after bottling; drink early, serve chilled.
- Fortification was traditionally used to protect wine from spoilage. All Port is sweet (fortification interrupts fermentation); most Sherry is dry, but some is sweetened later (p. 116).
- Three key dry Sherry styles (Fino, Oloroso, Amontillado) differ mainly through ageing period and conditions in the solera (p. 116).

L2-card-03.head: APPEARANCE DETAIL
L2-card-03.body:
- Clarity: most wines are clear. Hazy = unusually high suspended particles; may indicate a fault (identify on nose/palate) or that the wine was not clarified before packaging.
- Intensity: glass at 45 degrees, look from core to rim. Whites always look colourless right at the rim. White with broad watery rim = pale; pigment almost to rim = deep. Red lightly pigmented rim to core = pale (stem easy to see through upright glass); intensely pigmented to rim = deep (stem impossible to see).
- Whites: lemon most common; noticeable green = lemon-green; hint of orange/brown = gold; very noticeable browning = amber or brown.
- Reds: ruby most common; noticeable blue/purple = purple; orange/brown but still more red than brown = garnet; more brown than red = tawny; no redness left = brown.
- Rosé: pure pink = pink; pink with hint of orange = pink-orange; orange dominant = orange (very rare).

L2-card-92.head: CH 25: SHERRY
L2-card-92.body:
- Oloroso: no flor; fortified to about 17% (flor can't survive) -> oxidative ageing. Turns brown; raisin, prune, walnut, caramel.
- Amontillado: under flor for a time, then refortified to about 17% (kills flor) -> oxidative ageing. Deeper than Fino; bread dough plus walnut, caramel.
- Sweetened: Pale Cream = sweetened Fino; Medium and Cream = often sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso.
- PX (Pedro Ximénez): white PX grapes sun-dried; fortified, aged oxidatively; deep brown, sweet, fig, prune, raisin, liquorice, molasses. Often the sweetener in Cream Sherry.
- Dry Sherries can be sweetened, but must then carry a different or supplementary label term (p. 118).
